      ENVIRONMENT


      Why data centers pose an outsized threat to
      Eastern Oregon’s air quality

                By April Ehrlich (OPB)
                July 22, 2026 6 a.m. Updated: July 23, 2026 12:50 p.m.



      Under an unstable grid, diesel pollution could threaten communities with
      large clusters of data centers.

                                                                                                                                      00:00 / 05:01

                                                                             Experience this story in an audio version created by OPB journalists



              STREAMING NOW
              HIGHLIGHTS

https://www.opb.org/article/2026/07/22/data-center-eastern-oregon-air-quality-umatilla-basin/                                                                1/25
9/24/26, 1:29 PM                                     Why data centers pose an outsized threat to Eastern Oregon’s air quality - OPB

                   Data centers use train car-sized diesel generators for backup power during blackouts.

                   The Pacific Northwest’s unstable grid is at risk of longer, more frequent blackouts,
                   making some areas more vulnerable to harmful diesel exhaust from large data centers.

                   An hour-long, region-wide power outage in the Lower Umatilla Basin — where there are 14
                   large data centers — could generate as much pollution as 38,000 semi-trucks driving for
                   an hour.

                   Air pollution is a risk that some local officials say is worth bearing, as their small towns
                   see growing economies for the first time in decades.

https://www.opb.org/article/2026/07/22/data-center-eastern-oregon-air-quality-umatilla-basin/                                         2/25
9/24/26, 1:29 PM                                     Why data centers pose an outsized threat to Eastern Oregon’s air quality - OPB


   A cow on Josh Walton's property walks in front of a data center in Umatilla, Ore., in April 2026. The Waltons' home was once
   surrounded by cornfields and farms. Now, a large swath of their property looks out onto an Amazon data center. Many of the
   data centers across Oregon rely on diesel generators to provide backup power —which, if used, could release massive
   amounts of diesel pollution into nearby communities.
   Saskia Hatvany / OPB




      When the Waltons built their lemon-colored ranch home outside Umatilla in northeast
      Oregon, they were drawn to the area’s rolling hills.

      “All of our neighbors were farmers,” Josh Walton said on a sunny afternoon this spring.
      “So, all this used to be a cornfield.”

      The landscape has changed a lot in the last 15 years. Instead of overlooking crop fields
      and the Columbia River in the distance, the Waltons’ backyard view is now the towering
      white walls of a data center operated by Amazon.

      This complex of four boxy buildings is roughly the size of nine Walmart Supercenters. At
      night, its stadium-level lighting shines into the Waltons’ bedroom windows, making sleep
      difficult for Walton, his wife and their two teenage sons. Most summer days, the data
      center’s cooling fans drone like low-flying passenger jets.

      “Except it’s constant and doesn’t fade away,” Walton said.

      The family could face another intrusion from their super-sized neighbors: diesel
      pollution.




              STREAMING NOW



https://www.opb.org/article/2026/07/22/data-center-eastern-oregon-air-quality-umatilla-basin/                                         3/25
9/24/26, 1:29 PM                                     Why data centers pose an outsized threat to Eastern Oregon’s air quality - OPB




   Mason Walton, 14, does chores at his family's home in Umatilla, Ore., in April 2026.
   Saskia Hatvany / OPB




      Across the country, Amazon, Google and other tech companies have stocked up on
      diesel generators to keep their data centers humming during power outages. Like diesel-
      powered buses, these generators chug out black exhaust full of air pollutants that can
      cause cancer, asthma and heart disease.

      At a time when the risk of major blackouts is growing, that could add massive air
      pollution to Oregon and the Northwest. Yet Oregon air regulators haven’t modeled the
      potential risk from Oregon’s growing data center market, and policymakers haven’t
      asked them to.

      While the precise risk to the public is unknown, it could be enormous.

      Related: How we reported the story about emissions from data center generators


      To measure    the potential harm, OPB used pollution permits to calculate emissions
          STREAMING NOW

      based on a possible blackout scenario and then checked those estimates with regulators
https://www.opb.org/article/2026/07/22/data-center-eastern-oregon-air-quality-umatilla-basin/                                         4/25
9/24/26, 1:29 PM                                     Why data centers pose an outsized threat to Eastern Oregon’s air quality - OPB

      and industry analysts for accuracy.

      OPB focused on the Lower Umatilla Basin because that is where Oregon’s largest, most
      power-hungry data centers are clustered. All are owned by Amazon. We found the
      company has amassed enough diesel generators to cloud the nearby cluster of small,
      rural towns along the Columbia River with smog. For each hour that an outage lasts,
      they would emit about twice as much pollution as all of the exhaust from cars and trucks
      on Oregon’s roads over the same hour.


       Data centers in the Lower Umatilla Basin
       Amazon owns 14 data center complexes in the Lower Umatilla Basin in Northeast Oregon.




                                                                                                                      © OpenStreetMap contributors



       Source: Oregon Department of Environmental Quality pollution permits
              STREAMING NOW



https://www.opb.org/article/2026/07/22/data-center-eastern-oregon-air-quality-umatilla-basin/                                                        5/25
9/24/26, 1:29 PM                                     Why data centers pose an outsized threat to Eastern Oregon’s air quality - OPB

      If a region-wide blackout forced Amazon to run its generators for an hour, it would
      create more diesel pollution than 38,000 semi-trucks driving through town over the
      same period.

      That extreme level of pollution would only occur during a blackout stretching across a
      30-mile-wide region, which Amazon says is highly unlikely.

      OPB’s “calculation relies on a scenario in which the entire Umatilla Electric Cooperative
      territory loses power simultaneously,” Amazon spokesperson Adrienne Talbot said in an
      email. “This has never happened in the utility’s 89 years of operation and would be an
      extraordinarily rare event anywhere in the United States.”

      But widescale power outages are not unheard of. In 2021, an ice storm knocked out
      power for more than 300,000 Oregonians in the Willamette Valley. Some were without
      power for hours. Others were in the dark for days. And two weeks after Talbot said
      Umatilla Electric had never experienced a large-scale outage, a neighboring utility — the
      Oregon Trail Electric Cooperative — did experience a territory-wide power failure
      across about 4 million acres for about an hour. The outage was triggered by a wildfire.

      Amazon has cleaner alternatives it could use for backup power. It could replace its
      current generators with new ones that have pollution controls. A company spokesperson
      said its new data centers will all have generators with pollution controls. But that won’t
      help the Watsons if the power goes out today.

      If electrical grids become increasingly unstable, the chances of a region-wide outage
      increase. The Western Electricity Coordinating Council projects that by 2034, Pacific
      Northwest residents could see more than 700 hours of potential power failures annually.

      “It’s certainly something that could happen,” said Jay Dietrich, research director of
      sustainability at Uptime Institute, a data center consultancy. “You have to be aware that
      it could happen and you have to plan for it.”

      Other parts of the country are already experiencing grid strain during extreme weather
      events, like storms and heatwaves, prompting data center operators to run their
      generators nonstop for multiple days, even when their local permits expressly prohibit
      that.

      Five times this year, the Trump administration used a 1930s law originally written for
      wartime to allow data centers to tap their diesel generators and stop drawing power from
      the electrical grid. These emergency orders enabled data center operators to run their
           STREAMING NOW
      generators for multiple days, forgoing local pollution regulations.
https://www.opb.org/article/2026/07/22/data-center-eastern-oregon-air-quality-umatilla-basin/                                         6/25
9/24/26, 1:29 PM                                     Why data centers pose an outsized threat to Eastern Oregon’s air quality - OPB

      Potential air pollution is one of the tradeoffs Oregon’s city and county leaders are
      making as they welcome data centers. These high-tech projects have brought public
      revenue and jobs. For the first time in years, these small farming towns are seeing their
      budgets and populations grow.




   An Amazon data center is seen from Oregon Trail Boulevard, in a neighborhood of Boardman, Ore., in April 2026.
   Saskia Hatvany / OPB




      Some officials in these communities say they trust the state to keep the air clean.

      “We’re not air quality experts and don’t have to really deal with it in any other
      circumstance,” said Hermiston Assistant City Manager Mark Morgan.

      Morgan said they rely on the state’s environmental regulators to ensure air quality is
      safe. Those regulators say they’re concerned about air pollution from data centers’
      generators, but they’re limited in what they can do.

      This year, Gov. Tina Kotek convened a data center advisory committee to address issues
          STREAMING NOW
      from data center growth and recommend policy solutions. Air quality was added to the
https://www.opb.org/article/2026/07/22/data-center-eastern-oregon-air-quality-umatilla-basin/                                         7/25
9/24/26, 1:29 PM                                     Why data centers pose an outsized threat to Eastern Oregon’s air quality - OPB

      committee’s to-discuss list on Friday, after OPB contacted the governor’s office for this
      story. It will be on the agenda on July 31.

      In a statement to OPB, the governor’s office said the committee will “certainly be
      considering diesel generator impacts in their deliberations.”

      “The Governor believes there should be intentional statewide planning on data centers
      to ensure Oregon is effectively mitigating adverse impacts while maintaining strong
      economic growth and responsible stewardship of local tax revenues,” Press Secretary
      Luke Harkins said. “That’s why she convened the Data Center Advisory Committee and
      looks forward to their recommendations later this year.”



      Backbone of the internet




   A data center in Umatilla, Ore., in April 2026. Data centers often have power stations built adjacent to them to meet their
   extensive energy needs.
   Saskia Hatvany / OPB



              STREAMING NOW



https://www.opb.org/article/2026/07/22/data-center-eastern-oregon-air-quality-umatilla-basin/                                         8/25
9/24/26, 1:29 PM                                     Why data centers pose an outsized threat to Eastern Oregon’s air quality - OPB

      Just about everything on the internet runs through data centers. Their computer servers
      host streaming movies, video games and business documents, and they train and host
      artificial intelligence models.

      Processing all of that data requires an exorbitant amount of electricity. The data center
      behind the Waltons’ home is part of a class of massive data centers called “hyperscale.” It
      uses more than 100 megawatts of electricity at once, enough to power about 80,000
      homes.

      That energy must be constant. Over the last three years, one in five data center operators
      experienced a loss of more than $1 million — some of them from power outages,
      according to an analysis by Uptime Institute.

      “If my airline reservation system goes down, I can’t sell new tickets. I can’t put people
      on planes, right?” Dietrich of Uptime Institute said. “There are different ways those
      losses materialize, but they can easily get into the millions of dollars if it’s a really critical
      system.”

      Meta, Apple and other tech companies own dozens of data centers across Oregon,
      varying in size and power load.

      It’s difficult to gauge the scale of data centers in Oregon compared to other states, partly
      because multiple buildings might be clumped together as a single campus sharing the
      same address. The Pew Research Center lists Oregon among the ten states with the
      highest number of operating data centers, though its figures don’t consider their size or
      capacity.

      Hillsboro, outside Portland, is home to about 40 individual data center buildings, but
      many of those have a small footprint. Prineville in Central Oregon has about 13
      hyperscale buildings.

      The Lower Umatilla Basin — which includes the towns of Boardman, Hermiston and
      Umatilla — has about 45 hyperscale buildings. Those structures dwarf most other data
      centers in the state.



      Where life is sweet

              STREAMING NOW



https://www.opb.org/article/2026/07/22/data-center-eastern-oregon-air-quality-umatilla-basin/                                         9/25
9/24/26, 1:29 PM                                     Why data centers pose an outsized threat to Eastern Oregon’s air quality - OPB




   A Google Earth image, southwest of Hermiston, shows crop circles between Morrow and Umatilla counties.
   Maps data: Google Earth/Airbus




      Satellite images of Umatilla and Morrow counties show a grid of circular crop fields, like
      a collection of verdant coins, where farmers grow potatoes, onions and watermelons.
      Hermiston is “where life is sweet,” as the city motto goes, with murals of watermelons
      painted around town.

      Farmers across the country have been struggling in recent decades due to rising costs
      and market consolidation. Some Oregon farmers have sold or leased their land to make
      ends meet. Over time, some of those verdant coins have given way to solar panel farms,
      wind turbines and hyperscale data centers.

      The Lower Umatilla Basin is now a web of industrial power lines.

      Those power lines are partly what has brought data centers to this area. Data center
      operators want affordable power, lots of water, vast stretches of land — and friendly
      local governments.




              STREAMING NOW



https://www.opb.org/article/2026/07/22/data-center-eastern-oregon-air-quality-umatilla-basin/                                         10/25
9/24/26, 1:29 PM                                     Why data centers pose an outsized threat to Eastern Oregon’s air quality - OPB

        First image: A hyperscale data center owned by Amazon can be seen on the outskirts of Hermiston, Ore., in April
        2026. Second image: A train makes its way through Umatilla County in April 2026.
        All images: Saskia Hatvany / OPB.




      In Hermiston, Amazon has hired hundreds of employees and contractors to staff its two
      hyperscale data center campuses. Hermiston has given the company 15-year tax breaks
      for each campus. So instead of property taxes, Amazon pays annual fees amounting to
      about $9.5 million. Amazon also pays annual franchise fees, which businesses pay when
      their power lines or cables encroach on public rights-of-way. Hermiston’s revenues from
      franchise fees have more than tripled since Amazon came to town, from $1 million in
      2024 to a projected $3.4 million by the end of this year.

      Amazon also contributed about $25 million toward water and other utility
      infrastructure, so the city can deliver water to Amazon. Another $9 million helped the
      city build an RV park for Amazon’s construction workers.

      That money has funded new city buildings, services
      and infrastructure. City staff say these financial
      exchanges are not quid-pro-quo deals, and that each
      agreement between the city and Amazon stands on its
      own.

      “This is paid for by Amazon,” said Morgan,
      Hermiston’s assistant city manager, waving toward
      the city’s newly constructed City Hall.

      The building’s front overhang is made of green glass
      circles, a tribute to the region’s farming industry.

      An analysis by city staff estimated about 4,200 people
      in the Lower Umatilla Basin work at data centers —
      about 9% of this region’s total population. These
      locations hire technicians to install, maintain and
                                                                                                      Assistant City Manager Mark Morgan
      repair hardware and network infrastructure, as well as

      contractors for security, building maintenance and                                              Hall in April 2026 in Hermiston, Ore.
      construction.
                                                                                                      Saskia Hatvany / OPB

      Between these jobs and the public fees Amazon pays,
      Morgan   said,
          STREAMING   the benefits of becoming a data center
                    NOW

      hub have outweighed the costs.
https://www.opb.org/article/2026/07/22/data-center-eastern-oregon-air-quality-umatilla-basin/                                                    11/25
9/24/26, 1:29 PM                                     Why data centers pose an outsized threat to Eastern Oregon’s air quality - OPB

      “We’re just comfortable in the discussions we’ve had that they can operate safely,”
      Morgan said.



      ‘The cumulative impact … is going to be incredibly
      high’




   Generators and their exhaust pipes are visible outside of an Amazon data center in Umatilla, Ore., in April 2026.
   Saskia Hatvany / OPB




                                              THANKS TO OUR SPONSOR:                            Become a Sponsor




      When a power outage strikes, large data centers first switch to their battery backups.
      Those run out of juice in about 10 minutes, according to Uptime Institute. Operators
      then fire up dozens — sometimes hundreds — of train car-sized diesel generators to
      keep the power flowing.
              STREAMING NOW



https://www.opb.org/article/2026/07/22/data-center-eastern-oregon-air-quality-umatilla-basin/                                         12/25
9/24/26, 1:29 PM                                     Why data centers pose an outsized threat to Eastern Oregon’s air quality - OPB

      Diesel exhaust is part gas, part soot. It’s what creates smog around freeways and traffic-
      heavy cities like Los Angeles. Its most harmful pollutants include nitrogen oxides, or
      NOx, and particulate matter. The World Health Organization has classified both as
      carcinogens.

      Oregonians might already be familiar with the term particulate matter, or PM 2.5, from
      wildfire smoke. Similar to smoke, tiny particles from diesel exhaust can lodge in people’s
      lungs and enter their bloodstream, elevating their risk of heart attacks and lung disease.
      Severe health effects can occur within a day of exposure.

      Hospitals, grocery stores and large corporate buildings commonly rely on diesel
      generators for backup power. They’re sturdy, reliable and relatively cheap. But those
      buildings use a small fraction of the electricity of hyperscale data centers, so they only
      need a few diesel generators to power their essential services.

      At OHSU, Oregon’s only public academic hospital system, much smaller generators can
      cumulatively generate 18 megawatts of electricity.

      The backup diesel generators at Amazon’s 14 data centers in the Lower Umatilla Basin
      are collectively rated for about 3,700 megawatts of power. That’s over 200 times more
      than OHSU’s backups.

      Last year, data centers in Oregon had about 6,000 megawatts of backup electrical
      generating capacity — double the average power usage of all the homes in the state.

      An Amazon spokesperson declined an on-the-record interview with OPB, but in
      background conversations, staff said the company is investing in alternative energy
      sources — including nuclear, solar and wind — to help ease local grid strain.

      In a statement, Kerry Person, Amazon’s vice president of global operations and data
      center delivery, said the company’s generators aren’t currently high polluters.




              STREAMING NOW



https://www.opb.org/article/2026/07/22/data-center-eastern-oregon-air-quality-umatilla-basin/                                         13/25
9/24/26, 1:29 PM                                     Why data centers pose an outsized threat to Eastern Oregon’s air quality - OPB




   Generators and their exhaust pipes are visible outside of an Amazon data center in Umatilla, Ore., in April 2026.
   Saskia Hatvany / OPB




      “Our emergency generators run approximately 12 hours per year, almost entirely for
      brief compliance testing,” Person said. “These systems exist solely to protect continuity
      of essential services during rare power interruptions.”

      When there isn’t an emergency or a blackout, data centers have to maintain their
      generators by running each of them at low capacity for a minimum of 30 minutes a
      month. State environmental regulators say that maintenance doesn’t release a
      concerning amount of pollution.

      What does worry them, though, is what would happen during a summer heatwave or
      wildfire-induced blackout, when multiple data centers might crank up many of their
      generators at once.

      “The cumulative impact, in terms of NOx emissions, in terms of PM 2.5, is going to be
      incredibly high,” DEQ air quality administrator Ali Mirzakhalili said.


              STREAMING NOW



https://www.opb.org/article/2026/07/22/data-center-eastern-oregon-air-quality-umatilla-basin/                                         14/25
9/24/26, 1:29 PM                                     Why data centers pose an outsized threat to Eastern Oregon’s air quality - OPB

       Nitrogen oxides emissions
       If the Umatilla Basin experienced a 24-hour blackout, Amazon's data centers would turn on their
       back-up diesel generators. Those generators release pollutants called nitrogen oxides, or NOx.
       This chart shows how much these data centers could release compared to other major
       polluters.
           Amazon's potential NOx emissions, tons per day
           Oregon's 2022 statewide NOx emissions, tons per day

       On-road vehicles                                 107

       engines

       Marine vessels                                   12

       Construction equipment                           9




      Oregon isn’t tracking data center air pollution risks

      On paper, Oregon limits how much diesel fuel a data center can use in a year — around
      700,000 gallons for each campus. Amazon would likely exceed those limits during an
      extended blackout, Mirzakhalili said.

      “​Is that fuel sufficient to satisfy a long-duration emergency? I don’t think so,”
      Mirzakhalili said. “Should that happen, they’re going to use more fuel than that, and
      we’re not going to stop that.”

      Amazon didn’t directly respond when asked about the possibility it might exceed state
      limits. It stressed the importance of preparing for severe weather or other disruptions to
      the electrical grid.

      Data center operators can reduce their diesel pollution by installing generators that
      include pollution controls, like filters. Those generators can cut emissions by about 90%,
      but they are pricey. Just one pollution-controlled generator could cost upwards of $1
      million, almost twice as much as a standard industrial generator.
              STREAMING NOW



https://www.opb.org/article/2026/07/22/data-center-eastern-oregon-air-quality-umatilla-basin/                                         15/25
9/24/26, 1:29 PM                                     Why data centers pose an outsized threat to Eastern Oregon’s air quality - OPB

      Amazon is the fifth most valuable company in the world, valued at $2.6 trillion, with $78
      billion in profits last year.




        First image: An Amazon data center in Boardman, Ore. Second image: A data center is under construction in
        Umatilla, Ore.
        All images: Saskia Hatvany / OPB.




      Staff with Amazon told OPB that they plan to equip their new data centers entirely with
      pollution-controlled generators going forward. They did not directly respond when
      asked if the company had plans to replace its current generators that don’t include
      filters.

      DEQ now offers fast-tracked air pollution permits to operators who primarily use
      pollution-controlled generators, but no companies have taken up the offer in the last
      year.

      Staff with the agency say they’re worried about data centers releasing concentrated
      plumes of diesel exhaust.

      “It’s a carcinogen,” Mirzakhalili said. “That’s an additional load to the environment that
      we don’t want to see.”

      Other than its fast-tracked permits, Oregon doesn’t have statewide laws or policies
      specifically addressing diesel generators at data centers.

      “It’s a risk we have to understand,” said Shaolei Ren, an engineering professor at
      University of California, Riverside, who has studied the health impacts from data
      centers.
              STREAMING NOW



https://www.opb.org/article/2026/07/22/data-center-eastern-oregon-air-quality-umatilla-basin/                                         16/25
9/24/26, 1:29 PM                                     Why data centers pose an outsized threat to Eastern Oregon’s air quality - OPB

      Ren has advocated for state governments across the country to take a closer look at how
      data center emissions could impact the towns where they are concentrated.

      California, Virginia, Illinois and Washington have strictly limited data centers from using
      generators without pollution controls. Washington regulators are also tracking and
      modeling diesel pollution in regions with large numbers of data centers, so lawmakers
      can eventually develop policies that can protect people from pollution.

      Oregon isn’t tracking how much air pollution data center generators could release
      during a major power outage.



      Pausing environmental laws for data center power

      The risk of air pollution from data centers’ diesel generators goes beyond the Pacific
      Northwest.

      Diesel generator capacity at data centers in the U.S. nearly tripled from 2018 to 2024,
      according to a report by the Better Data Center Project, an organization that advocates
      for cleaner data centers. If they were all turned on at once, diesel generators at data
      centers across the country could provide enough electricity to power roughly 20 million
      American homes.

      That’s a lot of potential power — and a lot of potential exhaust.

      Trump administration policies may be increasing that potential health risk.

      Four researchers who spoke to OPB say they are worried about something called
      “demand response.” That’s when electric utilities request data centers stop pulling from
      the grid when overall electrical demand is high, like during heat waves or snowstorms.
      When that happens, most data centers turn to their backup power supplies.

      Oregon’s air pollution permits don’t allow industrial businesses like data centers to
      participate in demand response. They can only use their generators if they unexpectedly
      lose power.

      But those regulations can be cast aside by the federal government. During a winter
      storm that stretched across southern and northeastern states, three electric utilities
      serving  97 million customers asked the federal government to waive environmental
           STREAMING NOW
      limitations on data centers in order to prevent blackouts for residential customers.
https://www.opb.org/article/2026/07/22/data-center-eastern-oregon-air-quality-umatilla-basin/                                         17/25
9/24/26, 1:29 PM                                     Why data centers pose an outsized threat to Eastern Oregon’s air quality - OPB

      The U.S. Department of Energy granted their requests under a section of the Federal
      Power Act, a 1935 statute originally created to compel utilities to cooperate during war.
      The Trump administration has used these emergency powers to allow coal plants to
      continue operating past their retirement dates — and to allow data centers to use their
      backup diesel generators — regardless of environmental restrictions.

      During this year’s winter storms, the Energy Department’s emergency orders allowed
      data centers in 14 states and the District of Columbia to rely on their backup power
      instead of the electrical grid. The orders specifically excluded other businesses and
      agencies that have backup power — including hospitals, first responders, air traffic
      controllers, and facilities treating water and waste — from using those backups without
      environmental limitations.



      Looking for alternatives

      Not far from Hermiston, Umatilla has also seen financial benefits thanks to data centers.
      It has four in city limits, and three others in the works. All but one belong to Amazon.

      Umatilla has seen a seven-fold increase in its overall
      budget since Amazon started building more data
      centers here around 2018, according to city manager
      David Stockdale. Umatilla is now one of the few
      cities in Oregon with growing revenues. That’s helped
      the city repair roads and old buildings at a time when
      many Oregon communities are facing budget cuts.

      “Prior to data centers arriving here, quite literally                                           Umatilla City Manager David Stockdale
      everything was deferred maintenance,” Stockdale                                                 in his office in April 2026. Stockdale

      said. “Prior to 2018, it had been about 25 years since                                          says the arrival of the industry has
                                                                                                      provided much-needed cash flow to
      there had been even a road construction project in
                                                                                                      the town, and also acknowledges the
      the whole city.”                                                                                environmental costs of data centers.

      Amazon has also brought people. Housing                  Saskia Hatvany / OPB

      construction is at an all-time high, Stockdale said,
      with around 100 new homes entering the market
      every year — significant for a town with around 2,200 households.
              STREAMING NOW



https://www.opb.org/article/2026/07/22/data-center-eastern-oregon-air-quality-umatilla-basin/                                                  18/25
9/24/26, 1:29 PM                                     Why data centers pose an outsized threat to Eastern Oregon’s air quality - OPB

      But Stockdale also acknowledges data centers’ environmental impacts, including the
      potential for increased air pollution. He’s helping spearhead an effort to build a battery
      storage facility on about 1 million square feet, which could help power data centers
      during blackouts. Stockdale said the project is stalled by slow-moving negotiations with
      state land use regulators.

      Umatilla city officials are also hopeful that a business could turn carbon dioxide from
      diesel exhaust into clean, restaurant-quality carbon dioxide for carbonating sodas.
      They’re in the early stages of helping the company find suitable land in city limits.

      Stockdale sees this as an example of the city doing its best to mitigate environmental
      harms that could come from data center pollution.

      “We’ve tried to take a proactive approach rather than reactive,” Stockdale said.

      Even so, Josh Walton — whose home now sits in the shadow of that hyperscale data
      center near Umatilla — feels like he’s on the losing side of an industry that’s rapidly
      transformed his community.

      “It seems like it happened so quickly,” Walton said of the data center behind his home.
      “We were never notified. We never received a letter.”

      Walton’s property is 450 feet from the data center site — far enough that officials
      weren’t required to tell him of the plans.

      To Walton, it feels like his health, and that of his family, depends on the economic whims
      of local politicians.

      “There’s noise pollution, there’s light pollution, there’s increased traffic,” Walton said.
      “We just hope that the people that are in charge are doing the best for the community.”

    Modeling Localized Air Pollution Impacts from
          Data Centers in Northern Virginia

Dr. Damian Pitt,a,b Dr. Ivan Suen,a Ellie Plisko,a
    a.​ Urban and Regional Studies and Planning program, L. Douglas Wilder School of
        Government and Public Affairs, Virginia Commonwealth University
    b.​ Institute for Sustainable Energy and Environment, Virginia Commonwealth University
This project is supported by a research seed grant from the VCU Institute for Sustainable Energy
and Environment (ISEE), and with data provided by the Virginia Dept of Environmental Quality.

1.​ Background

The goal of this research is to examine the extent of current and potential future air pollution
emissions from data centers in Northern Virginia. As has been well documented, Northern Virginia
has the largest concentration of data centers in the world, which is greatly increasing electricity
demand and associated greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and other forms of air pollution from
fossil-fuel power plants. However, this study does not examine the implications of data centers’
electricity consumption. Rather our focus is on the direct criteria air pollution emissions (i.e.,
pollutants such as carbon monoxide and nitrous oxides that directly harm human health) resulting
from the data centers’ use of backup diesel and natural gas generators.

This project addresses the following research questions about the total current criteria emissions
from Northern Virginia data centers, as well as the much larger amount that is allowed under the
data centers’ air pollution permits from the Virginia Department of Environmental Quality (DEQ):
    ●​ What are the total current criteria air pollutant emissions from data centers in Northern
       Virginia, how much have those emissions increased from 2015 - 2023, and what
       percentage do they represent of total criteria air pollution in the region?
    ●​ How does the total criteria air pollution from data centers compare to the amount of air
       pollution emitted by other notable facilities in the region (electric power plants, etc.)?
    ●​ How much additional criteria air pollution would Northern Virginia’s data centers emit, if they
       were to reach the total level of emissions allowed by their DEQ air permits?

Additionally, given that many of Northern Virginia’s data centers are concentrated in certain parts
of the region, our research addresses the following additional questions about the localized air
pollution exposure from data centers in Northern Virginia:


Air Pollution Impacts from Data Centers in Northern Virginia - Final Report​   ​   ​   ​   ​      1
    ●​ What is the total cumulative exposure to criteria air pollution from data centers in individual
       Northern Virginia neighborhoods?
    ●​ What is the potential cumulative exposure to criteria air pollution from data centers in
       Northern Virginia neighborhoods, if they emit the total amounts allowed by their permits?
    ●​ To what degree does the current and potential neighborhood-level air pollution exposure
       from data centers compare to that from other notable facilities in the region?
    ●​ To what degree do the current and potential neighborhood-level air pollution levels in
       Northern Virginia correlate with demographic characteristics such as race, income, etc.?

2. Data Sources and Methodology

[Note: See Appendix A for a more detailed discussion of this report’s methodology]

To answer the first set of research questions, about current air pollution emissions from data
centers, we utilized back-end data provided directly by the Virginia DEQ. Additional contextual
data about air pollution in the region was sourced directly from the National Emissions Inventory
(NEI) website maintained by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA).

To evaluate potential future emissions from data centers, we downloaded all available data center
air pollution permits from the Virginia DEQ website on Issued Air Permits for Data Centers, as of
June, 2025, identified those within our Northern Virginia study area, and built a database of the
key details from those permits including their annual emission limits.

The study area for this project is the four counties in Northern Virginia (Arlington, Fairfax,
Loudoun, Prince William), and the five independent cities contained within those counties
(Alexandria, Fairfax, Falls Church, Manassas, and Manassas Park). This is a more narrowly
defined area than the Virginia DEQ’s “Northern” region, which also includes an outer perimeter of
localities such as Fauquier County, Culpepper, etc. This study area includes 138 of the 170 data
centers with air pollution permits identified on the DEQ website, as of June 2025, of which 106
have actual criteria air pollution emissions data available from DEQ and/or NEI. While no data
centers requiring air pollution permits currently operate in Arlington County or Alexandria, these
localities were included in our study area for the sake of regional comparison.

For the second set of research questions we imported the actual and potential air pollution
emissions data into GIS. Using this software we modeled the diffusion of air pollution emissions
from Northern Virginia’s data centers and other notable facilities, to estimate total emissions
exposure at the Census Block Group level. We then downloaded Census data for these same
block groups, in order to analyze the correlations between data center air pollution emissions
exposure and demographic characteristics such as race, income, and education level.




Air Pollution Impacts from Data Centers in Northern Virginia - Final Report​   ​   ​   ​   ​      2
3. Current Air Pollution Emission Totals from Data Centers in Northern Virginia

Total criteria air pollution emissions from Northern Virginia have increased substantially since
2015, as shown in Figures 1 and 2 below.

Figure 1. CO and NOx Emissions from Northern Virginia Data Centers, 2015-2023




Source: Virginia Department of Environmental Quality (DEQ)

Figure 2. Particulate Matter Emissions from Northern Virginia Data Centers, 2015-2023




Source: Virginia Department of Environmental Quality (DEQ)


Air Pollution Impacts from Data Centers in Northern Virginia - Final Report​   ​   ​   ​   ​   3
As indicated in Figure 1 above, the total reported carbon monoxide (CO) and nitrous oxides (NOx)
emissions from Northern Virginia data centers increased substantially between 2015 and 2023.
Emissions of CO increased 196% over that time, from 42.91 tons in 2015 to 169.29 tons in 2023.
Emissions of NOx increased 111%, from 218.03 to 562.01 tons. These increases are due in part to
the growth of data centers themselves, as the data provided by DEQ included 50 reporting
facilities in 2015, increasing to 92 reporting facilities by 2023. (While our data set includes 106
facilities, some have shut down since 2015, while others have not reported emissions every year).

Analysis of particulate matter (PM) emissions is more complicated, as permitting and reporting
standards have evolved over the years, and there is some overlap in the data between PM, PM
10, and PM 2.5. Nevertheless, Figure 2 demonstrates a clear increase in particulate matter
emissions overall, with PM 2.5 emissions – the most dangerous form of particulate matter, from a
public health perspective – increasing 139% from 2020 to 2023.

The actual current emissions from data centers represent a small percentage of total criteria air
pollution emissions within the Northern Virginia region. For example, as of 2022 the NEI data
shows over 187,000 tons of CO and over 21,000 tons of NOx. Much of these emissions comes
from onroad sources (i.e., vehicles), and other “mobile” or “non-point” sources. “Point sources”
such as power plants, factories, etc. make up less than 5% of Northern Virginia’s CO, SO2, and
VOC emissions, but much higher percentages of NOx (19%) and SO2 (50%) emissions. (See
here for an explanation of how the NEI defines these emissions source categories. This
information is summarized in Table 1 below. [Note that the data provided by DEQ does not include
SO2 and VOC emissions for 2015 - 2022, but does include those for 2023].

Table 1. Emissions from Data Centers Compared to NOVA Region Totals (tons)

Emissions Type                                              CO          NOx    PM 2.5         SO2          VOC

Regional Emissions - All Sources (2022)                  187,427      21,070   9,734          1,170    62,494

Regional Emissions – Point Sources (2022)                  4,432       4,061       368        581          762

Data Center Emissions (Actual, 2022)                        127         460        12        No Data   No Data

Actual DC Emissions as Pct of All Sources                  0.1%        2.2%    0.1%          No Data   No Data

Actual DC Emissions as Pct of Point Sources                2.9%        11.3%   3.2%          No Data   No Data

Sources: Virginia DEQ, U.S. EPA National Emissions Inventory 2022 v2 Emissions Modeling Platform.

Note that the percentage of total regional emissions coming from data centers will likely be higher
for 2023, once the baseline NEI data for that year becomes available, as the DEQ data shows
significant increases in data center emissions from 2022-2023.




Air Pollution Impacts from Data Centers in Northern Virginia - Final Report​   ​         ​      ​      ​         4
4. Permitted Air Pollution Emission Totals from Data Centers in Northern Virginia

While current air pollution emissions from Northern Virginia data centers is not insignificant, Table
2 shows that the total emissions allowed under the DEQ data center permits are far higher.

Table 2. Permitted Data Center Emissions Compared to NOVA Region Totals (tons per year)

Emissions Type                                                     CO          NOx         PM 2.5      SO2           VOC

Permitted Data Center Emissions (Totals)                          4,105        9,995        351            45        1,102

Actual DC Emissions (2022) as Pct of Permitted                    3.1%         4.6%        3.4%       No Data       No Data

Permitted DC Emissions as Pct of All Sources*                     2.1%         32.7%       3.5%        3.7%          1.7%

Permitted DC Emissions as Pct of Point Sources*                  48.8%         73.5%       49.6%       7.2%         59.1%

Permitted DC Emissions as Increase in All Sources**                2%          45%          3%             4%         2%

Permitted DC Emissions as Increase in Point Sources**             90%          235%         92%            8%        145%

Sources: Virginia DEQ, U.S. EPA National Emissions Inventory 2022 v2 Emissions Modeling Platform.
* These percentages are calculated by adding the additional permitted data center emissions to the total
2022 emissions, then dividing the total permitted data source emissions by those new regional totals
** These percentages are calculated as the difference between the actual 2022 emissions (both point
sources and all sources) and the total emissions once the additional permitted emissions are added

The key takeaways from the data summarized in Table 2 are as follows:
    ●​ The actual data center emissions from 2022 were between 3% - 5% of total permitted data
       center emissions. While not shown in the tables above, the actual data center emissions
       from 2023 are significantly higher (see Figures 1 and 2 on p. 3), and represent between 3%
       (VOC) and 10% (SO2) of total permitted data center emissions.
    ●​ If Northern Virginia data centers were to emit their total allowed pollution, per their DEQ
       permits, this would significantly increase the region’s total point source air pollution, for all
       pollutants other than SO2. Point-source emissions would increase by about 90% for CO
       and VOC, 145% for VOC, and 235% for NOx. Total emissions (including mobile, etc.) would
       only increase by less than 5% for most pollutants, but would increase 45% for NOx.
    ●​ After adding the additional permitted emissions, data centers would represent about 50 -
       75% of the new point source pollution totals for all pollutants, except SO2 (only 8%). The
       permitted data center emissions would then represent about 2% - 4% of regional totals for
       most air pollution emissions, but would be 33% of total regional NOx.

Following are some observations from the comparisons shown in Table 3:
    ●​ Current data center emissions of CO and NOx are far higher than in most of these other
       facilities, while the data center PM 2.5 and VOC emissions are comparable in many cases.
    ●​ The current data center emissions of CO, NOX, and VOC are substantially higher than the
       corresponding emissions from the Dominion Possum Point Power Station.
    ●​ Permitted data center emissions would be orders of magnitude higher than those from
       these other facilities, particularly for CO, NOx, and VOC.


Air Pollution Impacts from Data Centers in Northern Virginia - Final Report​             ​           ​    ​      ​          6
6. Localized Air Pollution Emissions from Data Centers in Northern Virginia

The next step in this research was to analyze the actual current neighborhood-level exposure to
criteria air pollution from data centers, at the Census block group level. Our study area includes
1,565 block groups, of which 338 are located within one mile of a data center identified in the 2023
data center emissions data set from DEQ. First, we used Geographic Information Systems (GIS)
tools to convert the tons of emissions from each data center facility into diffusion maps, which
illustrating how each facility’s emissions would spread into nearby neighborhoods, including the
combined effects where multiple data centers are clustered near each other (See figures B-1A,
B-2A, etc., in the Appendix). From these diffusion maps we were able to derive block-group-level
estimates of the emissions concentrations from these data centers, as can be seen in Figures 3 -
5 below. (See also full-sized versions of each map in Appendix B).

We used this same process to estimate the block-group-level emissions exposure from the other
notable facilities in the study area, listed above in Table 3. Those facilities are far enough apart
that we could isolate each one’s individual emissions impacts. However, three of the facilities are
in the same industrial complex in the Lorton area of South Fairfax County, requiring us to model
the combined block-group level emissions exposure from those facilities.
Figure 3. Concentrations of Carbon Monoxide (CO) Emissions (tons / sq. mi.) from
Northern Virginia Data Centers (2023) versus Select Other Facilities (2022)




Sources: Virginia DEQ data and U.S. EPA National Emissions Inventory 2022 v2 Emissions Modeling
Platform. Analysis by Virginia Commonwealth University research team.



Air Pollution Impacts from Data Centers in Northern Virginia - Final Report​   ​   ​   ​   ​      7
Comparing the data center (left) and non-data center (right) images in Figure 3 (above) reveals
the following takeaways:
    ●​ Current data center operations result in small amounts of CO exposure across much of
       eastern Loudoun County, western Prince William County, and parts of Fairfax County.
    ●​ In the areas with large clusters of data centers, CO pollution exposure can be equal to, or
       higher, than that from natural gas power plants and compressor stations.
    ●​ Data center CO exposure is much lower than that from some other notable facilities,
       including the Prince William County landfill, the Arlington / Alexandria municipal waste
       combustor, and the cluster of facilities – a municipal waste combustor, a landfill gas plant,
       and a wastewater treatment plant – in southeast Fairfax County.

Figure 4 compares nitrous oxide (NOx) exposure from current data center operations to those of
the other notable facilities in the region.

Figure 4. Concentrations of Nitrous Oxides (NOx) Emissions (tons / sq. mi.) from Northern
Virginia Data Centers (2023) versus Select Other Facilities (2022)




Sources: Virginia DEQ data and U.S. EPA National Emissions Inventory 2022 v2 Emissions Modeling
Platform. Analysis by Virginia Commonwealth University research team.

Key observations from Figure 4 are as follows:
    ●​ Data center pollution exposure, in tons per sq. mi., is generally higher for NOx than for CO.



Air Pollution Impacts from Data Centers in Northern Virginia - Final Report​   ​   ​   ​   ​      8
    ●​ NOx exposure from data centers meets or exceeds that from the natural gas power plants
       and compressor stations in Northern Virginia.
    ●​ Data center NOx emissions exposure also exceeds that from the Prince William Co. landfill,
       but remains much lower than the highest concentrations of NOx from the Alexandria /
       Arlington municipal waste combustor and the cluster of facilities in SE Fairfax County.

Figure 5 provides the same side-by-side comparison for particulate matter (PM 2.5) exposure.

Figure 5. Concentrations of Particulate Matter (PM 2.5) Emissions (tons / sq. mi.) from
Northern Virginia Data Centers (2023) versus Select Other Facilities (2022)




Sources: Virginia DEQ data and U.S. EPA National Emissions Inventory 2022 v2 Emissions Modeling
Platform. Analysis by Virginia Commonwealth University research team.

Comparing the PM 2.5 exposure from data centers (left image) and non-data-center facilities (right
image) in Figure 5 results in similar patterns as the other two pollutants shown in Figures 3 and 4:
    ●​ Exposure to PM 2.5 pollution, in total tons per sq. mi., is generally lower than those from
       the other two pollutants, for both the data centers and other non-data-center facilities.
    ●​ The highest concentrations of PM 2.5 are also found around the wastewater treatment
       plant and municipal waste facilities in southeast Fairfax County.
    ●​ PM 2.5 is the only pollutant for which the highest levels of emissions exposure from data
       center operations is lower than that from the two natural gas power plants in the study area.



Air Pollution Impacts from Data Centers in Northern Virginia - Final Report​   ​   ​   ​   ​      9
Table 4 below identifies the ten Census Block Groups in the study area with the highest current
emissions impacts from data centers, per our analysis of the 2023 DEQ data. These totals range
as high as 9.16 tons / sq. mi. of CO and 20.25 tons / sq. mi. of NOx. Several other block groups
not shown in Table 4 have higher PM 2.5 exposure, up to a maximum of 1.48 tons / sq. mi., but
lower exposure to CO and NOx. (See additional descriptive statistics in the Appendix, Table B-1).

The block groups with the highest NOx and/or CO exposure are all in the Sterling / Ashburn areas
of east Loudoun Co., or in the area of Prince William Co. just west of Manassas (e.g., around the
Broad Run Industrial Park), both of which are home to large clusters of active data centers. These
areas correspond to the two large “hot spots” of data center emissions shown in Figures 3 - 5.

The following are some key observations from the comparison of the highest block-group level air
pollution emissions exposure from data centers (Table 4) and notable non-data-center facilities
(Table 5) in the study area:
    ●​ Some of the Census block groups near the cluster of facilities in southeast Fairfax County
       (wastewater treatment plant, municipal waste combustor, and landfill gas power plant) have
       a much higher cumulative emissions exposure from those facilities – across all three
       pollutants – than anything seen in the areas of clustered data centers.
    ●​ The block groups around the Covanta Alexandria / Arlington municipal waste combustor
       also receive higher emissions exposure from that facility, across all three pollutants, than
       any block group receives from data center emissions.

However, comparing Tables 4 and 5 also reveals instances in which the cumulative data centers
exposure for certain block groups is greater than the emissions exposure from some of these
other notable facilities. For example:
    ●​ The block groups shown in Table 4 experience levels of carbon monoxide exposure from
       data centers that are much higher than the CO emissions from the Dominion - Leesburg or
       Transcontinental Gas natural gas pipeline compressor stations.
    ●​ The peak block-group level NOx emissions from data centers also far exceed the local NOx
       impacts from the Dominion - Leesburg compressor station, and are about equal to those
       from the Transcontinental Gas compressor station. Likewise the local PM 2.5 impacts from
       data centers are at times higher than those from either compressor station.

Perhaps more notably, the combined local emissions exposure from clusters of data centers can
sometimes even exceed the pollution exposure associated with a natural gas power plant:
    ●​ The highest levels of CO exposure from data centers are generally similar to those found in
       the block groups receiving the highest emissions from Possum Point.
    ●​ Some block groups receive much more NOx exposure from data centers, compared to the
       highest block group NOx exposures from Dominion - Possum Point.
    ●​ The highest amount of block-group level PM 2.5 exposure from the Dominion - Possum
       Point power plant (7.04 tons / sq. mi.) far exceeds any PM 2.5 exposure from data centers.
    ●​ The highest levels of local block-group-level CO and NOx impacts from data centers
       exceeds those associated with the Panda Stonewall / Potomac Energy Center natural gas
       power plant, but that gas plant has higher PM 2.5 impacts.

7. Permitted Localized Air Pollution Emissions from Data Centers In Northern Virginia

In this next phase of the research we evaluated the potential localized air pollution emissions from
data centers in Virginia, based on the total allowed emissions of CO, NOx, and PM 2.5 from their
use of back-up generators, as per the requirements of each data center’s respective air pollution
permits issued by the Virginia Department of Environmental Quality (DEQ).

As noted in Table 3 above, the actual emissions from data centers in 2023 was only about 4 - 7%
of the total permitted emissions for the three pollutants evaluated in this study. However, in
comparing the actual versus permitted emissions of individual data centers, we find that 14 out of
104 facilities emitted 20% or more of their allotted totals in 2023, for at least one of the three
pollutants. In some cases the data centers emitted more than 40% of their total permitted
emissions for a given pollutant. Table 6 shows some examples of data centers for which the tons
of emissions reported in 2023, per the data provided by DEQ, equaled at least 30% of the allowed
tons / year of a given pollutant on the applicable air permit issued by DEQ for that facility.

Given that the data center facility permits allow much higher levels of pollution than the current
totals, and that some facilities are already emitting far more than the average of 4 - 7% of their
allotment, we therefore find it instructive to model the potential pollution exposure from these
facilities, in the event that data center emissions were to reach their maximum allowed levels.

Following the same methodology as used for the actual emissions from data centers and non-data
center facilities, we converted the total permitted emissions levels for each data center in the
study area into diffusion maps, shown in Figures C-1A, C-2A, and C-3A of the Appendix, which
show how the potential criteria air pollution emissions from each data center would spread across
a 1-mile radius. From those diffusion maps we derived the potential emission concentrations for
each block group, in tons / year / sq. mi., thus creating the maps shown in Figures 6 - 8 below.

actual or potential pollution concentrations. In doing so, one can see that the potential emissions
concentrations from Northern Virginia data centers far exceed both the actual emissions
concentrations from current data center operations, and the concentrations associated with any of
the other notable facilities evaluated in this report (landfills, natural gas power plants, etc.)

Comparing these potential block-group-level emissions concentrations in Table 6 to the actual
estimated emissions concentrations in Tables 4 and 5 leads to the following observations:
    ●​ The highest potential data center emission concentrations are roughly 10 - 20 times greater
       than the highest actual data center emissions concentrations, across all three pollutants.
    ●​ The highest potential emissions concentrations from data centers also far exceed, in most
       cases, the highest actual estimated concentrations from the other non-data-center facilities.
    ●​ The potential CO and NOx concentrations shown in Table 6 dwarf the highest estimated
       concentrations from any of the natural gas compressor stations or power plants in the study
       area. The highest potential concentration of CO (125 tons / year / sq. mi.) is about 14 times
       greater than the highest estimated CO concentration (9.2 tons / year / sq. mi.) from the
       Possum Point Power Station. Likewise, the potential 312 tons / year / sq. mi. of NOx is
       nearly 25 times the highest estimated NOx (12.6 tons / year / sq. mi.) from Possum Point.
    ●​ The potential CO and NOx concentrations shown in Table 6 also exceed, to varying
       degrees, the estimated emissions exposure from other facilities such as landfills,
       wastewater treatment plants, and municipal waste combustors, including the estimated
       combined exposure from multiple such facilities in southeast Fairfax County.
    ●​ The potential PM 2.5 concentrations from data centers remains below the estimated
       combined exposure from the facilities in southeast Fairfax County, but significantly exceeds
       the estimated actual concentrations from any of the other non-data-center facilities,
       including the Possum Point and Potomac Energy Center natural gas power plants.

8. Demographics of Data Center Emissions In Northern Virginia

For the final step of this research, we investigated the potential for inequitable environmental
impacts from data center emissions, across various demographic categories. To do this, we
analyzed the correlations between estimated data center emissions exposure and key
socioeconomic indicators such as race, income, and education, among all Census block groups
within the Northern Virginia study area.

The results of these analyses are shown in Tables 8 and 9 below. The values shown in bold
indicate statistically significant correlations between the corresponding demographic
characteristics and estimated concentrations of data center emissions. These statistically
significant correlations can be summarized as follows:
    ●​ In Table 8, the estimated actual concentrations of CO and NOx, as reported in the 2023
       DEQ data, are negatively correlated with Median Household Income and Higher Education
       (percentage of residents with a college degree). Estimated NOx concentrations are also
       negatively correlated with home ownership percentage.
    ●​ In other words, Census block groups with higher estimated (2023) concentrations of CO
       and NOx from data centers tend to have lower household income levels, fewer residents
       with college degrees, and fewer owner-occupied housing units (in the case of NOx) than
       block groups in the study area that experience lower estimated data center emissions.
    ●​ In Table 9, the estimated potential emissions concentrations, from the DEQ data center air
       permits, are negatively correlated across all three pollutants (CO, NOx, and PM 2.5), for
       both median household income and higher education percentage. Estimated potential CO
       and NOx concentrations are also negatively correlated with home ownership percentage.
    ●​ This means that Census block groups with higher concentrations of potential CO, NOx, and
       PM 2.5 emissions tend to have lower household income levels, fewer residents with college
       degrees, and fewer owner-occupied housing units (in the case of CO and NOx) than block
       groups in the study area that experience lower estimated data center emissions.
    ●​ There are no statistically significant correlations between data center emission
       concentrations and non-white population percentage, neither with estimated actual (Table
       8) nor potential (Table 9) data center emissions.
    ●​ Population density is for the most part not correlated with any of the estimated actual or
       potential data center emissions metrics. The only exception is a statistically significant
       negative correlation with estimated actual PM 2.5 emission concentrations (Table 8), which
       would suggest that areas with lower population density tend to have higher estimated
       concentrations of PM 2.5 emissions from data centers.

Appendix A. Detailed Methodology

To answer the first set of research questions, about current air pollution emissions from data
centers, we utilized back-end data provided directly by the Virginia DEQ. Additional contextual
data about air pollution in the region was sourced directly from the National Emissions Inventory
(NEI) website maintained by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA).

To evaluate potential future emissions from data centers, we downloaded all available data center
air pollution permits from the Virginia DEQ website on Issued Air Permits for Data Centers,
identified those within our Northern Virginia study area, and built a database of the key details
from those permits including their annual emission limits.

The study area for this project is the four counties in Northern Virginia (Arlington, Fairfax,
Loudoun, Prince William), and the five independent cities contained within those counties
(Alexandria, Fairfax, Falls Church, Manassas, and Manassas Park). This is a more narrowly
defined area than the Virginia DEQ’s “Northern” region, which also includes an outer perimeter of
localities such as Fauquier County, Culpepper, etc. This study area includes 138 of the 170 data
centers with air pollution permits as identified on the DEQ website, of which 106 have actual
criteria air pollution emissions data available from DEQ and/or NEI. While no data centers
requiring air pollution permits currently operate in Arlington County or Alexandria, they were
included in our study area for the sake of regional comparison.

For the second set of research questions we imported the actual and potential air pollution
emissions data into GIS. Using this software we modeled the diffusion of air pollution emissions
from Northern Virginia’s data centers and other notable facilities, to estimate total emissions
exposure at the Census Block Group level. As shown in the subsequent figures, each pollutant’s
emissions was interpolated to create a continuous surface of emission levels using ArcGIS Pro’s
Diffusion Interpolation with Barriers tool. (See diffusion maps in Figures B-1A, B-2A, etc.). The
resulting surface was then processed to derive the total emission in tons per year (TPY) for each
block group. To adjust for varying geographic areas, block group level TPYs were further divided
by their areas measured in square miles. (See derived emissions in Figures B-1B, B-2B, etc.).

We then downloaded Census data for these same block groups, in order to analyze the
correlations between data center air pollution emissions exposure and demographic
characteristics such as race, income, education level, and home ownership. We obtained this
demographic data from the following 2023 American Community Survey (ACS) 5-Year Estimates
data tables: B02001 (race), B19013 (median household income), B15003 (educational
attainment), and B25003 (housing tenure).

Finally, we used SPSS to compute the descriptive statistics of emissions exposure (Tables B-1
and C-1), as well as the correlation coefficients to examine the strength and direction of
relationships between emissions exposure and demographic characteristics (Tables B-2 and C-2).


Air Pollution Impacts from Data Centers in Northern Virginia - Final Report​   ​   ​   ​   ​   20
