       Ireland                                       >22% of national electricity               Limited grid capacity



     Backup Power and Reliability Strategies
     Operators are building on‑site generation and energy storage to reduce their reliance on
     fragile regional grids. Natural gas generators, fuel cells, and big battery energy storage
     systems (BESS) are some of the go-to options.




https://cc-techgroup.com/blog/how-much-power-does-a-hyperscale-data-center-use/                                                     10/18
9/24/26, 2:35 PM                       How Much Power Does a Hyperscale Data Center Use? In-Depth Analysis - C&C Technology Group

     These technologies help keep things running when the grid can’t deliver. Many companies
     now design “microgrid” setups that combine renewables with backup power.


     Hybrid sites in Texas and Arizona, for instance, use solar with lithium‑ion batteries to stay
     online during peak demand. Some firms experiment with small modular nuclear units or
     geothermal, looking for more stable sources—a trend Orrick’s energy guide covers in detail.


     Highly reliable on-site backup keeps data flowing and can even help balance the wider grid
     during outages or congestion.



     Cooling Systems and Non-IT Energy Use
     Large data centers spend a big chunk of their electricity on things that don’t process data
     directly. Most of it goes to cooling servers, distributing power, and running the building.

     Boosting the efficiency of these systems can make a real dent in overall energy use.


     Cooling Technology Innovations
     Cooling systems keep servers from overheating and make up one of the biggest non-IT
     power draws. In some hyperscale sites, cooling eats up anywhere from 7% to over 30% of
     total electricity, depending on how things are set up (Pew Research Center).

     Modern data centers mix and match cooling methods:

          Air cooling with aisle containment to separate hot and cold air.

          Liquid cooling for high-density AI servers—it just works better.

          Evaporative and adiabatic systems that use water sparingly for efficient heat exchange.


     Some operators let machine learning fine-tune temperatures and fan speeds in real time.
     That helps avoid wasting power.


     Others capture waste heat and send it to nearby buildings or district heating systems. Every
     method aims to lower the Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE) ratio—a key efficiency metric.


https://cc-techgroup.com/blog/how-much-power-does-a-hyperscale-data-center-use/                                                     11/18
9/24/26, 2:35 PM                       How Much Power Does a Hyperscale Data Center Use? In-Depth Analysis - C&C Technology Group

     Other Major Power Consumers in Data Centers
     Non-IT energy use doesn’t stop at cooling. Power distribution units, uninterruptible power
     supplies, and lighting systems also draw a surprising amount of juice.


     In some facilities, these can add up to 10–15% of total energy use (Enconnex’s analysis).

     Facilities also use energy for fire suppression, security equipment, and building
     ventilation. Even little things—humidity controls, battery chargers—add up.


     Newer centers use efficient transformers, LED lighting, and management software to direct
     power only where it’s needed. Staying on top of maintenance and monitoring in real time
     helps keep small inefficiencies from growing into big problems.



     Sustainability Initiatives and Renewable Energy Integration
     Hyperscale data centers burn through a lot of electricity, but operators are pouring
     resources into sustainable operations to shrink their carbon footprint.

     They’re chasing cleaner power sources, transparent environmental reporting, and
     partnerships that push renewable tech forward.


     Shift Toward Clean Power Sources
     Modern data centers lean on renewable energy—solar, wind, hydro, sometimes even
     nuclear—to cut down on fossil fuels. Many pick locations with abundant renewables or
     generate their own on-site to hit sustainability targets.

     The Environmental and Energy Study Institute says that choosing efficient sites and building
     renewables into facility design can really lower grid demand.

     Companies are also putting money into energy storage and distribution to keep things
     steady during peak times. Cloud providers use battery storage and microgrids to balance
     local supply and guarantee uptime.




https://cc-techgroup.com/blog/how-much-power-does-a-hyperscale-data-center-use/                                                     12/18
9/24/26, 2:35 PM                       How Much Power Does a Hyperscale Data Center Use? In-Depth Analysis - C&C Technology Group

     For cooling, some centers take advantage of cold climates or reuse water to keep power
     needs down. Cleaner energy and smarter site design make the whole operation more
     resilient and efficient.


     Hyperscaler Commitments and Industry Collaborations
     Big tech leads the way on sustainability. Amazon Web Services (AWS), for example, plans
     to run on 100% renewable energy worldwide by 2025—five years ahead of schedule
     (TechTarget). Other hyperscalers have made similar promises to hit carbon neutrality or net-
     zero in the next couple decades.

     Collaboration is everywhere. Hyperscalers, utilities, and grid operators are dreaming up new
     energy procurement models together.

     Initiatives like Bring Your Own Power (BYOP) help facilities and utilities design flexible
     energy-sharing strategies, as Data Center Frontier explains.

     When companies work together, they set new efficiency standards and get more
     transparent about power usage effectiveness (PUE). It’s not just talk—these partnerships
     turn sustainability into actual performance gains.


     Role of Government and Research Institutions
     Government and research outfits play a huge role in nudging data centers toward energy
     efficiency. The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) funds studies on national energy trends,
     including work at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory looking at how U.S. data
     centers use and optimize electricity.


     Their research calls out the need for infrastructure that balances performance and
     sustainability. DOE’s assessments, summed up by ScienceDirect, dig into this.

     Regulations now push for renewable integration, energy reporting, and incentives for
     innovation. These policies encourage centers to try advanced cooling, smarter energy
     management, and modular designs.


https://cc-techgroup.com/blog/how-much-power-does-a-hyperscale-data-center-use/                                                     13/18
9/24/26, 2:35 PM                       How Much Power Does a Hyperscale Data Center Use? In-Depth Analysis - C&C Technology Group

     The International Energy Agency (IEA) tracks how AI and hyperscale growth impact
     global electricity demand. By encouraging international teamwork, these agencies help the
     industry grow without blowing past sustainable limits.

      Where will the power come from? As AI workloads explode and U.S. data center
      power demand races toward 134 GW by 2030, the industry faces a fundamental
      constraint: the grid can’t keep up. This deep dive maps the regions, tools, and
      hidden power corridors that will define AI growth over the next decade, and where
      operators must look next to secure their megawatts.

      Melissa Farney Dec. 1, 2025                            19 min read                                                 ADD US ON GOOGLE




      Key Highlights

https://www.datacenterfrontier.com/energy/article/55333263/the-data-center-power-squeeze-mapping-the-real-limits-of-ai-scale-growth            1/9
9/24/26, 2:34 PM                         The Data Center Power Squeeze: Mapping the Real Limits of AI-Scale Growth | Data Center Frontier

              AI workloads are significantly more energy-intensive, with data center
              electricity consumption expected to reach 134 GW by 2030, nearly tripling
              current levels.
              Mapping tools like national capacity maps, hosting capacity maps, and
              real-time congestion dashboards are vital for site selection and risk
              management amid grid constraints.
              Regions such as Pennsylvania, Texas, Atlanta, Ohio, and emerging
              markets like Phoenix and Las Vegas are identified as strategic hubs due to
              their power potential, infrastructure, and untapped resources.
              The industry must innovate in energy sourcing, including utilizing
              underused assets like non-powered dams and retired industrial sites, to
              meet future demand sustainably.
              Overcoming grid bottlenecks requires collaboration between public and
              private sectors, policy innovation, and technological advancements to
              unlock new power sources and expand capacity.

        WHEREAS, the Economic Opportunities Analysis (EOA) is a planning document that is
 incorporated into the Hillsboro Comprehensive Plan (HCP) in its entirety by reference and the existing
 EOA was adopted by Ordinance No. 6249 on November 21, 2017, and was effective January 2, 2018;

 hearing by the Planning Commission on a City-initiated Comprehensive Plan Minor Text Amendment;

 EOA adoption process and the EOA-related Comprehensive Plan Amendment; and

        WHEREAS, on October 12, 2022, the Planning Commission approved Order No. 8374,
 recommending that the City Council amend the HCP to incorporate the 2021 EOA and 2021 EOA
 Technical Appendices, based on the testimony, the evidence in the Record, and the supporting findings;
 and

         WHEREAS, on November 15, 2022, based on the evidence, testimony, and argument in the
 record, the City Council approved Ordinance No. 6420, amending the HCP, Part III, Chapter 14, Section
 23.4 and adopting the 2021 EOA and 2021 EOA Technical Appendices in their entirety; and

        WHEREAS, on July 20, 2023 the Oregon Land Use Board of Appeals (LUBA) remanded the
 City’s decision on two issues, compliance with Hillsboro Community Development Code (CDC)
 Section 12.80.164 (Minor Text Amendment), and the standards in state law for the buildable lands
 inventory; and

 continued the item to May 22, 2024; and

                        GLOSSARY OF TERMS
A listing of key terms used in this EOA report is noted and defined as follows:

   •   Buildable Lands Inventory (BLI) as described in this EOA represents the City of
       Hillsboro’s parcel-by-parcel inventory of the supply of buildable acreage within the City’s
       Urban Growth Boundary (UGB) designated for employment uses amended in March
       2024 based on December 2020 data. Potentially developable acreage comprises the
       sum of undeveloped portions of tax lots not already built, environmentally constrained,
       and/or allocated for rights-of-way.
   •   Covered Employment refers to employees covered by regular unemployment insurance
       typically excluding sole proprietor and gig workers. Data is compiled and made available
       by the Oregon Employment Department (OED) through the Quarterly Census of
       Employment and Wages (QCEW). Published data is available at the state, county and
       metropolitan statistical area (MSA) levels. For this EOA, OED has provided customized
       data runs specific to the City of Hillsboro.
   •   Economic Opportunities Analysis (EOA) is a document required as consistent with
       Oregon land use planning law (OAR 660-009-0015) to “compare the demand for land for
       industrial and other employment uses to the existing supply of such land.”
   •   NAICS is the North American Industry Classification System used by the U.S. Department
       of Commerce to categorize all industrial, commercial and institutional employment.
   •   OAR 660-009 provides the Oregon Administrative Rules as an official compilation of
       rules and regulations having the force of law in Oregon as applied to Division 9
       Economic Development to implement Goal 9 Economy of the State in compliance with
       Oregon Revised Statutes [ORS 197.712(2) (a) to (d)].
   •   Target Industries represent industrial and commercial sectors of the economy that are
       prioritized for business expansion and/or recruitment by state and local jurisdictions as
       well as regional public-private economic development organizations. Targeted sectors
       may include business clusters encompassing disparate industrial or commercial sectors
       important in the local or regional supply chain – whether as vendors or customers.
   •   Urban Growth Boundary (UGB) is a land use planning tool to separate land
       characterized by urban services and development from farms and forest lands protected
       from urban development. Hillsboro’s UGB encompasses land within the current city
       limits and areas as yet not annexed but anticipated for future growth – as part of the
       Metro determined regional UGB for urban portions of the three-county area of
       Washington, Multnomah and Clackamas Counties.
   •   Urban Growth Report (UGR) is a publication of Metro as required by Oregon law to
       periodically evaluate the capacity of the Portland region’s UGB to accommodate a 20-
       year forecast of housing needs and employment growth. The most recent regional
       update is provided by the 2018 UGR.




                     City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis ♦ Page i
                               EOA SUMMARY
This report is intended to provide an updated Economic Opportunities Analysis (EOA) for the
City of Hillsboro – addressing conditions of rapid employment growth in recent years including
changing conditions prior and subsequent to the 2020 COVID pandemic together with an
associated employment land needs analysis. Added detail is provided on the following pages.


                                      EOA Take-Aways
Background
✓ An EOA articulates community priorities for economic development and addresses statewide land
  use planning Goal 9 together with Metro Urban Growth Boundary UGB considerations.
✓ This 2021 EOA updates a prior pre-pandemic EOA last completed in 2017 and adopted in 2018, also
  addressing federal and state initiatives for revitalized tech (notably semiconductor) manufacturing.
Employment Trends & Outlook
✓   Pre-pandemic, Hillsboro had 81,000+ jobs, up by 30% in 11 years, twice the metro-wide % increase.
✓   Manufacturing accounts for 1/3 of all Hillsboro jobs, three times the metro-wide proportion.
✓   As tech center of the state and metro region, Hillsboro firms pay well above average wage rates.
✓   20-year forecast is for 36,910 more jobs (with straight line growth) to 87,800 (exponential growth).
✓   Recommended is a hybrid scenario for 61,895 added jobs based on detailed review of sector-by-
    sector job trends together with prioritization for Hillsboro’s high-tech target industry clusters.
Community Economic Potential
✓   Business and community stakeholder input prior to and through the pandemic augments the data.
✓   Forces of disruptive technology and improved live-work connection accelerated thru the pandemic.
✓   The next economic cycle will redefine pivotal technologies and alter historic live-work boundaries.
✓   Target industry clusters serve to focus economic opportunities for: computers & electronics,
    software & information technology, advanced manufacturing, bioscience & medical devices
Employment Land Needs (Amended in March 2024 with BLI data from December 2020)
✓ Hillsboro has over 6,210 acres of employment land, of which 1,225 acres remain developable.
✓ Growth areas outside the current city limits but in the UGB represent 46% of future job potential.
✓ By 2040, Hillsboro faces a land need for 2,228-5,329 acres (3,481 acres with a hybrid scenario).
✓ Bringing land availability and needs into alignment may require adjustment on multiple fronts.
✓ For example, BLI capacity might expand by up to 12% with more redevelopment on low value land.
Implementation Policies
✓ Adopt a 20-year jobs and land use forecast similar to Scenario C Hybrid Growth together with
  implementing measures for supportive annexation and large site employer campuses.
✓ Target transportation/utility infrastructure and annexation to meet short-term (5-year) land needs.
✓ Adapt target industries to emerging traded sector opportunity and supporting community amenity.
✓ Support workforce readiness for employers and opportunities for under-represented businesses.
✓ Orient state and local incentives to support land readiness and support traded sector investment.
✓ Encourage support for Hillsboro tech as an economic engine benefiting the metro region and state.



                     City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis ♦ Page ii
Employment Trends & Outlook
As the tech center of the Portland metro region, Hillsboro is a major economic contributor to
the metro area and state. Of note is the significance of manufacturing – accounting for nearly
one-third of all Hillsboro employment versus just 11% of the sector’s job-count metro-wide.
This is largely due to the economic performance of Hillsboro’s semiconductor industry.

From 2007-18, employment in Hillsboro increased by nearly 30%, double the approximately
15% increase in regional-wide employment (pre-pandemic). Annual payroll of Hillsboro firms in
2018 averaged $87,635 per job, 46% above the average per job wage of $59,900 metro-wide.

Covered employment (for jobs covered by unemployment insurance) has increased from
62,430 jobs located in Hillsboro as of 2007 to nearly 81,000 in 2018 (pre-pandemic).

As detailed by the Section II Employment Trends and Outlook portion of this EOA, three
scenarios of potential employment growth to 2040 have been prepared (as illustrated above):

   •        Scenario A Straight-Line Growth results in 121,300 in-city jobs by 2040, with 36,910 net
            new jobs added over the 20-year forecast period of 2020-40, a 44% increase.
   •        Scenario B Exponential Growth predicated on compound annual growth rates (CAGRs)
            specific to each employment sector results in a substantially higher forecast of 173,570
            jobs by 2040. An estimated 87,800 net new jobs would be added in the two decades
            from 2020-40 – a virtual doubling of employment over this 20-year forecast horizon.
   •        Scenario C Hybrid Growth results in an estimated 146,975 jobs in Hillsboro by 2040,
            based on assumption of compounding growth for sectors evidencing this trend and/or


                        City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis ♦ Page iii
       associated with cluster industry targets versus lesser rates of growth for other sectors.
       With this scenario, 61,895 net new jobs would be added over 20 years from 2020-40.

Since the Great Recession of 2007-09, Hillsboro has outperformed the U.S. and metro region in
rates of job growth. And during the pandemic and economic downturn unfolding in 2020,
Hillsboro’s semiconductor and manufacturing industries have lost fewer jobs than experienced
across other sectors of the Portland metro economy.

With about 21,400 employees as of early 2021, Intel is the largest private employer in Hillsboro
and the state of Oregon. Hillsboro’s 18 largest firms employ 35,200 – with 12 of the 18 firms
directly connected to semiconductor, high tech research/support and bio-tech sectors. These
top employers provide an economic foundation of good paying/high wage jobs, supporting the
economic vitality of the metro area and state as well as for the immediate Hillsboro community.

After the recession of the 2007-09, Hillsboro’s job counts recovered more quickly and exceeded
pre-recession levels more fully than was the case for the entire U.S. and Portland metro region.
Stronger employment performance was apparent across manufacturing sectors – most notably
for computer/electronics products – together with information services. And during the most
recent pandemic-related downturn of 2020, Hillsboro was less adversely affected than the rest
of the region, due to lesser reliance on hospitality and retail coupled with resilience of its
industrial sectors.

To summarize, Hillsboro’s current and prospective employment mix appears to offer benefits
both of economic resilience and long-term growth potential:

   •   Hillsboro’s business and industry mix demonstrates a path toward economic recovery
       and resilience beyond what has been achievable across the rest of the metro region.
   •   The community’s nurturing of technology industries aligns well with the best
       opportunities for economic growth regionally and nationally – in recent years, through
       the 2020 economic downturn and post-pandemic.

These demonstrated advantages position the community to be an even more significant source
of job stability and renewed growth for the PDX metro region and state of Oregon in the
technology-driven economy of the years just ahead. These opportunities are best realized with
land use planning for added tech-led industrial investment and are supportive of the EOA
recommendation for selection of a Scenario C Hybrid Growth approach.

Community Economic Potential
Discussion of Community Economic Potential draws from the quantitative data analysis
combined with qualitative research consistent with ORS 660-009 guidance. Background
research has included focus group and interview discussions with business and community
stakeholders. Initial conversations were conducted in early 2020 – just prior to the pandemic. A
second round of interviews was conducted in late summer 2020 as firms were in the midst of
adaptation to rapidly changing regulatory and market conditions.


                    City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis ♦ Page iv
This sequential research approach has proven useful to better identify economic opportunities
that remain as before vis-à-vis those that clearly point in new directions. Two themes have
emerged from pre-pandemic conversations with local and regional stakeholders:

   •   Disruptive technology – exemplified by emerging opportunities as for autonomous
       vehicles with less parking need, artificial intelligence (AI), internet of things (IoT), 5G
       telecommunications, exponential growth of data needs, and decarbonization.
   •   Live-work connection – as tech workforce has become more mobile. Employees don’t
       want to get stuck in a location or sector with few options for re-employment. As
       millennials age, there is a shift in live-work preferences, less toward center cities and
       more to full-service communities meeting a greater array of family and job interests.

For stakeholders contacted over the summer of 2020, the post-pandemic world of work and
business has become a different place than in early 2020. However, underlying forces of change
already at work globally and locally remain in place. Existing trends for Hillsboro of disruptive
technology and live-work connection have not changed markedly, but rather have accelerated.

An assessment of Hillsboro’s competitive position has been conducted from the perspective of
strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats (or SWOT) with key results as follows.

  Summary Hillsboro Economic Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities & Threats
                     Strengths                                              Weaknesses

• Market-driven 50-year urbanization                      • Non-market regulation


A clear message from business and community leaders is that this next economic cycle will be
about more than economic recovery or a simple return to the business and economic
development practices of the last decade. In addition to accelerating trends of disruptive
technology and live-work connection, the next decade may well serve to redefine the
technologies viewed as most pivotal globally and to alter current live-work boundaries – further
changing traditional distinctions between employment and residential land uses.

to the extent possible to attract and retain campus-oriented manufacturing and support uses.

review set the stage for resumed quantitative and qualitative analysis of associated
employment land needs over 5-, 20- and 50-year planning horizons.

The remaining 1,225 acres (approximately 20% of the total inventory) comprise Hillsboro’s
currently remaining buildable area for employment use. Adequacy of this net buildable
employment land inventory to meet projected needs over short- and long-term planning
horizons is a major focus of this EOA. The 1,225 net buildable acres result of this refined BLI
methodology is 132 acres (10%) less than the 1,357 acres indicated by the previously prepared
land inventory as noted with the 2021 EOA. However, “strike-price” analysis (as detailed by
Appendix E) of low value already developed parcels indicates that potentially up to 143 acres
could be shifted from the category of “developed” to “remaining buildable” area for
redevelopment – a nearly 12% increase in remaining buildable (i.e., net employment) acreage.
Given the numerous variables that determine whether an individual site will redevelop,
including property owner willingness, the availability of other suitable sites, and
macroeconomic factors, the 143 acres of potentially redevelopable land was not included in the
clearly identified 1,225 acres of remaining buildable area for employment use.

Properties in the City comprise 83% of gross acres – both developed and vacant but only 54% of
Hillsboro’s land for job growth. In effect, realization of Hillsboro’s employment opportunity will
depend on development of net buildable lands both within and outside current city limits but
all in Hillsboro’s current UGB – including sites not yet annexed as with the Jackson East area.

In addition to consideration of overall land availability versus needs, an important component
of a Goal 9 EOA is to evaluate the adequacy of parcel size distribution. Parcels of 50+ acres
comprise only 18% of Hillsboro’s current vacant inventory though current trends indicate
greater demand for large lots ahead. Employment land needs likely will be further affected in
ways not yet fully foreseen by post-pandemic conditions – as for mixed-use development, site
utilization, remote work trends, industrial automation including robotization, and e-commerce.

Key components of employment need – for each of three job growth scenarios – can be
compared with the primary categories of BLI capacity – industrial, commercial and mixed-use

   •    Assuring that there will be adequate economic opportunity not just for the current
        generation but for the next – by planning now for future urban land reserves
   •    Being better prepared if employment growth and land needs prove to be greater than
        expected and planned for within a 20-year Comprehensive Plan time frame

                    City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis ♦ Page ix
Qualitatively, technological change may well have the most profound effects across Hillsboro’s
economic landscape – in 20 years and yet more so over 50 years. How Hillsboro and the metro
region address the gap between land need and supply will affect the question of whether
Hillsboro asserts an even stronger position on the U.S. and global stage – or just holds its own.

This EOA clearly indicates that Hillsboro’s current inventory of employment lands (including
potential growth areas) will not come close to accommodating a continuation of strong local
employment growth over the next 20 years. There is a pronounced shortfall of employment
land with even with a base case Scenario A forecast. The shortfall intensifies with Scenario B or
C outcomes and is especially severe for capacity to serve major large campus employers.

Bringing Hillsboro’s land availability and needs into alignment may require substantial
adjustments on multiple fronts – likely involving revisions to forecast outcomes, BLI
adjustments and/or supportive state/regional land use policy.

Potential options for consideration include any or some combination of actions to:

   •   Reduce the EOA employment forecast to match current BLI capacity
   •   Focus EOA forecast reductions on the most land extensive sectors
   •   Adjust employment to land need conversion factors toward a more urban profile
   •   Increase the planned BLI supply, especially for growth areas around Hillsboro
   •   Pursue Metro region and statewide recognition of Hillsboro’s strategic significance to
       long-term competitiveness and high wage jobs integral to long-term economic vitality

Advantages and disadvantages of these options are further described with the Section V
Implementation Policies portion of this EOA report.

Implementation Policies
Hillsboro implementation policies and measures are closely linked to 2018 Hillsboro
Comprehensive Plan goals for competitive advantage, facilities/utilities/services, land supply,
equity and livability. The more recently adopted Hillsboro 2035 Community Plan focuses on five
vision-based initiatives – all related to economic development:

   •   Initiative 1: Promote Hillsboro’s business-friendly culture and proactive workforce
       development initiatives.
   •   Initiative 2: Encourage and support the growth of emerging industries, small business,
       and the spirit of entrepreneurship.
   •   Initiative 3: Expand shopping, entertainment, and dining destinations.
   •   Initiative 4: Continue efforts to develop a vibrant, mixed-use downtown as a unique
       attraction.
   •   Initiative 5: Implement efforts to ease congestion in and around Hillsboro.

Implementation policies and measures are made consistent with the EOA recommendation for

                   City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis ♦ Page xii
I. HILLSBORO EOA INTRODUCTION
This report provides an updated Economic Opportunities Analysis (EOA) for the City of
Hillsboro. This EOA addresses conditions of rapid employment growth in recent years including
changing conditions prior and immediately subsequent to the 2020 COVID pandemic, together
with an associated land needs analysis.

EOA BACKGROUND & PURPOSES
As with other cities throughout Oregon, an EOA is intended to serve two related purposes:

   •   Clearly articulate community priorities for economic development over a 20+ year
       planning horizon – for jobs, employment land needs, business and associated
       infrastructure development
   •   Address requirements of Oregon Land Use Planning (Goal 9) and Metro regional
       determinations of Urban Growth Boundaries (UGBs), as reviewed every six years

Prior to this updated analysis, an earlier EOA report was completed in 2017 and then adopted
by the City of Hillsboro and subsequently acknowledged by the state in 2018. Work on this
updated EOA was initiated in 2019, then revised to reflect COVID-related experience and post-
pandemic emerging trends. The updated EOA provides both pre- and post-pandemic
information as well as more detailed specification and updating of recommended
implementation measures – ranging from local initiatives to recommendations for added
employment land in Hillsboro as an economic engine for the city, Metro region and state. 1

COMMUNITY ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT OBJECTIVES
In addition to the EOA, there are two primary documents that serve to frame community
economic development objectives for the City of Hillsboro – the 2018 Hillsboro Comprehensive
Plan and the Hillsboro 2035 Community Plan.

Hillsboro Comprehensive Plan
Chapter 11 of the Hillsboro Comprehensive Plan addresses Building Economy & Infrastructure
with the goal statement stating that:

       Hillsboro’s world class economy, advanced technical training, and innovative, business-
       friendly culture attract investments and support businesses of all sizes. The city boasts a
       diverse and sustainable employment base, with jobs accessible to all community
       residents. State of the art infrastructure systems including communications, roads,
       transit, and water supply are in place and continually updated to accommodate the
       city’s growth and evolution. Hillsboro is a vibrant, regional destination for arts,
       recreation, cuisine, and entertainment.



                   City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis ♦ Page 13
The Comprehensive Plan addresses five goals, each of which is supported by more specific and
detailed policy and implementation measures – with the goal statements reading as follows:

   •   Goal 1 – Competitive Advantage: Diversify and expand the economy to give Hillsboro,
       the region, and the state a competitive advantage.
   •   Goal 2 – Facilities, Utilities & Services: Catalyze economic development through high-
       quality public facilities, utilities and services.
   •   Goal 3 – Land Supply: Manage land supply to meet short and long-term economic
       development needs of Hillsboro, the region, and the state.
   •   Goal 4 – Equity: Promote economic development opportunities for individuals and small
       and emerging businesses to ensure equitable access to resources.
   •   Goal 5 – Livability: Develop and sustain a vibrant City to support economic
       development.

Hillsboro 2035 Community Plan
Building on the success of the original award-winning Hillsboro 2020 Vision and Action Plan, in
2020 the City completed an updated Hillsboro 2035 Community Plan as representing “a shared
vision for a sustainable future.” 2 Economy and Infrastructure comprises the first of five focus
areas for 2035 accompanied by a goal statement representing continued high aspiration:

       Hillsboro’s world-class economy, advanced technical training, and innovative, business-
       friendly culture attracts investment and supports businesses of all sizes. State of the art
       infrastructure systems including communications, roads, transit, and water supply are in
       place and continually updated to accommodate the city’s growth and evolution.
       Hillsboro is a vibrant, regional destination for arts, recreation, cuisine, and
       entertainment.

Five supportive initiatives and actions are detailed as part of the updated Community Plan:

   •   Initiative 1: Promote Hillsboro’s business-friendly culture and proactive workforce
       development initiatives.
   •   Initiative 2: Encourage and support the growth of emerging industries, small business,
       and the spirit of entrepreneurship.
   •   Initiative 3: Expand shopping, entertainment, and dining destinations.
   •   Initiative 4: Continue efforts to develop a vibrant, mixed-use downtown as a unique
       attraction.
   •   Initiative 5: Implement efforts to ease congestion in and around Hillsboro.

This updated EOA aims to both reinforce adopted City-wide planning priorities and to identify
potential new initiatives as appropriate to facilitate economic recovery and resilience for
Hillsboro and the metro region going forward.



                   City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis ♦ Page 14
EOA APPROACH & REPORT ORGANIZATION
This EOA has been prepared to address planning requirements of Oregon’s Division 9 LCDC
Economic Development guidance, with particular attention to:

   •   OAR 660-009-0015 for economic opportunities analysis
   •   OAR 660-009-0020 for industrial and other employment development policies
   •   OAR 660-009-0025 designation of lands for industrial and other employment use

EOA Approach
While a primary focus of the analysis is on determination of 20-year employment land needs,
the EOA analysis also addresses the short-term land supply deficiencies associated with 25% of
the long-term need. Also considered is a longer 50-year planning horizon. Added attention is
given to land needs not met within the current urban growth boundary (UGB) as within the
purview of Metro for potential boundary expansion.

Work on this EOA update was initiated in the last half of 2019 just prior to the pandemic and
associated economic downturn of 2020. EOA completion was then suspended through the early
stages of the pandemic with EOA preparation resumed in the autumn of 2020. Much of the
economic data has been maintained as of the time of the initial work, due to specialized data
runs but representative of trends over the most recent economic cycle.

Qualitative data regarding community economic potential is updated to reflect pre- and post-
pandemic conditions. A buildable lands inventory (BLI) based on data from December 2020 was
prepared together with analysis of industrial land demand through the pandemic and recession.

Report Organization
The remainder of this report is organized to cover the following topics:

   •   Employment trends and outlook – focused on Hillsboro in the context of regional to
       national experience prior to the COVID-19 pandemic and with recovery to date
   •   Community economic potential – incorporating stakeholder interview input together
       with analysis of Hillsboro’s changing competitive position and target industry clusters
   •   Employment land needs – reflecting an updated employment buildable lands inventory
       as compared with employment-driven land need and associated site size requirements
       over the next 20 years and as might be realized over a longer-term 50-year plan horizon
   •   Implementation policies – addressing key drivers of economic recovery and resilience
       together with recommended implementation policies and related measures

This EOA report is organized to cover highlights of the full analysis. Standing behind the analysis
is supporting research provided as a separate and more detailed Technical Appendices
document with references as appropriate in this report. This EOA also references statewide and
federal initiatives affecting economic opportunities taken over the summer of 2022.

                    City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis ♦ Page 15
II. EMPLOYMENT TRENDS & OUTLOOK
In cooperation with the Oregon Employment Department (OED), it has been possible to
assemble a consistent employment dataset in recent years for the City of Hillsboro in
comparison to trends experienced for the 7-county Portland metro region. Topics covered are:

   •   Metro Region Employment Trends – focused on experience of the last economic cycle
   •   Hillsboro Employment Trends – for top employers and by employment sector
   •   Shift-Share Analysis – as a means to assess comparative advantage with the metro area
   •   Employment Forecast Scenarios – for straight-line, exponential or hybrid job growth

Trend data evaluated for the City of Hillsboro and the 7-county Portland-Vancouver-Hillsboro
metropolitan statistical area (MSA) for 2007 and 2018 was compiled from the Quarterly Census
of Employment and Wages (QCEW) by the Oregon Employment Department (OED). This data is
for jobs covered by unemployment insurance, excluding some workers as with sole proprietors.

This dataset reflects experience from a peak employment year in advance of the Great
Recession of 2007-09, followed by subsequent change through 2018 in advance of the COVID-
19 pandemic and associated economic downturn of 2020. More detailed technical
documentation for this employment analysis is provided by Appendix A to this EOA report.

METRO REGION EMPLOYMENT TRENDS
Evaluation of employment trends begins with a review of employment change for the full 7-
county Portland-Vancouver-Hillsboro MSA. As depicted by the following graph, as of 2019 there
were an estimated 1.2 million QCEW covered workers employed region-wide, followed by an
approximate 7% decline averaged across the full year of 2020.

Since the Great Recession, metro wide employment increased by 25-26% from the 2010 low
point of 961,000 persons employed, equating to an annual average compound annual growth


                    City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis ♦ Page 16
rate of (CAGR) of 2.6% per year through 2019. When considered from the last employment
peak of 1.03 million in 2007 to the more recent annual 2019 peak of 1.21 million, employment
region-wide has experienced a net increase approaching 18%, equating to a job growth rate
approaching 1.4% per year.

A peak-to-peak analysis offers the logical benefit of calculating job growth over the time period
of what appears to be approaching a full economic cycle. In effect, the ups and downs are
averaged out over this business cycle. Consequently, the years 2007 and 2019 could serve as
primary employment benchmarks for this updated EOA analysis – for Hillsboro as well as for
sustained economic vitality of the greater metro region.

In this case, due to availability of customized OED data runs specific to Hillsboro prepared as of
late 2019 for full-year data then available through 2018, a similar 2007-18 average growth rate
also in the range of 1.3-1.4% per year has been applied for this analysis. This is also consistent
with a somewhat greater fall-off of employment in 2020 than occurred in the prior trough years
of 2008-10.

HILLSBORO EMPLOYMENT TRENDS
This analysis now shifts to consideration of employment trends specific to Hillsboro. Topics
reviewed include consideration of Hillsboro’s top employers, employment trends, employment
by sector and manufacturing focus. As of a 2018 benchmark year, Hillsboro firms accounted for
88,980 jobs.

Hillsboro’s Top Employers
While detailed data reflects experience of the local and regional economy pre-pandemic, it is
useful to begin with a review of more recent job counts associated with Hillsboro’s major
employers as of the first quarter of 2021. As indicated by the listing on the following page, 18
Hillsboro firms account for an estimated 35,180 jobs as of early 2021. These firms range in size
from 400 to over 21,000 employees.

Unlike the rest of the region for which employment had yet to recover to pre-pandemic levels
(as of mid-2021), these 18 firms have experienced a net increase of over 2,000 jobs in a little
over a year from October 2019 to the first quarter of 2021, an increase of 6%. Seven of the 18
companies account for this employment gain, with the other 11 remaining stable or with minor
reductions in job counts.

Twelve of the 18 firms are directly connected to semiconductor, high tech research/support
and bio-tech sectors. The other six include firms in apparel and food manufacture, health care
and financial services.

Accounting for about 40% of Hillsboro employment, these top employers provide an
economic foundation of good paying/high wage jobs, supporting the economic vitality of the
metro area and state as well as for the immediate Hillsboro community.

As has been noted by the City of Hillsboro website, Oregon has the fourth-highest
concentration of computer and electronics companies in the U.S. Intel tops this list but there is
also a clear network of supporting tech infrastructure and with pivotal supply chain linkages.
This extends beyond the list of top employers to include a range of other tech-related firms –
including communications, software, information technology and data centers together with
advanced manufacturing, bioscience and medical device companies.

Taken together, this tech cluster has given Hillsboro and Oregon global recognition as The
Silicon Forest.


                      City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis ♦ Page 18
Employment Trend (2007-18)
This EOA now turns to a broader review of employment activities across all economic sectors,
extending over the period of the last U.S. and regional economic cycle prior to the COVID
pandemic. As noted, the EOA analysis relies on data of the Oregon Employment Department
(OED) compiled for QCEW employees covered by unemployment insurance.

As of 2018, Hillsboro had a covered count of approximately 88,980 employees. Hillsboro has
accounted for an estimated 6.8% of the region’s employment. By comparison, with a
population of 101,920 as of 2018, Hillsboro represented 4.1% of the metro area’s population of
nearly 2.5 million. This illustrates the extent to which the city serves as a regional job magnet.

For the 2007-18 benchmark period, employment in Hillsboro increased by nearly 30%, almost
double the just over 15% increase in regional-wide employment. Annual payroll of Hillsboro
firms averages $87,635 per job, 46% above the average per job wage of $59,900 region-wide.

In effect, these overview statistics indicate that Hillsboro makes disproportionately high
contributions to the region’s economic vitality, evidenced by:

   •   Accounting for 1.66 times the share of the region’s job versus population base.
   •   Experiencing a rate of employment growth over the prior 11 years double that of the
       rest of the region.
   •   Serving as home to firms that pay 46% above the average wage across the metro region.

Employment by Sector
What stands out is the dominant role played by manufacturing in Hillsboro’s economy. With
29,950 jobs, manufacturing accounted for 32% of all employment in Hillsboro as of 2018. By
comparison, manufacturing has represented only 11% of the job count metro-wide.

From 2017-18, manufacturing jobs locally increased by 3,400 (+15%) as compared with
manufacturing job growth of only 1% for the full 7-county metro region. Excluding Hillsboro,
the rest of the metro area experienced a net loss of 1,800 manufacturing jobs pre-pandemic.

Most other sectors of the Hillsboro’s economy also have experienced increasing employment
since the pre-recession peak of 2007. Health care and social assistance experienced an increase
of 4,390 jobs – outpacing the gains even of manufacturing employment in absolute numbers.
Significant employment growth – of more than 1,000 net new jobs each – also was experienced
in the sectors of wholesale trade, information, professional services, administrative services,
accommodation and food services, and other private services.

In percentage terms, the biggest gains are noted for arts, entertainment and recreation – up by
over 150%. One sector – management of companies and enterprises – is noted as having
experienced a net reduction of nearly 1,660 jobs. Other sectors experiencing minor job losses of
about 200 or less apiece are ag/mining/utilities, educational services, and public administration.

wages are above MSA-wide industry-specific averages for printing, chemical, non-metallic,
furniture and miscellaneous manufacturing.

SHIFT-SHARE ANALYSIS
As an added step, it is useful to consider the current and changing competitive relationship
between key clusters of economic activity in Hillsboro relative to the metro region. One way of
presenting this information is by way of what is termed as shift-share analysis. With the graphic
on the next page, the following information is illustrated for each of 16 major employment
sectors:

   •   Location Quotient (LQ) – illustrated on the Y-axis of the graph to depict the
       concentration of a sector in Hillsboro vis-à-vis the metro region. (An LQ above 100%
       indicates above average local job concentration).
   •   LQ Shift (2007-18) – shown on the X-axis as the % change in sectoral LQ from 2007-18.
   •   Relative size of employment (2018) – as depicted by the size of the circles shown for
       each sector.

In terms of total employment, Hillsboro’s most prominent sector is manufacturing at nearly
26,000 jobs – equating to 32% of total employment city-wide. Manufacturing has nearly three
times the job count of health and social services (with nearly 9,000 jobs) as the city’s second
largest source of employment. The other major standouts – in terms of job count – are the
sectors of retail, administrative and hospitality services which each account for between 5,700-
7,200 jobs per sector.

These sectors may be further distinguished by their current and changing LQ as follows:

                  •               Strong and growing – for sectors with above average and increasing industry
                                  concentration relative to the metro region (including manufacturing, information,
                                  administrative and other service sectors).
                  •               Strong but declining – for sectors with above average but declining Hillsboro industry
                                  concentration (currently noted only for public administration).
                  •               Weak & declining – describing sectors that have below average and declining industry
                                  concentration (including retail, management, educational and hospitality services).
                  •               Weak but strengthening – for sectors with below average but improving industrial
                                  concentration (including construction, wholesale trade, transport/warehousing, FIRE (or
                                  financial/insurance/real estate), professional, health/social, and
                                  arts/entertainment/recreation services).

By far and away, manufacturing is the employment sector with the highest local concentration,
comprising 32% of employment in Hillsboro versus 11% metro-wide – for an LQ that is nearly
300% of (or three times) the region-wide manufacturing representation. However, Hillsboro
appears to have plateaued out with its manufacturing LQ – increasing by only about 1% from
2007-18. Strong gains in computer/electronic products have been offset by slow or declining
performance in some other manufacturing sectors (as further considered below).



                                              City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis ♦ Page 24
Looking beyond manufacturing, the other high performer in the strong and growing quadrant
of the shift-share chart is information (with an LQ of over 150% and positive 11-year shift of
nearly 60%). Also noted is the healthy performance of administrative services (with LQ of over
140% and LQ shift of +20%). Other services (largely personal services) lie at 101% of the
regional share but with a noticeable positive 25% shift in regional share over the last decade.

As the only strong but declining sector, public administration (as a portion of governmental
activity) has an LQ that is about 120% of the regional average (as of 2018), but with a 12%
negative LQ shift since 2011.

Of the four weak and declining sectors, three are clearly linked to local consumer or
population-driven services – retail, educational, and hospitality (covering both dining and
lodging). Hillsboro residents and businesses clearly exhibit some tendency to obtain a large
share of these services outside of the immediate community. The fourth weak and declining
sector involves management of companies and enterprises – with an LQ of 20% (lowest of all
employment sectors). Despite Hillsboro’s strong manufacturing base, these functions appear to
have gravitated pre-pandemic more toward Portland’s central business district,

Seven of 16 employment sectors fall into the weak but strengthening quadrant of the shift-
share chart. Three of these sectors have experienced a strong positive LQ shift of 60% or better
since 2007 – wholesale trade, transportation/warehouse and arts/entertainment/recreation.
Two of these sectors are bolstered by proximity to Hillsboro’s manufacturing center while
growth in arts-related activity reflects a maturing, more diverse and more affluent community.
The other four sectors – construction, finance/insurance/real estate (FIRE), professional and
health/social services – are also seeing some positive LQ change but not to the same extent (in
percentage terms).

In terms of the number of jobs, employment in health and social service activities represents
the single largest job gainer of Hillsboro’s 16 employment sectors over the last decade.
However, health care employment has also increased rapidly across the full metro region –
leaving Hillsboro with a 25%+ positive LQ gain (but still 28% below the region-wide average job
share as of 2018).

manufacturing in Hillsboro is dominated by computer and electronic related products.

Other manufacturing sectors are not as readily discerned, by comparison. This is due to the
much lesser employment counts together with less dominant location quotients (relative to the

       manufacturing. These are all relatively small sectors – ranging in size from wood
       products with less than 80 employees to food/textile manufacturing at a combined total
       about 640. The biggest positive shift relative to the rest of the region is noted for
       food/textile manufacturing with a Hillsboro LQ increasing by 250%. Another strong
       positive shift is noted for Hillsboro’s chemical, plastic (and rubber) industry – up by over
       90% relative to the rest of the metro area since 2007.

Shift-Share Implications
To summarize, four overview observations are suggested by this shift-share evaluation:

   •   The economy of Hillsboro functions quite differently from the rest of the region – less
       affected by metro-wide growth factors and more by competitiveness of the city’s key
       computer and related electronic products within much broader domestic and
       international markets.
   •   While there are early signs of economic diversification with complementary producer
       functions taking hold in Hillsboro, it remains unclear as to whether and how these will
       emerge to also exhibit substantial comparative advantage relative to the rest of the
       metro region in the years ahead.
   •   The production side of the local economy has tended to fare better and more
       competitively than the consumer economy which has lagged behind – with the noted
       exception of a potential break-through arts/entertainment/recreation sector. Whether
       and in what fashion consumer-driven retail, hospitality and service functions emerge as
       the community further matures likely depends on marketplace competitiveness
       together with pandemic resilience as well as public planning and policy response.
   •   Looking ahead, Hillsboro’s economic potential likely remains more tethered to global
       technology and market influences together with local supply initiatives than is the case
       for much of the rest of the Portland metro region. Continued success with the path
       taken to date is by no means assured. Taking advantage of this distinct opportunity will
       nonetheless depend on cooperative regional initiatives, recognizing Hillsboro’s role as a
       competitive and dynamic economic engine for growth, both regionally and statewide.

These implications (and caveats) are important as this report now transitions to consider future
economic opportunity – in the context of anticipated continuing employment growth.

EMPLOYMENT FORECAST SCENARIOS
With many communities, there may be multiple scenarios of future economic pathways and
outcomes to consider. The challenge lies in adequately understanding the regional economic
environment in which the community is working, then pulling the right mix of public policy and
private investment levers that will come closest to achieving desired outcomes.

In Hillsboro’s case, potentially viable scenarios appear to be shaped more by forces external
than internal to the metro region or state of Oregon. Consequently, potential forecast


                   City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis ♦ Page 27
alternatives for Hillsboro are driven by extrapolation of documented local trends, then checking
these as appropriate against regional forecasts for a sense of forecast reasonableness.

Boundaries of the External Drivers?
To begin, it is useful to reflect on the experience of the Great Recession of 2007-09 and ensuing
recovery as a potential backdrop for future expectations. Consistent with key drivers of the
Hillsboro economy, this discussion considers recent trends and forecast implications – going
from the macro to micro level across four metrics:

   •   Starting with total employment
   •   Proceeding to manufacturing employment
   •   Then with more exclusive focus on computer/electronics as a proven job driver
   •   And add information as an emerging driver of Hillsboro job growth going forward

With this most likely regional employment scenario, Metro has forecast that total non-

the region-wide job growth for this sector that has proven pivotal to Hillsboro is expected to be
much less robust than for other sectors of the metro region’s economy.

Metro’s long-term outlook for the information sector has been considerably more bullish. This
sector dipped below the rest of the MSA economy through to about 2018 but is projected by
Metro to move toward a more rapid growth trajectory in the years ahead – with internet
related applications even as the traditional publishing side of the information industry slows or
fades.

Hillsboro Forecast Scenarios Defined
Recognizing that Hillsboro’s economy has been driven in large part by computer/electronics
traded sector activity which is dependent largely on market forces external to the Portland
MSA, two initial scenarios considered with this EOA have been to project the sector-by-sector
growth rates of the recent 2007-18 economic cycle forward over the 2020-40 EOA time frame.

A third hybrid scenario was then added to better reflect Hillsboro’s competitive advantage and
priority given to clearly defined target industry sectors. These alternative forecast scenarios
have then been compared with job growth projected for the region as a first test to assess
reasonableness of Hillsboro forecast scenarios.

The three sectoral forecast scenarios considered with this EOA are described as follows:


                      City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis ♦ Page 29
   •   Scenario A – Straight-Line (Linear) Growth forecasts employment change assuming that
       the recent employment trend is extrapolated forward in straight-line or linear fashion –
       with the same number of jobs per year added through 2040 as occurred (on average)
       from 2007-18. This equates to over 1,830 jobs added (on average) in Hillsboro each year
       to 2040. If calculated at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR), the CAGR rate
       averages about 1.8% per year from 2020-40.
   •   Scenario B – Exponential (Non-Linear) Growth forecasts employment change assuming
       that growth occurs at a compound average growth rate (CAGR), with the compounding
       factor meaning that the number of jobs added in one year is greater than the jobs
       added the previous year. From 2007-18, Hillsboro’s employment increased at a CAGR
       averaging about 2.4% per year.
       Going forward, the rate of employment increase is forecast to increase by 3.6% per year
       from 2020-40 (or 3.5% per year from 2018-40). A higher overall job growth rate in the
       years ahead occurs as the effect of already large and rapidly growing industry sectors
       outweighs the effects of smaller and/or slow growth/declining sectors.
   •   Scenario C – Hybrid Growth was added as a third in-between forecast scenario based on
       review of Scenarios A/B and consideration of Hillsboro target industry and associated
       sectors (or industry clusters). 4 The net effect of these applications is for an overall
       employment growth rate (CAGR) averaging 2.8% per year from 2020-40 (or a CAGR of
       2.7% from 2018-40).
       Sectors of construction, manufacturing, transportation/warehousing, information, real
       estate and professional services are forecast for growth at continued exponential CAGRs
       as experienced over the last economic cycle. Finance/insurance, health care/social
       assistance, accommodation and food services, and other services are expected to
       experience results at a mid-point between the CAGR and linear extrapolation models.
       Wholesale, retail, administrative and arts/entertainment/recreation sectors are forecast
       for linearly trended growth consistent with historically observed rates calculated on a
       straight-line basis. And employment sectors related to management, educational
       services and public administration which experienced net job loss in recent years are
       forecast to experience no further job loss going forward.

All three scenarios are reported in terms of QCEW covered employment – but also adjusted to
provide for a meaningful apples-to-apples comparison with the Metro UGR prepared regional
non-agricultural employment forecast.

The 2020 pandemic, economic downturn and subsequent recovery may well alter longer-term
job growth patterns going forward. However, in spite of uncertainty as to changing trajectories,
these forecast scenarios assume an eventual return to trends as experienced with the last
economic cycle. For Hillsboro, the most significant question is whether job growth resumes at
an even year-to-year growth increment or accelerates as with the effects of compounding
interest in an investment portfolio.

   Results of the three alternative forecast scenarios considered are summarized as follows:

   •   Scenario A Straight-Line Growth results in 121,300 in-city jobs by 2040, with 36,910 net
       new jobs added over the 20-year forecast period of 2020-40, a 44% increase.
   •   Scenario B Exponential Growth predicated on compound annual growth rates (CAGRs)
       applied across all employment sectors results in a substantially higher forecast of
       173,570 jobs by 2040. An estimated 87,800 net new jobs would be added in the two
       decades from 2020-40 – a virtual doubling of employment over this 20-year forecast
       horizon.

       associated with cluster industry targets versus lesser rates of growth for other sectors.

As noted, job growth is not expected to increase on a smooth path as illustrated for these three
scenarios. Rather, year to year variations can be expected in response to economic cycles or
external events as the COVID-19 pandemic demonstrated in 2020. In effect, net job losses as
experienced in 2020 also will need to be made up within subsequent years to achieve the
scenario projections indicated.

Outcomes for each of the three scenarios considered with this EOA are summarized as follows.



                    City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis ♦ Page 32
Scenario A Straight-Line Growth. With the lowest growth overall of the three scenarios,
health care and social assistance would add an estimated 7,980 jobs over 20 years (the most of
any sector) – followed by manufacturing at 6,200 added jobs. Job growth is more modest for
other sectors with small potential reductions noted for sectors of management, educational
services and public administration (assuming the continuation of recent trends).

Considered in terms of region-wide employment, Hillsboro would increase from just under 7%
of the region’s employment currently to about 8.5% in 2040. Manufacturing would increase
from 20-21% to just under 28% of the sector’s MSA count, information from 10-11% to 15%,
and health care/social assistance from 5-6% to nearly 8% of that sector’s regional job count.

Scenario B Exponential Job Growth. As with Scenario A, health care and social services
would add the most jobs, followed by wholesale trade and manufacturing. From 2007-18,
Hillsboro health care employment nearly doubled. Assuming continued growth at a 6.3% CAGR,
health care and social assistance alone could add 24,370 jobs over 20 years – with a total count
nearly 34,500 jobs and even exceeding manufacturing’s total job count by 2040. 5

Wholesale trade has experienced 6.7% per year job growth since 2007 and at this continued
rate could see a net gain of as many as 9,650 jobs in the next 20 years. The related sector of
transportation/warehousing could add another 5,290 jobs – reflecting the creation of a second
regional distribution hub on the westside to support continued area-wide manufacturing and
health care growth.

Manufacturing would add an estimated 7,770 jobs – for about 25% more new jobs than with
Scenario A.6 Strong growth is likely predicated on availability of large campus sites for major
employers. Job growth in the range of 5-7,000 jobs per sector might also be experienced for the
transportation/warehousing, information, professional services, administrative,
arts/education/recreation, and other services sectors.

With Scenario B, Hillsboro would increase from about 7% currently to 12% of metro-wide most
likely employment by 2040. Within 20 years, Hillsboro could account for 30% of the
arts/entertainment/recreation, 29% of the manufacturing, 25% of the information, 22% of the
wholesale trade, 16% of the transportation/warehousing, and 15% of the health care/social
assistance jobs metro-wide.

Scenario C Hybrid Job Growth. This hybrid or targeted job growth scenario would be led
by health care with an added 16,175 jobs followed by manufacturing at an added 7,770 jobs.
Strong job growth (in the range of 5-6,000 added jobs each) would be experienced by the
information, professional services and transportation/warehouse sectors.

With Scenario C, Hillsboro would increase from about 7% (as of 2018) to more than 10% of
metro-wide employment by 2040. Hillsboro would account for similar shares of the region’s
employment in manufacturing, information, and transportation/warehouse sectors as with
Scenario B. Hillsboro would increase from 5-6% to about 11-12% of the region’s employment in
health care and social services.

                   City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis ♦ Page 33
Comparison With National & Regional Expectations
As an added step in the employment outlook and planning process, it is useful to set Hillsboro’s
prospective jobs scenarios in the context of nation-wide employment trends and forecasts – as
well as in conjunction with the metro-wide experience of the COVID pandemic, associated
recession and subsequent recovery. What follows represents a synopsis of more detailed
review and analysis provided by Appendix A to this EOA.

National Employment Trend & Forecast. The employment forecast associated with
Metro’s current 2018 Urban Growth Report (UGR) is driven by national assumptions and
resulting employment forecasting conducted by IHS Global Insight – all of which predate the
events of 2020. Based on pre-pandemic trends, IHS previously forecast that manufacturing
together with associated sectors of wholesale trade and transportation/warehousing w ould
continue to decline as a share of U.S. employment through 2040.

These expectations all run counter to Hillsboro’s employment experience and now to clear signs
of a resurgence in industrial activity through the pandemic and with increased emphasis on
industrial re-shoring to the U.S. Also forecast by IHS is little change in information as a share of
all U.S. employment, though this sector now appears to have increasing potential for Hillsboro.

IHS also has forecast that health and social services together with administrative and also
arts/entertainment/recreation services will represent growing shares of U.S. employment. This
is a trend that appears to be reflected in Hillsboro’s experience and future growth projections.

Overall, Hillsboro appears well positioned to support and reinforce the most recent national
shift back to strengthened industrial activity including freight-intensive transportation and
distribution functions while at the same time capturing other national growth sectors, for
example, with health-related services including bio-tech applications. In addition, with changing
national priorities, there appear to be emerging opportunities for clean-tech industries
addressing climate change (as with energy storage, transportation electrification, and
manufacturing of energy generation equipment).

Metro-Wide 2020-21 Employment Experience. Observations noted with the national
perspective are reinforced by review of metro region experience through the 2020 pandemic
and recession together with ensuing partial recovery up through year-end 2021. While the
nation. state and metro area all experienced similar proportionate job loss early in the
pandemic, the subsequent bounce-back nationally has been stronger than for the state or
metro area. Hillsboro-specific data for 2020 indicates that employment dropped by only 2.8% in
versus a 6.8% drop metro-wide from 2019-20.

As of December 2021, the metro region had 3.3% fewer jobs than in February 2020 versus U.S.
under-performance of 2.1%. On average up through year-end 2021, Portland metro cumulative
job loss has averaged 1.7% points above the nation-wide average job loss. This equates to net
metro-wide loss of about 21,200 jobs more than would be the case if the bounce-back
experience parallel that of the nation.


                    City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis ♦ Page 34
Regardless, Hillsboro has consistently maintained one of the lowest unemployment rates in the
region, for example at 2.5% (as of May 2022). Much of this can be attributed to the
complimentary key industries Hillsboro chooses to foster and grow; computer and electronics
(semiconductor), information technology, advanced manufacturing, and bioscience/medical
devices. Hillsboro supports these existing industries and has aimed to continually improve the
business climate at the local, regional, and state levels to help business succeed.

Hillsboro has a smaller share of employment in sectors that were most affected by business
and employment restrictions during the pandemic – notably hospitality and retail. These
sectors represent continued vulnerability ahead to the extent that pandemic-related conditions
prove resurgent over time. Professional services represent the only commercial sector for
employment that rebounded to pre-pandemic levels starting March 2021 with subsequent
added new hires to year-end 2021 – followed by retail and finance/insurance/real estate (FIRE)
sectors also returning to more employment than experienced pre-pandemic.

Industrial uses held up considerably better through 2020 to year-end 2021. Pre-recession,
industrial sectors have accounted for 29% of PDX metro and 46% of Hillsboro employment.
Industrial uses accounted for 14% of all metro area jobs lost in April 2020, but returned to
exceed pre-pandemic job counts by the autumn of 2021. By comparison, commercial uses have
accounted for all of the remaining metro-wide job loss as of year-end 2021.

Transportation/warehousing activities proved to be a star performer through the pandemic
and recession – with more job growth than any other commercial or industrial sector. This
sector benefits from the renewed attention to supply chain management across multiple
industries and coupled with the Amazon effect of dramatically increased shipments to
residences including newly created home offices.

With the exception of construction (since rebounded), other industrial sectors maintained
relatively stable employment through the pandemic with minimal net job loss. Metro area
manufacturing employment (as of May 2022) has exceeded pre-pandemic levels – especially
with regard to employment in computer and electronic manufacturing (including
semiconductors). In 2020, Hillsboro represented 25% of the region’s manufacturing
employment and over 50% of the region’s high-tech manufacturing. Food and advanced
manufacturing employment have remained steady with some job growth. Companies like
Beaverton Foods, Meta Fab and FiberSensys reportedly have expanded their facilities and
operations.

The semiconductor industry expansion presents Hillsboro and Oregon with an extraordinary
opportunity to intentionally create the kind of jobs and investment the state needs to emerge
from the pandemic with a stronger, more deliberately equitable economy. Globally,
semiconductor demand has soared beyond expectations due to strong performance for
everything from cloud storage to mobile devices to notebook computers due to work from
home options. There is also the anticipation of accelerating growth related to new
technologies, as for artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning and the internet of things (IoT) –
compounded by backlogged demand. This paired with national attention and funding to restore

                    City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis ♦ Page 35
domestic semiconductor innovation and manufacturing, and the industry’s preference to have
manufacturers and suppliers located near each other focuses Hillsboro and Washington County
to encourage more of these investment opportunities.

To summarize, Hillsboro’s current and prospective employment mix including recent pandemic
experience appears to offer benefits of economic resilience and long-term growth potential:

   •   Hillsboro’s business and industry mix demonstrates a path toward economic recovery
       and resilience beyond what has been achievable across the rest of the metro region.
   •   The community’s nurturing of technology industries aligns well with the best
       opportunities for economic growth regionally and nationally – in recent years, through
       the 2020 economic downturn and post-pandemic.
   •   The growth and resilience of these industries have led to a more stable and predictable
       tax base ensuring a more consistent level of service for community members.
   •   The additional growth of manufacturing jobs also presents opportunity for area
       residents and workers with a variety of backgrounds, educational levels and socio-
       economic diversity to access higher wage careers.

Bottom line, these demonstrated advantages position Hillsboro to be an even more significant
source of job stability and renewed growth for the PDX metro region and state of Oregon post-
pandemic. This sets the stage for sharing in the longer-term transition to a more resilient and
sustainable global as well as domestic U.S. economy.
