              Federal & State Tech Manufacturing Initiatives

Hillsboro’s updated EOA coincides with key federal and state initiatives, notably:
   •   The federal CHIPS and Science Act of 2022 as approved by Congress and signed
       into law by the President on August 9, 2022.
   •   The Initial Report and Subcommittee Findings of the Oregon Semiconductor
       Competitiveness Task Force released as of August 17, 2022.
Taken separately and when viewed together, these initiatives are consistent with the robust
strategy of the Hillsboro EOA for continued rapid tech industry investment and job growth –
anchored by on-going semiconductor R&D innovation, manufacturing and expansion – with
this region continuing as the #1semiconductor industry cluster in the U.S.

CHIPS and Science Act
Renewed investment in domestic semiconductor manufacturing is viewed as pivotal to
American competitiveness and national security. A major rationale provided with the CHIPS
and Science Act legislation is recognition that only 12% of chips globally are currently
manufactured domestically, down from 37% in the 1990s.
As stated by a White House issued Fact Sheet of August 9, a major objective of the CHIPS
legislation is to encourage the re-shoring of American manufacturing, “bringing good-
paying manufacturing jobs back home.”
The Fact Sheet further elaborates that this legislation is intended to “strengthen American
manufacturing, supply chains, and national security, and invest in research and
development, science and technology, and the workforce of the future to keep the United
States the leader in the industries of tomorrow, including nanotechnology, clean energy,
quantum computing, and artificial intelligence.”
More specifically, the CHIPS and Science Act provides $52.7 billion in funding for American
semiconductor research, development, manufacturing, workforce development. Included is
$39 billion in manufacturing incentives, $13.2 billion in research and development and
workforce development, and $500 million for international information, communications
technology security and semiconductor supply chain activities.
Also provided is a 25% investment tax credit for capital expenses for manufacturing of
semiconductors and related equipment. The bill requires recipients to “demonstrate
significant worker and community investments, including opportunities for small businesses
and disadvantaged communities, ensuring semiconductor incentives support equitable
growth and development.”
The Act further authorizes $10 billion for regional innovation and technology hubs across the
U.S. as “regional partnerships to develop technology, innovation and manufacturing sectors.
And the Act will provide science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM)
workforce development critical to skills needed for emerging industries and technologies of
the future.
$2 billion is reserved for the formation of a National Semiconductor Technology Center
(NSTC). A proposal for an Advanced Lithography Center to be located in Oregon and
funded under the NSTC is under development. If successful, regional location of an
advanced lithography focused NSTC hub would draw billions of federal investments to
Oregon and serve to significantly increase the level of industry interest and investment
regionally and statewide.


                   City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis ♦ Page 37
Oregon Semiconductor Competitiveness Task Force
Recognizing that the “global semiconductor industry is investing billions to fill a worldwide chip
shortage," a statewide Semiconductor Task Force was convened to frame a strategy to
“secure this once-in-a-generation opportunity for all Oregonians.”
Co-chaired by Senator Ron Wyden, Governor Kate Brown and Portland General Electric CEO
Maria Pope, the task force comprised industry, educator and elected official representation
with participation from the City of Hillsboro.
Intel’s Gordon Moore Park at Ronler Acres Research Campus in Hillsboro is one of the global
centers of semiconductor research and development, Impressively, Intel’s Gordon Moore
Research Campus is responsible for the creation of 1,000 patents a year – a level of R&D and
innovation that exceeds the patent output of more than 21 U.S. states. So immense is the
semiconductor patent activity that Oregon ranks 5th in the nation in patents per capita.
The impact of that technological leadership and impact is evident across the state.
Semiconductors represent nearly half of Oregon exports. And it is widely recognized that
export-sector businesses bring-in wealth that circulates through benefiting communities and
expands state and local budgets.
As depicted by the graphic at the introduction to this discussion, the work of the Task Force
was organized around five subcommittees – addressing industrial land, incentives, university-
industry partnerships, talent and workforce and environmental regulations. Much of this work is
also addressed with implementation measures for economic development and opportunity as
outlined in the last chapter of this EOA report.
Principal findings and recommendations of the Task Force are summarized as follows:
   •   R&D Strength: Semiconductor research and development is Oregon’s unique
       competitive advantage. Oregon’s strategy to secure chip investment should focus on
       solidifying a world-class innovation ecosystem around chip research and production.
   •   Talent: Premier access to talent and a robust, private sector-led innovation ecosystem
       separates Oregon from others. To preserve this advantage, Oregon needs to invest
       across the talent continuum, from entry-level positions to PhDs.
   •   Land: To attract semiconductor manufacturers, the state needs more buildable
       industrial land. Oregon’s land use system and infrastructure investment programs
       require urgent legislative attention and investment to address this need. Of pivotal
       importance for this EOA, the Task Force concluded that “there are no development
       ready sites of the size needed to attract a major semiconductor investment, or to
       support larger size suppliers.” With the Metro region cited as key to semiconductor
       growth, specifically recommended are two sites of 500+ acres, four sites of 50-100
       acres and at least eight sites of 15-35 acres (for key suppliers to the semiconductor
       cluster).
   •   Incentives: Oregon needs to become more competitive on incentives. Other states
       offer incentive packages that are both larger and more specifically tailored to the
       semiconductor industry.
   •   Regulation: When it comes to governmental oversight, from permitting facilities to
       environmental regulations, the subcommittee reviewed “best practices” from
       competing states and identified the importance of forming stronger partnerships with
       manufacturers and streamlining the permitting process.

The three 20-year employment growth scenarios evaluated with this EOA indicate a possible
range of 36,910 - 87,800 added jobs (as covered by unemployment insurance) over the 20-year
period of 2020-40. If adjustments are made for non-covered workers as was with Hillsboro’s
2017 EOA, the range of the current forecast would be from 44,650 - 106,870 added jobs:

   •   The lower Scenario A straight-line forecast associated with this current analysis comes
       closest to the results of the prior 2017 EOA alternative forecast – albeit with a
       somewhat modified methodology.
   •   The higher Scenario B exponential sectoral growth approach yields a result that well
       exceeds what was presented by earlier EOA alternatives – but better reflects the
       exponential growth curve of key industries in Hillsboro in recent years as well as
       national economic restructuring currently underway.
   •   The mid-range and hybrid Scenario C approach best reflects Hillsboro’s target industry
       and business clustering approach as reinforced by economic development activity up to
       and through the pandemic. This scenario emphasizes building on existing strengths
       consistent with national economic strategies for industrial re-shoring, offering catalytic
       benefits for the Portland metro region and state. Recommended with this EOA update
       is adoption of a Scenario C approach for hybrid growth.

Forecast Scenario Implications & Decision-Making
Five key implications of the three forecast scenarios are noted with this employment analysis:

   •   Widely differing results in employment outcomes are possible with the scenarios
       considered – for example, with Scenario B resulting in more than twice the 20-year job
       growth associated with Scenario A.
   •   In addition to input from those knowledgeable about Hillsboro’s key employment
       sectors, an important check on “reasonableness” is with comparison to the Metro UGR
       forecast – including a regional high growth jobs scenario (although Metro’s high growth
       projection is only 6% more than the most likely scenario identified by the 2018 UGR).
       Hillsboro’s experience likely will continue to be more robust for industrial employment
       and for related diversification as the local economy further matures in the years ahead.
   •   Employment sectors for which declining employment has been observed and
       extrapolated forward may warrant added attention – especially as to either the lower
       reasonable bounds for continued employment decline or regarding the potential for
       sector turnaround in the years ahead.
   •   Any employment outcomes substantially more aggressive than Scenario A will benefit
       from continued articulation of targeted industry marketing and implementation
       strategies – especially for sectors that can be demonstrated as mutually reinforcing.
   •   NAICS-defined employment sector potentials may then need to be overlaid with
       Hillsboro’s groupings of targeted industry clusters – defined as including advanced
       electronics manufacturing, specialized machinery and equipment, clean tech
       manufacturing, biotechnology and pharmaceuticals, and software.


                   City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis ♦ Page 40
These implications receive added consideration and discussion in subsequent sections of this
EOA pertaining to community economic potential, employment land needs, and
implementation policies.

Forecast Approach
OAR 660-009-0015 for EOAs stipulates that forecast demand is to be based on what could
“reasonably be expected to locate or expand in the planning area based on information about
national, state, regional, county or local trends.” While the OAR does not require the use of a
specific methodology, the application of a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) reflects typical
practice for EOA employment and land needs analyses – as well as for Metro’s Urban Growth
Report (UGR). With this EOA forecast, the approach is to apply an approach most consistent
with local job trend data. Details of the forecast approach utilized including statistical testing of
sector-by-sector trends is provided with Appendix A to this EOA. What follows is a summary of
the approach as applied.

Straight Line versus Exponential Job Growth. In communities experiencing relatively
slow job growth, there may be relatively little difference in extrapolation of straight-line or
annually compounded growth (where each year’s growth is built on the higher base number as
calculated for the previous year). Hillsboro presents a different situation as growth rates have
been relatively rapid across a number of employment sectors in recent years. In this situation,
there can be a substantial difference in future growth potentials depending on whether the job
trend is extrapolated forward based on a straight line or exponential (CAGR) methodology.

Sector-by-Sector Approach. A second consideration is that, in Hillsboro, widely varied job
growth rates have been experienced in recent years depending on the sector being considered.
Not all sectors have experienced rapid or accelerated job growth. Some have experienced job
change at relatively low (or negative) growth rates. Consequently, as in other similarly affected
communities, forecasts of future employment are often made sector-by-sector, with results
then summed across all sectors to achieve an overall employment forecast result.

Consistency of Job Trend. Job change also does not always occur on a consistent basis
from year-to-year. In these cases, it may not be readily apparent whether growth over a multi-
year period reflects more of a linear or exponential growth pattern. This situation is
exacerbated by the experience of the COVID pandemic with sudden and severe employment
loss followed by varying degrees of subsequent partial to full job recovery. Some sectors have
recovered more fully than others. When coupled with emergent workforce shortages, this
suggests potential for longer term job displacement, especially in lower paid employment
sectors. Also of significance may be local, state or national policy considerations.

Sector Toggle Application. The forecast methodology applied with this EOA reflects the
empirically demonstrated experience of Hillsboro employment sectors consistent with the data
available. A toggle approach is taken to the forecast, applying a linear, exponential, or mid-
course (mid-point) forecast to each sector – depending on experience as recorded sector-by-
sector including evaluation of regional capture rates as detailed by Appendix A to this report.

                  City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis ♦ Page 43
Employment Forecast Recap
This EOA employment forecast process reflects a customized methodology based on experience
and anticipated flexibility of response to as yet uncertain post-pandemic economic prospects.

Methodology. Key features of the approach taken with this EOA update are that it is:

   •   Experience based – drawing from experience of the last economic cycle together with
       short- and long-term employment-related implications of the COVID pandemic
   •   Scenario driven – distinguishing between outcomes potentially associated with straight-
       line (linear) versus exponential (CAGR) job growth
   •   Sector-by-sector focused – as individualized sector determinations of linear,
       exponential or mid-case growth summing to a recommended hybrid growth scenario
   •   Qualitative as well as quantitative – reflecting community priorities together with
       federal and state initiatives as for substantially increased semiconductor manufacturing

Prior Experience. Two key points of reference are of note with this EOA update:

   •   Comparison with prior 2017 EOA – which after consideration of three alternatives
       recommended a growth projection an added 40,326 jobs over 20 years – above the
       current Scenario A 20-year projection of an added 36.910 jobs in the updated 20-year
       time frame and below the 61,895 added jobs associated the preferred Scenario C for
       hybrid growth. The prior 2017 EOA was predicated on a 2010-15 observed job CAGR of
       3.3% but with the 2015-35 projection trimmed to a 2.0% CAGR. The recommended
       Scenario C approach with this EOA reflects a higher 2.7% CAGR from 2018-40 – lower
       than observed experience with the prior EOA but above the 2017 projection.
   •   Comparison with recent job growth – as a more pertinent point of reference for this
       update. Over the last economic cycle of 2007-18, Hillsboro’s employment increased at
       an observed 2.4% CAGR. When projected forward on a sector-by-sector basis, sectors
       with high historically experienced CAGRs (as with health care, transportation and
       wholesale trade) become ever larger proportions of the total over 20 years. This
       increases the overall CAGR going forward to 2.7%, above what was experienced in the
       last economic cycle. This is the case even with tempered prospects as for health care.

Flexible Response for an Uncertain Future. As recommended, Scenario C provides:

   •   Consistency – with EOA analyses statewide together with observed trends locally
   •   Priority – emphasizing added opportunity for the community’s targeted traded sectors
   •   Flexibility – for future EOA updates as post-pandemic changes become more apparent
   •   Opportunity – for metro/state-wide benefit to harness economic engines of the future

Looking beyond job numbers, this EOA now shifts to review of community economic potential –
addressing qualitative considerations of industry, business and community stakeholders.


                   City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis ♦ Page 44
III. COMMUNITY ECONOMIC POTENTIAL
Discussion of community economic potential draws from the quantitative analysis of economic
trends and forecasts combined with qualitative research including focus group and interview
discussion with business and community stakeholders. Also covered is a review of pertinent
regional to global trends research. This EOA chapter represents a summary of a more detailed
discussion as provided by EOA Technical Appendix B.

Key elements of this community economic development potential assessment address:

   •   Qualifying Economic Development Potential – complementing the quantitative
       assessment with qualitative judgements informed by stakeholder input
   •   Factors Affecting Community Economic Development Potential – addressing Goal 9
       requirements and setting the stage for a next step competitive position analysis
   •   Competitive Position – articulating strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats
       (SWOT) affecting Hillsboro’s economic potential currently and prospectively
   •   Target Industry Clusters – assessing what has already been outlined for Hillsboro as
       similar to and distinct from the Portland metro region and state of Oregon

As initially conceived, the purpose of this assessment of community economic potential has
been to serve as a bridge between the quantitative review of economic trends with associated
land use needs and subsequent implementation policies. This work was initiated prior to and
then was interrupted by the March-April 2020 recognition of the profound health and
economic effects of the then emergent global COVID-19 pandemic.

An initial draft of this analysis was completed in mid-March 2020. Consequently, the approach
taken with an updated assessment has been to retain much of the material of the initial
analysis – subsequently supplemented by new and potentially altered directions reflecting
changing perspectives resulting from the pandemic, economic downturn and subsequent
recovery.

When in the middle of sweeping change, it is difficult to reliably assess both short- and long-
term prospects for the global economy, let alone implications for any particular jurisdiction. A
pivotal question for this EOA is: Will the economy re-stabilize to pre-COVID conditions, or is this
new-new normal to be fundamentally different from what has occurred over recent business
cycles, especially as most recently experienced since the Great Recession of 2007-09?

This assessment takes an approach that looks to the past as one potential guide to the future
while also considering the character and extent of potential transformative changes that may
now be underway. The decision of a viable path to pursue involves a risk-reward assessment.
The analysis and recommendations resulting from this assessment suggest a risk mitigation
strategy that might involve elements of both approaches – working to keep the best of the past
while being an early adapter of the post-pandemic changes most likely to endure.


                    City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis ♦ Page 45
QUALIFYING ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT POTENTIAL
Identifying and characterizing economic development potential to this point has been, in large
part, driven by the numbers. Addressing the statewide land use planning Goal 9 Economic
Development requires quantification of potential employment change and associated land
requirements.

However, understanding and preparing for the future is about more than numerical modeling
alone. Qualitative assessment is also important – especially when it comes to setting policies to
implement the plan in a way that also will fit with broader community objectives.

For this 2021 EOA, a stakeholder outreach process was conducted in two phases. An initial
round of interviews was conducted in early 2020 (pre-pandemic). A second round of phone
interviews was conducted over the summer of 2020, as initial steps toward economic recovery
were getting underway.

In addition to the topics noted with the first round, the second round also involved asking
participants to comment on two key items – the near-term pace and timing for pandemic-
related economic recovery together with implications for sustained economic recovery and
resiliency longer-term over the next 5-20 years.

What follows is a composite synopsis of what was gathered from initial stakeholder
conversations conducted pre-pandemic followed by more recent perspectives including added
contacts made over the summer of 2020 as early steps toward national and local economic
recovery were beginning to take hold. More detailed discussion of the interview process and
results is provided by Appendix B to this EOA.

Pre-Pandemic Global to Local Trends
Two major themes emerged from pre-pandemic conversations with business and public
decision makers:

   •   Disruptive technology – exemplified by emerging opportunities for autonomous
       vehicles with less parking need, artificial intelligence (AI), internet of things (IoT), 5G
       telecommunications, exponential growth of data needs, and decarbonization.
   •   Live-work connection – as tech workforce needs to be mobile, often work remotely,
       and reduce the length of the commute trip. Workers don’t want to get stuck in a metro
       or community location with few options for re-employment if their current job goes
       away. As millennials age, there also is now a shift in live-work preferences, less toward
       center cities and more to full-service communities meeting a greater array of family as
       well as job interests.

Pre- and now post-pandemic, Hillsboro has been described as well positioned to capitalize on
these trends over the next 20 years.



                    City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis ♦ Page 46
Working Through & Beyond the Pandemic
For virtually all stakeholders contacted through the summer of 2020, the world of work and
business has clearly become a different place than it was pre-pandemic. However, many of the
fundamental forces of change already at work globally and locally still appear to remain in
place. Existing trends for Hillsboro of disruptive technology and live-work connection have not
necessarily changed, but rather have dramatically accelerated.

Industrial & Commercial Land Needs
Recognizing that a primary purpose of this EOA update is to define short- and long-term needs
for industrial and commercial land, an important question is: What employment land needs are
most important to address?

Again, two overall observations emerged from stakeholder discussions:

   •   First, priority should be placed on assuring that shovel-ready land required to
       accommodate new employment will be there as demand warrants. Hillsboro has a
       strong track record of serving major employers requiring large sites – making possible
       development that otherwise would not likely have occurred in the metro region. In the
       wake of the pandemic, there is growing recognition that employment land use needs
       may change in ways not previously expected – ranging from more work-at-home to
       office reconfiguration and retail downsizing to more large-site demand for industrial
       manufacturing and distribution functions led by major corporate investment.
       Suggested is a need to be more flexible with land use planning and regulation than in
       the past. Greater flexibility may include consideration of mid-course adjustments as the
       character and extent of these emerging land demand changes become more apparent.
   •   Second, there is growing recognition of the need to accommodate both exclusive
       industrial zones and mixed-use development. Business requirements and priorities vary
       depending on the specific characteristics of different industrial and commercial uses.
       With potential reduced commercial space demand, horizontal rather than vertical
       mixed-use may become a more pronounced market opportunity, at least near-term.

Other Public & Private Initiatives
A final topic of discussion has been on identifying other public and private initiatives that
should be considered with this EOA. These are initiatives that extend beyond but support the
City’s land use policies. Priorities suggested by stakeholders interviewed center on workforce
training, smart transport investment, long-term utility investment and targeted economic
development incentives.

FACTORS AFFECTING ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT POTENTIAL
An element of the EOA process involves consideration of location or market factors affecting
where a particular type of industrial or other employment use may locate. As defined by ORS


                   City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis ♦ Page 47
660-009-0005, these locational factors “include but are not limited to, proximity to raw
materials, supplies, labor, services, markets, or educational institutions; access to
transportation and freight facilities such as rail, marine ports and airports, multimodal freight or
transshipment facilities, and major transportation routes; and workforce factors (e.g., skill level,
education, age distribution).”

Separately outlined by OAR 660-009-0015 (4) are potential advantages and disadvantages to be
considered with the assessment of community economic development potential as topics that
“may include but are not limited to” the following:

   (a) Location, size and buying power of markets
   (b) Availability of transportation facilities for access and freight mobility
   (c) Public facilities and public services
   (d) Labor market factors
   (e) Access to suppliers and utilities
   (f) Necessary support services
   (g) Limits on development due to federal and state environmental protection laws
   (h) Educational and technical training programs

Due to the overlap of the locational and market factors stipulated by OAR Definitions (0005)
and Economic Opportunities Analysis (0015), these factors are considered together and also
organized around topics that have emerged as most germane to Hillsboro’s current and
prospective community economic potential.

With this EOA, 11 factors are identified as pivotal both now and going forward for economic
development in Hillsboro. As further detailed by EOA Appendix B, these are factors related to:

   •   Globalization/Localization – with e-commerce suggesting less localization while a
       transition back from global to local may significantly affect manufacturing decisions by
       re-shoring closer to a U.S. home base
   •   Technology – as a continued if not accelerating source of innovation affecting virtually
       every aspect of business, consumer and residential choice
   •   Workforce – with key industry issues related to availability of workers and to workforce
       skills and training
   •   Vendor & Customer Networks – with growing opportunity for Hillsboro and metro area
       businesses to draw from a widening network of other local businesses for key business-
       to-business relationships where the market is large enough to support key local vendors
   •   Incomes & Buying Power – for added local consumer buying power driven by Hillsboro
       wage levels that average 46% more than the average wage across the entire metro area
   •   Transportation – important in a more congested metro area for reliable freight
       transport, reasonable workforce commute, and retail/consumer business accessibility




                    City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis ♦ Page 48
   •   Utility Infrastructure – notably electric power, redundant fiber, and wastewater
       treatment – the availability, quality and cost of which has been a significant location
       consideration and attraction for major Hillsboro area employers
   •   Civic Infrastructure – including critical community infrastructure as for City services, K-
       12 schools, health care, parks/open spaces, and cultural amenities
   •   Environmental Conservation – with protection of wetlands, other critical areas and
       open spaces serving as an economic amenity, drawing business facilities that value a
       campus setting
   •   Housing – with job-housing balance of growing significance amid a more geographically
       limited commute-shed and with need for greater diversity of affordable housing product
       including expanded live-work opportunity
   •   Quality of Life – which for Oregon residents is rooted in access to active and passive
       outdoor recreation including mountains, ocean areas and, more recently, to regional
       attractions ranging from internationally recognized wineries to locally sourced foods

A major objective of this EOA is to build on existing strengths and emerging opportunities while
addressing and, where possible, mitigating critical weaknesses and threats. As observed by one
stakeholder, “We have the second most manufacturing economy in the U.S. and Hillsboro is the

                      City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis ♦ Page 49
most important traded sector in Oregon.” These existing conditions represent building blocks
for renewed economic prosperity not only locally but regionally and state-wide.

The aftermath of the 2007-09 Great Recession was focused on the transition to what was then
termed as a new normal. With COVID and the economic contraction of 2020, the focus now
shifts perhaps even more dramatically to what might be considered as a new-new normal.

Historical economic data presents often useful guideposts of where the economy has been, but
not necessarily of where it is now headed. Qualitative evidence from stakeholders provides
critical insights as to the transition now underway but not yet with a fully clear picture of where
Hillsboro will be five years from now, let alone over the next 20 or 50 years.

However, a clear message from business and community leaders is that this next economic
cycle will be about more than economic recovery or a simple return to the business and
economic development practices of the last decade. In addition to accelerating trends of
disruptive technology and live-work connection, this next
decade may well serve to redefine the technologies viewed
as most pivotal and to alter current live-work boundaries.         Emerging Economic

This approach recognizes the reality of the marketplace – especially where there are
opportunities for a particular industry to be supported by local vendors or customers within a
related industry segment.

As in the past, Hillsboro may modify its industry clusters to reflect and serve new or emerging
industry opportunities in the years ahead. This would recognize the potential to step in
alongside and encourage sectors that currently relatively may be weakly represented in
Hillsboro but with growing competitive presence.

Priority consideration for business targeting might be provided to those emerging sectors (or
specific businesses) offering potential for strong employment, tax revenue, and/or
supplemental business leveraging (or “pull-through”) benefits.7 Consistent with a hybrid
development scenario, an adaptive industry cluster approach can be positioned to address both
national and regionally-driven opportunities.

This target industry strategy also reflects recent federal policy and strategic industry
initiatives. The congressionally approved CHIPS and Science Act provides both the incentive
and impetus for increased U.S. semiconductor manufacturing. This policy initiative is reinforced
for Oregon and the metro region with 2022 findings and recommendations of the Oregon
Semiconductor Competitiveness Task Force – with emphasis on the need for more buildable
industrial land. As these or other policy or industry driven initiatives emerge in ways not
previously anticipated, the City of Hillsboro also expects to increasingly focus on securing the
capacity to better assure variable land parcel availability.

As discussed with both Chapters II and III of this EOA, significant market and policy shifts have
materialized in response to unanticipated external shocks domestically and globally. These
changes have occurred not only in response to the COVID-19 pandemic health and economic
conditions, but also as a result of widespread supply chain disruptions.

From a land use perspective, it is increasingly necessary to highlight the need or impact of
having or not having a variable range of land parcels available and ready-to-build. Of pivotal
importance, the realization of Hillsboro’s community economic potential requires maintaining
large lots to the extent possible as needed to attract and retain major employer manufacturing
and support functions.

Even with a continuing if not accelerated shift to increased automation, parcels suitable to
serve large campus needs of major employers may serve not only as a means to increase direct
employment but also to enhance the value of output and contribution to other employment
generating functions locally, regionally and statewide. This points to a need to encourage
adaptive build-out of facility needs, including recycling of older or obsolete facilities to meet
state-of-the-art industrial and technology practices.

These more qualitative and forward-looking portions of this Community Economic Potential
discussion set the stage for resumed quantitative analysis with Chapter IV Employment Land
Needs which now follows.


                    City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis ♦ Page 51
IV. EMPLOYMENT LAND NEEDS
The determination of needs for commercial and industrial employment lands draws on results
of the employment forecast scenarios coupled with the more qualitative perspectives
describing community economic potential. In effect, this portion of the EOA analysis compares
land supply with projected employment driven demand to assess site availability over 5- and
20-year planning horizons with alternate employment scenarios considered. Also included is
summary consideration of potential longer-term, 50-year employment land needs.

The land needs analysis is intended to identify and characterize the demand and supply for
industrial and commercial sites. Also described are the types of sites needed to accommodate
targeted growth industries and existing employers that could potentially expand – together
with opportunities for spin-off employers and entities that provide support for existing business
and industry clusters.

The analysis aims to further identify specific site sizes, special site requirements or other
characteristics affecting the needed land supply. In addition, the analysis includes a brief review
and comparison to Metro’s regional buildable lands inventory associated with the 2018 Urban
Growth Report. Key elements of this land needs assessment include discussion of:

   •   Hillsboro’s Employment Buildable Lands Inventory (BLI) – based on data from
       December 2020.
   •   Employment-Driven Land Need – for each of three employment scenarios
   •   Reconciliation of Land Need & Capacity – addressing shortfalls with each jobs scenario
   •   Site Size Requirements – with large sites of pivotal importance for Hillsboro industries
   •   50-year Outlook – extrapolating the three job scenarios forward from 20 to 50 years
   •   EOA implications & Options – for bringing land capacity into alignment with demand

HILLSBORO’S EMPLOYMENT BLI
The City of Hillsboro has coordinated with Metro to evaluate the city’s supply of buildable lands
available for employment uses. The City utilized Metro’s Buildable Land Inventory (BLI)
methodology to revise portions of the 2018 Draft Urban Growth Report (UGR) pertaining to
Hillsboro’s Urban Growth Boundary (and future growth areas).

Hillsboro serves as a major source of employment – especially higher wage jobs – in
Washington County. For example, as of 2018 QCEW employment data indicates that Hillsboro
accounted for 27% of all jobs in Washington County, well above its 17% share of population
county-wide.8

A supply-focused BLI was initially prepared by the City of Hillsboro in late 2019. The amended
BLI also reflects a similar data benchmark date of December 2020. This approximates a similar
2020 starting point for the 20-year 2020-40 EOA employment forecast period.

                    City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis ♦ Page 52
The 2021 EOA was adopted in 2022 and was appealed to the Land Use Board of Appeals (LUBA)
by 1000 Friends of Oregon (Friends) and Metro. While Friends and Metro raised several
assignments of error relating to employment growth forecasting and the Comprehensive Plan
status, most of these arguments were denied by LUBA. However, LUBA agreed with Friends
that the 2019 buildable lands inventory (BLI) for employment land that was included in the
2021 EOA did not apply the correct analysis for determining the redevelopment potential of
“developed lands.” LUBA thus remanded the decision to the City to address that issue.

Consequently, this 2021 EOA has been amended to incorporate an employment BLI based on
December 2020 data as prepared by the planning firm MIG in compliance with the terms of the
LUBA remand. The results of the amended BLI are summarized in this chapter with further
detail as provided by MIG included as Appendix E.

Amended BLI Methodology & Mapping
As with the initial 2019 BLI, the amended BLI based on data from December 2020 utilizes:

   •   GIS analysis based on Washington County tax parcel data (limited to the City of
       Hillsboro and associated future growth areas).
   •   Focus on parcels for which some form of employment use is permitted, differentiated
       between COM commercial, IND Industrial, and MUR mixed use residential and
       commercially zoned properties (with employment capacity varied to reflect allocations
       differentiated by mixed use zoning designation).
   •   Both the initial and amended BLI inventories reflect land use conditions as of 2019-20
       consistent with the baseline year for forecasting of employment growth over the
       ensuing 2020-40 time period. As noted, the revised BLI reflects employment land
       inventory conditions as of December 2020.

Refined BLI Methodology. The MIG prepared BLI (included in full as Appendix E) is summarized
as part of a five-step process:

   •   Step 1: Land classification. This step identifies the land in the City that is available for
       employment uses.
   •   Step 2: Constraints to Development. This step identifies constraints such as natural
       resources, steep slopes, and utility easements that limit development.
   •   Step 3: Development Status. This step assigns a “Development Status” of vacant,
       partially vacant, or developed to tax lots in the inventory.
   •   Step 4: Net Buildable Area. This step removes land for future rights-of-way and other
       land needs to provide a net number of buildable acres for each City zoning designation.
   •   Step 5: Redevelopment. This analysis includes an assessment of potentially
       redevelopable sites in the City and adjacent growth areas.

Land Classification. Parcels in the inventory are categorized based on their Comprehensive Plan
designations, zoning designations, property ownership, and other characteristics. Employment

                   City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis ♦ Page 53
classifications include designation of lands with Comprehensive Plan designation as industrial,
commercial and as a portion of mixed use land. Residential as well as publicly owned and other
uses not consistent with employment activity are excluded from the employment BLI.

Constraints to Development. Employment land that is constrained from development is
excluded from net buildable acreage based on constraints including:

   •   Steep slopes
   •   Water bodies
   •   FEMA floodway
   •   FEMA 100 Year floodplain
   •   Significant wetlands
   •   Significant forest resources
   •   Significant natural resources overlay (SNRO)
   •   BPA easements
   •   Airport runway protection area

Unconstrained or buildable areas of are defined as unconstrained vacant and partially vacant
sites minus constrained acreage.

Development Status. Each parcel in the study area including employment designated
properties in the City and the unincorporated urban growth boundary is categorized as vacant,
partially vacant, or developed (further screened for redevelopment potential). Parcels partially
vacant have existing development but with some portion of the site identified as potentially
available for future development subject to minimum site or use requirements for
development suitability (as specific to industrial, commercial and mixed use zones).

Converting Gross Acreage to Net Employment Area. Land for roads, infrastructure, open space
and other needs constitutes reductions of two primary types to calculate net developable
acreage for each parcel:

   •   An overall 25% reduction applied to commercial, industrial and mixed use zones; and
   •   Proportions of land area in mixed use zones expected to occur as employment uses
       (with varied deductions applied as specific to each of 16 applicable mixed use zones)

Employment BLI Mapping. Provided on the following four pages are maps illustrating
geographies across which the revised employment BLI has been conducted – together with
associated employment land categorizations.

The first map identifies boundaries of the Hillsboro city limits as of 2020. A second map depicts
comprehensive plan designations for the city and unincorporated UGB. The third map shows
portions of Hillsboro’s employment land categorized as fully developed, partially vacant, or fully
vacant. The fourth map depicts parcels with redevelopment potential using a strike price test.

As detailed by Appendix E, this employment BLI further evaluates the redevelopment potential
of employment parcels categorized as “Developed.” This test is an estimate that has been used,

representing a per square foot value of land at which a developer can afford to purchase
property and theoretically redevelop profitably.

property owner willingness, the availability of other suitable sites, and macroeconomic factors,
the 143 acres of potentially redevelopable land was evaluated separately from the remaining
buildable area for employment use.

land supply over 5- and 20-year time horizons. A longer-term 50-year outlook is also provided

The 1,225 net buildable acres of this refined BLI methodology is 132 acres (or 10%) less than the
1,357 acres indicated by the previous 2019 prepared BLI inventory. This difference could be

Industrial, commercial and mixed-use employment opportunities can occur via 29 distinct
zoning designations in the City of Hillsboro. This includes 8 industrial (IND), two commercial
(COM) and 19 mixed-use commercial/residential (MUR) zones (detailed by Appendix E).

The planned Jackson East industrial area represents by far the single largest potential
employment zone in terms of accommodating job growth – with just over 561 net employment
acres accounting for 46% of Hillsboro’s acreage for future employment-related development. In
terms of acreage potential, the next largest zone is Industrial Park (I-P) – with 264 acres
accounting for 22% of net buildable employment land in Hillsboro and its identified growth
areas. The area designated for Industrial Sanctuary (I-S) use comprises another 107 acres or 9%
of net buildable acreage for future employment development.

In August 2022, Hillsboro City Council adopted Industrial Comprehensive Plan and Community
Development Code amendments for the Jackson East Area. Adopted, codes allow for economic
development as property owners determine how and when to voluntarily annex into the City of
Hillsboro. Tools considered to encourage employment growth in this area include amending the
nearby North Hillsboro Industrial Renewal Area, master planning and delivering infrastructure,
and expanding the Enterprise Zone to include this larger future development area.

While commercial uses are intended to be accommodated primarily on commercial and mixed-
use zoned lands, there is opportunity for some additional complementary and ancillary
commercial development with virtually all of the industrial zoning designations. Office is
outright permitted in a majority of the city’s industrial zones, with limited and/or conditional
approval required in some zones, and not permitted in one industrial zone.

Greater limitations are indicated for retail, service, and institutional uses on industrial lands –
with the greatest restrictions on residential use (as least compatible with large site industrial
activity). Also noted is that, to a relatively limited extent, some (generally smaller scale)
industrial uses are allowed on a limited or conditional use basis in some non-industrial zones.

BLI Comparison with Metro UGR
Metro’s 2018 Urban Growth Report identified 2,150-2,530 net buildable acres of commercial
(including mixed-use) employment land and 8,600 net buildable acres of industrial land inside
the region’s UGB. With just under 107 net buildable acres of commercial and mixed-use
employment land, Hillsboro accounts for about 4-5% of the region’s commercial inventory.

By comparison, this amended Hillsboro reported inventory of 1,225 acres of net industrial
employment land represents an estimated 14% of the region’s inventory of net buildable


                    City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis ♦ Page 60
acreage. On a combined basis, Hillsboro would account for about 12% of the Metro UGB’s
commercial and industrial employment land inventory.

EMPLOYMENT DRIVEN LAND DEMAND
As described in the prior chapter of this EOA report, three employment scenarios have been
identified and quantified – with substantially different potential forecast outcomes:

   •   Scenario A Straight-Line Growth
       (forecast for a net addition of 36,910 Hillsboro jobs from 2020-40)
   •   Scenario B Exponential Growth
       (with net addition of as many as 87,800 net new jobs from 2020-40)
   •   Scenario C Hybrid Growth
       (focused on target industry sectors with 61,895 net new jobs from 2020-40)

For purposes of this EOA, forecast scenario results may be categorized in three separate ways:
by NAICS or overall employment sector (as noted in the prior chapter), by building type (as the
main focus of this EOA for purposes of allocating employment to buildings and land), and by
overall Comprehensive Plan designation.

Categorization of Employment by Building Type
A useful means of categorizing employment is by the type(s) of buildings that a particular
employment sector typically inhabits. This categorization system was first applied with Metro’s
2009 UGR as a means of translating employment growth to building and associated land needs.
This methodology also was applied with the most recent 2017 Hillsboro EOA.

For purposes of this updated EOA, seven employment-related building types are identified –
covering office, institutional, flex/business park, general industrial, warehouse, data center and
retail uses. NAICS specific employment is allocated to each of these building types using an
allocation matrix that cross-references building type by employment sector. Percentage
allocations of each employment sector to building types are based on prior research as initially
conducted for the 2009 Metro UGR and as reflected (with Hillsboro-specific refinements) with
the 2017 Hillsboro EOA (as further detailed by Appendix C to this EOA).

By building typology, office buildings are expected to account for the largest share of forecast
employment growth – 31% of job growth with Scenario A and 33% in Scenarios B and C.
Retail/storefront space accounts for 18-20% of anticipated job growth, general industrial for 12-
16%, warehouse space for 9%, flex/business park (BP) space for 10-11%, and institutional for
another 11-15% (depending on the scenario).

The next steps in this demand or needs analysis require the translation of employment growth
into associated employment land need. The analysis begins with discussion of the conversion
factors utilized, followed by presentation of resulting land need outputs for each of the three
employment forecast scenarios considered.


                    City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis ♦ Page 61
Conversion Factors
Translating employment growth to land demand involves three sets of conversion factors:

   •   Conversion of employment need to building space requirement – by applying typical
       ratios of building square footage per employee as applicable to each building typology.
   •   Conversion of building space need to associated land demand – by applying a floor area
       ratio (FAR) factor specific to each building typology.
   •   Application of a market vacancy factor – recognizing space turnover at normalized
       occupancy typical for each building type.

Applying these three factors in sequence makes it possible to estimate employment densities
(as jobs per acre) for each of the seven building types considered. For industrial uses, resulting
employment densities range from an estimated three employees per acre with data center uses
to about 17 jobs per acre for general industrial. With commercial uses, densities range from 18
jobs per acre for institutional to nearly 45 jobs per acre with office uses. These conversion
factors are applied consistently across all three employment forecast scenarios.

Ratios applied are those previously used with Hillsboro’s 2017 EOA. These factors also are
generally consistent with conversion factors first utilized with Metro’s 2009 UGR (including sub-
regional variations), but with some modifications apparent with the city’s 2017 EOA – including
addition of market vacancy factors.

Employment-Driven Land Needs by Scenario
Net industrial land acreage needs associated with the three employment scenarios are
estimated as follows:

   •   With the straight-line growth forecast of Scenario A, close to 2,230 net acres of
       employment land would be required from 2020-40. This is 12% less than the 2,530 net
       developable acreage need over a 20-year time frame as estimated with the prior 2017
       EOA.
   •   With a more robust compound growth rate applied based on experience of the current
       economic cycle as estimated with Scenario B, the employment land need more than
       doubles to a net total of nearly 5,330 acres over the same 2020-40 time horizon.
   •   With the hybrid or targeted growth projection of Scenario C, land demand over a 20-
       year planning horizon is estimated at a net total of just over 3,840 acres.

With any of these three scenarios, the largest single source of land need would be for
warehouse-related uses – at 26-28% of total net land demand (depending on the scenario). This
is followed by flex/business park need at 16-18%, and general industrial demand at 11-15%.

Data center acreage demand is estimated at 6-10% of the total employment land need. Major
generators of commercial related demand are institutional building needs at 10-13% of net land
need, with office and retail each at about 11-12%.

                    City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis ♦ Page 62
Employment-Driven Land Needs by Job Sector
When reviewed by NAICS employment sector, the largest sources of land demand are noted as:

   •   Manufacturing with Scenario A – at 21% of the net developable acreage need. Other
       major sources of land demand would be health care and social assistance (16%),
       wholesale trade (15%), information (11%), and transportation/warehousing (10%).
   •   A changed relative ordering of employment land needs with Scenario B – with
       wholesale trade and health care/social assistance each accounting for as much as 20%
       of total land need. Information and transportation/warehousing would each account for
       12% of land need with manufacturing at 11%.
   •   A further re-shuffling resulting in more sectoral balance for priority sectors with
       Scenario C – as transportation/warehousing, information and health care/social
       assistance each account for between 15-18% of total 20-year land need. Manufacturing
       would represent 15% of total net developable acreage required – a figure about mid-
       way between the Scenario A and B proportions.

RECONCILIATION OF LAND NEED & CAPACITY
The next step of this EOA needs analysis is to compare forecast employment land need with the
BLI-identified supply of net buildable sites. This analysis starts by comparing demand and supply
in aggregate, followed by a closer look at the composition of major employment generators.

Employment Land Need vs Capacity Overview
With this analysis, employment land needs are evaluated in terms of both a 20-year plan
horizon and also over a 5-year short-term period – for each of three forecast scenarios. As
shown by the following chart, employment land capacity appears inadequate to meet
anticipated employer needs over both 20-year and 5-year time horizons.

The long-term 20-year plan horizon assumes the availability of in-city lands plus lands currently

Short-term, in-city lands could accommodate essentially all of 5-year demand, assuming the
lower growth of a Scenario A forecast scenario. However, substantial deficits occur over a 20-

periods – with either of the high growth Scenario B and hybrid Scenario C projections. In effect,
securing more land becomes pivotal as a key step toward realization of Hillsboro’s full
employment potential – also for added higher wage regional job opportunity.

   •    Forecast land demand over 20 years is 1.8 times existing BLI land supply with Scenario A,

   •    With the limited BLI capacity comprised primarily of industrially designated land, not

Going forward, land need can be expected to be further affected in ways not yet fully foreseen
as for horizontal and vertical mixed-use development, remote work trends, e-commerce and
new technologies including artificial intelligence (AI). This EOA assumes land needs similar to
patterns of the last economic cycle but recognizes that future forecast methodologies will
adapt to new patterns of employment development as emerging trends become more evident.

Comparing Forecast Need with Observed Absorption
Forecasts of employment and resulting land need scenarios can be compared with actual land
absorption experience recently in North Hillsboro. The City’s Economic and Community
Development department has compiled data for industrial area development occurring since
2014 – in effect covering a 5-6 year time period through August 2021.

Over this time period, industrial development has occurred on 48 parcels totaling
approximately 595 acres. This equates to average annual absorption of 100+ acres per year –
not counting development outside the North Hillsboro area (including on commercial and
mixed-use designated lands).

By comparison, annualized land needs associated with the three EOA forecast scenarios are
estimated at forecast need of 111 acres per year with Scenario A, 266 acres annually with
Scenario B and 192 acres per year with Scenario C. This indicates clear support for more than
Scenario A straight-line growth as a base expectation going forward, with opportunity for added
absorption if Hillsboro continues active pursuit of major tech-related employer commitments.

the standpoint of comparing parcel sizes for the full existing inventory of all employment
designated lands with parcel sizes of the current vacant and redevelopable employment land
inventory. Detailed parcel size classifications are the same as were provided by the 2017 EOA.

Key observations from this review include the following:

   •   Hillsboro’s amended BLI indicates that out of a total employment designated land base
       of 6,210 acres, 3,753 acres (60%) are already developed with 1,232 acres (20%)
       identified as unbuildable for a net remaining inventory of 1,225 acres (or just 20% of the
       Hillsboro’s land area designated for employment use).
   •   Out of more than 6,210 acres of gross employment designated land area, more than
       2,456 acres (or 40% of the total) consist of tax parcels that are fully or partially vacant
       with potential for some amounts of added employment development (before
       environmental, infrastructure and other set-asides are taken into consideration.
   •   Not shown by the chart on the previous page but indicated by the detailed inventory
       database (provided with Appendix E) is that an estimated 128 parcels are noted as
       partially vacant. Taken together, these partially vacant properties account for an
       estimated 1,203 acres. Of this amount, 398 acres are viewed as potentially developable
       with 805 acres unbuildable. Overall average parcel size is about 9.4 acres for these
       parcels that are developed but with potentially vacant area.
   •   A total of 361 vacant land parcels comprise 1,253 acres for an average parcel size of just
       3.5 acres. Approximately 826 acres are estimated as net buildable with 427 acres
       classified as unbuildable. In effect, while Hillsboro’s vacant inventory is comprised of
       relatively small parcels, a higher proportion of this vacant lot inventory is assumed to be
       ultimately developable than with remaining vacant portions of partially vacant sites.
   •   Because industrial (IND) designated lands account for over 90% of the vacant inventory
       (with COM and MUR parcels the remainder), detailed breakouts by zoning class are not
       provided for each acreage size class. However, it is noted that IND lands identified as
       suitable for future employment use average about eight acres per remaining land
       parcels for which full or partial development potential is noted as compared with only
       1.2-1.6 acres per lot for the average commercial and mixed uses sites, respectively.
   •   Of final note is that properties situated in the North Hillsboro area – both in and outside
       the city limits – are associated with above average size lots for vacant and partially
       vacant properties. Jackson East properties average about 11 acres per vacant and
       partially vacant tax lot with development potential. This is also the case for properties
       designated for industrial sanctuary (I-S) use. The average lot size for industrial park (I-P)
       designated property is about 7 acres per parcel with development potential.

50-YEAR OUTLOOK
While focused on 5- and 20-year forecast scenarios, this EOA also addresses the longer-term
horizon of the next 50 years. This is significant for Hillsboro from two perspectives:

   •   Assuring that there will be adequate economic opportunity not just for the current
       generation but for the next – by planning now for future reserves
   •   Also the opportunity to be better prepared if job growth and land needs prove to be
       greater than expected and planned for within a 20-year Comprehensive Plan time frame

50-Year Employment Framework
The features of three forecast scenarios differ more substantially when extrapolated beyond
20-years to a 50-year time horizon. These implications are compared in summary fashion by the
chart on the following page. Primary considerations addressed with this comparison are:

   •   Ratio of jobs in the forecast period (20 or 50 years) to 2020 base year employment
   •   Key technology shifts of significance to Hillsboro employers
   •   Land supply (assumed for initial discussion to be essentially the same in all scenarios)
   •   Land need (with 20-year as previously estimated and 50-year as rough approximations)
   •   Gap strategies (or how shortages in land supply might most reasonably be addressed)

Summary Comparison
From a quantitative perspective, observations from this review are summarized as follows:

   •   With the Scenario A Straight-Line forecast, employment in Hillsboro could be 44%
       greater by 2040 than in 2020. Extending this scenario forward to 50 years, employment
       in Hillsboro by 2070 would be double that of 2020.
   •   With a Scenario B Exponential job growth forecast, employment in Hillsboro could
       double by 2040. If this compounded growth rate of 3.6% per year is extrapolated out to
       50 years, Hillsboro job base in 2070 could be as much as six times more than in 2020.
   •   With a Scenario C Hybrid and targeted job growth projection, Hillsboro employment
       could be 73% greater by 2040 than at the start of the forecast period. By 2070,
       employment would be nearly four times current conditions.

From a qualitative perspective, technological change may facilitate the most profound effects
across Hillsboro’s economic landscape – in 20 years and yet more so over 50 years. How
Hillsboro and the metro area address the gap between land need and supply will affect whether
Hillsboro asserts a stronger position on the U.S. and global stage – or just holds its own.

                    City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis ♦ Page 69
EOA IMPLICATIONS & OPTIONS
The juxtaposition of future employment growth with anticipated land capacity provides the
quantitative underpinnings for Hillsboro’s updated Economic Opportunities Analysis. Two
overall implications for the community’s economic future are of most significance.

First and foremost, this EOA clearly indicates that Hillsboro’s current inventory of employment
lands (including potential growth areas) will not come close to accommodating a continuation
of strong local employment growth over the next 20 years. There is a pronounced shortfall of
employment land with even with a base case Scenario A forecast. The shortfall further
intensifies with Scenario B or C outcomes.

Second, bringing Hillsboro’s land availability and needs into alignment may require substantial
adjustments on multiple fronts – likely involving revisions to forecast outcomes, BLI
adjustments and/or supportive state and regional land use policy.

Potential mitigation options for consideration to address the gap between employment land
demand and supply include any or some combination of the following:

   •   Reduce the EOA employment forecast to match current BLI capacity. If this is to be the
       primary option, it is clear that the high growth Scenario B forecast would need to be
       discarded. Even the more conservative Scenario A jobs forecast would need to be
       reduced by about 45% – assuming a pro-rata cut across all economic sectors.
   •   Focus EOA forecast reductions on the most land extensive sectors. This likely would
       mean that the most significant cuts would be made to allocations for lower employment
       density data center, warehouse and flex/business park uses.
   •   Adjust employment to land need conversion factors with a more urban profile. One
       option could be to increase building space utilization (with fewer square feet per
       employee) and/or floor area ratios (FARs) for more intensive land utilization in the past.
       This might be done by targeting higher density uses – both generally and within each
       primary employment sector or industry cluster. Also possible would be to eliminate the
       market vacancy factor which is not explicitly included in some EOA analyses.
   •   Increase the planned BLI supply, especially for growth areas around Hillsboro. While
       the prime focus might be on increasing gross employment acreage, options might also
       be considered for addressing environmental constraint and ROW patterns to minimize
       reductions from gross to net acreage amounts. Of added potential importance might be
       consideration of actions to encourage more rapid conversion of land being held for
       future expansion – as shown feasible without impairing corporate user strategic options.
   •   Pursue Metro region and statewide recognition of Hillsboro’s strategic significance to
       long-term competitiveness and high wage jobs as integral to long-term economic
       vitality. With respect to high technology clusters (especially semiconductors), reduced
       competitiveness of a Hillsboro location likely will not be readily or fully offset at other
       locations regionally or statewide. Any loss to Hillsboro can reasonably be expected to be
       only partially offset elsewhere in Oregon – with resulting statewide economic impact.

                   City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis ♦ Page 70
V. IMPLEMENTATION POLICIES
The final chapter of this Hillsboro EOA update draws from the quantitative and qualitative
analyses of Chapters I-IV to outline a strategic direction for policies that can serve to implement
community economic development objectives for the City of Hillsboro. As stipulated by OAR
660-009-0020, these policies are to provide a statement of community development objectives,
commitment to provide a competitive short-term supply of land for industrial and other
employment uses, and a commitment to provide adequate sites and facilities.

This Chapter V discussion begins with a brief review of Hillsboro’s economic development-
related objectives and policies. This is followed by discussion of key drivers of economic change,
recommended implementation policies and measures with anticipated updating of
Comprehensive Plan goals and policies. An expanded version of this Chapter V discussion is
provided by EOA Appendix D.

CURRENT FRAMEWORK FOR HILLSBORO ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT
The current status of City policy related to economic development appears to be covered
primarily from three documents – the 2017 EOA, the most recent adopted Hillsboro
Comprehensive Plan (dated November 21, 2017 and effective as of January 2, 2018), and the
2020-prepared Hillsboro 2035 Community Plan.

2017 EOA
The 2017 EOA does not include a direct statement of community economic development
objectives as stipulated by OAR 660-009-0020 but does contain a series of recommendations
organized around three topics – capacity, business environment and recruitment/retention.
The 2017 EOA also provided a “summary list of implementation measures to encourage
effective utilization of the City’s employment capacity.”

2018 Hillsboro Comprehensive Plan
Chapter 11 of the Hillsboro Comprehensive Plan addresses “Building Economy & Infrastructure”
including five goals, each of which is supported by more specific and detailed policy measures.
The adopted five goals read as follows:

   •   Goal 1 – Competitive Advantage: Diversify and expand the economy to give Hillsboro,
       the region, and the state a competitive advantage.
   •   Goal 2 – Facilities, Utilities & Services: Catalyze economic development through high-
       quality public facilities, utilities and services.
   •   Goal 3 – Land Supply: Manage land supply to meet short and long-term economic
       development needs of Hillsboro, the region, and the state.
   •   Goal 4 – Equity: Promote economic development opportunities for individuals and small
       and emerging businesses to ensure equitable access to resources.


                    City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis ♦ Page 71
   •   Goal 5 – Livability: Develop and sustain a vibrant City to support economic
       development.

Hillsboro 2035 Community Plan
Building on the success of the original award-winning Hillsboro 2020 Vision and Action Plan, in
2020 the City completed an updated Hillsboro 2035 Community Plan as representing “a shared
vision for a sustainable future.”

As noted in the introduction to this EOA, Economy and Infrastructure comprises the first of five
2035 focus areas for 2035 accompanied by a goal statement representing continued high
aspirations:

       Hillsboro’s world-class economy, advanced technical training, and innovative, business-
       friendly culture attracts investment and supports businesses of all sizes. State of the art
       infrastructure systems including communications, roads, transit, and water supply are in
       place and continually updated to accommodate the city’s growth and evolution.
       Hillsboro is a vibrant, regional destination for arts, recreation, cuisine, and
       entertainment.

Five supportive initiatives and actions are further detailed as part of the updated Community
Plan:

   •   Initiative 1: Promote Hillsboro’s business-friendly culture and proactive workforce
       development initiatives.
   •   Initiative 2: Encourage and support the growth of emerging industries, small business,
       and the spirit of entrepreneurship.
   •   Initiative 3: Expand shopping, entertainment, and dining destinations.
   •   Initiative 4: Continue efforts to develop a vibrant, mixed-use downtown as a unique
       attraction.
   •   Initiative 5: Implement efforts to ease congestion in and around Hillsboro.

This 2021 EOA aims to both reinforce adopted City-wide planning priorities and identify new
initiatives as appropriate to facilitate economic recovery and resilience for Hillsboro and the
metro region going forward.




                    City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis ♦ Page 72
KEY DRIVERS OF ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT CHANGE
This EOA update reflects key drivers of economic development changes globally that have
emerged since the 2017 EOA:

   •   The COVID pandemic and economic downturn which have accelerated temporary and
       likely lasting changes to work and shop from home at the expense of brick-and-mortar
       commercial office and retail space – but also creating demand for upsized housing and
       new innovative live-work options
   •   Resurgence of industrial space demand due to e-commerce distribution, accelerated
       technological change, added data center requirements, and re-shoring of traditional
       manufacturing
   •   Changing competitive advantage of tech leadership particularly with respect to
       semiconductors, to the potential disadvantage of American firms including Intel as
       Oregon’s largest private employer if not addressed both regionally and nationally
   •   Federal and state government commitment to a reinvigorated domestic tech and
       semiconductor industry exemplified by congressional approval of the CHIPS and Science
       Act of 2022 coupled with parallel August 2022 findings and recommendations of the
       Oregon Semiconductor Competitiveness Task Force.

Hillsboro has great opportunity to capitalize on these emerging trends – increasingly as
Oregon’s economic engine – as a key source of new wealth generated by traded sector
businesses. However, securing and building on the community’s comparative and competitive
advantages likely depends, in large part, on further reinforcing Hillsboro’s core semiconductor
technology manufacturing prowess. This will require larger shovel-ready campus sites suitable
for major corporate investment than are now available as part of the Hillsboro’s buildable lands
inventory.

There is also new downside risk, dependent on the changing fortunes and continued industry
leadership of the community’s major employer. And on local and regional capacity to better
leverage the next waves of tech-forward investment. These considerations serve as a backdrop
to implementation policies outlined with this EOA update.

Implementation policies are organized to cover topics stipulated by OAR 660-009-0020 to
reflect key issues and objectives. Topics covered are employment land use, transportation and
utility infrastructure, target and supporting industry clusters, economic development
incentives, workforce readiness, and partnership opportunity.

A full summary listing of recommended implementation policies and measures is provided by
the chart on the following two pages. This is followed by more detailed discussion of
