Employment Land Use
Following the articulation of community economic development objectives, the first policies
identified by OAR 660-009 are to provide an adequate employment land inventory with priority
emphasis on short term supply defined as “suitable land that is ready for construction within
one year of an application.”

Hybrid Scenario Recommended for Starters. Based on national and regional recovery
experience from the pandemic and related economic downturn, the Scenario C Hybrid Growth
forecast option is viewed as providing the best opportunity for short- as well as long-term
economic resilience. In addition to playing to Hillsboro’s demonstrated competitive advantages,
this scenario enhances regional and state-wide competitiveness for high wage employment
growth.

The scenario takes into account:

   •   Continued concentration in semiconductor/chip and electronics manufacturing
       addressing global supply chain issues with emphasis on domestic re-shoring and
       national defense considerations together with on-going research and commercialization
       as with artificial intelligence and electronic vehicles.
   •   Further expansion of bio-tech which pairs well with the west coast data center hub that
       Hillsboro has become along with future investments by firms such as Rosch/Genentech.

This strategic focus supports a broader industry cluster with support construction readiness,
manufacturing, increasing wholesale and distribution functions, information and professional
services. Further detail as to prospective industry opportunities is provided by Section III
discussion of Community Economic Potential.

Options for Achieving Scenario C Land Needs. Attention also is needed to assure
adequacy of total land supply as determined to be “adequate to accommodate industrial and

                   City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis ♦ Page 75
other employment uses for a 20-year planning period.” Cities are to provide at least 25% of the
total land supply within their UGB as short-term supply – albeit with exceptions noted for
jurisdictions unable to meet this target. 10

With both the prior 2017 and the current 2021 EOAs, the clear indication is that Hillsboro does
not have adequate employment land capacity to accommodate either short-term (5-year) or
long-term (20-year) employment growth. Several options have been outlined with this EOA –
together with identification of associated advantages and disadvantages – as potential means
to better reconcile employment land demand and supply:

   •   Reduce the EOA employment forecast to match current BLI capacity – essentially
       discarding Scenarios B/C and reducing the Scenario A jobs forecast by about 45%. This
       option may avoid the need to expand Hillsboro’s UGB and future annexations of land for
       industrial development – but at the expense of foregoing significant high-wage job
       potential for Hillsboro, the metro region and state in the years ahead.
   •   Focus EOA forecast reductions on the most land extensive sectors – likely resulting in
       reduced allocations for lower job density uses as for data centers, warehouse and some
       flex/business park uses. This option may reduce but not necessarily eliminate the
       impetus for added land outside of Hillsboro’s current city boundaries even from higher
       density major potential employers. Lack of property inventory for some land-extensive
       supply-chain uses may also dampen the appeal of Hillsboro for major tech employers.
   •   Adjust employment to land need conversion factors toward a more urban profile –
       emphasizing increased building FAR and job densities together with site redevelopment.
       This option is associated with advantages and disadvantages similar to those with
       focused on discouraging land extensive sectors (as noted above). Also possible would be
       to eliminate the market vacancy factor which is not explicitly included in some EOA
       analyses.
   •   Increase the planned BLI supply, especially for growth areas around Hillsboro – most
       notably with further annexation and urban service provision but also via mitigation
       measures to increase net to gross acreage use ratios – as a significant portion of the
       vacant and partially vacant employment land inventory is categorized as undevelopable
       due, in part, to wetland and other environmental constraints. This approach to
       increasing in-city land supply might be accomplished, for example, with off-site
       mitigation but would depend on significant and regional planning and regulatory review
       and approvals.
   •   Pursue Metro region and statewide recognition of Hillsboro’s strategic significance –
       for long-term competitiveness and high wage jobs as integral to long-term economic
       vitality, both metro and state-wide. Of the options considered, this is perhaps the most
       pivotal to ensuring the continued competitiveness of Hillsboro as Oregon’s center of
       high-tech investment but depends on broad recognition of current and prospective
       benefits for sustained community and economic vitality regionally and statewide.




                   City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis ♦ Page 76
As a result of the pandemic and changing work patterns, yet another option might be
considered – allocating more of employment growth (on an FTE equivalent basis) away from
work and more to home sites. There are two potential downsides with this option: a) no
sustained post-pandemic experience as yet to reliably ascertain the extent of a permanent shift
to work from home (primarily affecting office workers); and b) uncertainty as to whether and
how much space needs in traditional single use employment settings may change per on-site
employee (either decreasing or possibly increasing as from robotization and improved supply
change management), especially for manufacturing and warehouse/distribution functions.

Implementation Measures. The following measures are recommended for consideration:

   •   As a minimum measure, adopt a 20-year jobs and land use forecast similar to Scenario
       C Hybrid Growth. This scenario best serves Hillsboro existing and prospective
       competitive advantages for sectors targeted to clustered business growth opportunities.
   •   Annex and serve added employment land as needed to meet at least the 5-year
       Scenario A Straight-Line short-term supply requirement. While it is possible that a slow
       or delayed economic recovery may dampen demand near-term, this is less likely for
       industrial than commercial use. Having the full complement of shovel-ready site supply
       in place also better positions Hillsboro and the region from the mutual and reinforcing
       perspectives of economic recovery and resilience.
   •   Utilize the Scenario B forecast as an initial means to begin determination of longer-
       term needs for added industrial reserves and land capacity. This will help set the stage
       for 20-50 year UGB expansions – adjusted as needed to reflect actual experience with
       economic recovery and sustained economic vitality going forward.
   •   Provide more opportunity to accommodate both exclusive industrial zones and mixed-
       use development. For large industrial users, it can be important to provide a clear
       separation or buffer from residential development and other non-industrial uses that
       would pose an unreasonable risk to public health or safety. For smaller scale uses as
       with creative and support service firms together with potential reduction in commercial
       space demand, horizontal rather than vertical mixed-use may become the more
       pronounced market opportunity for closely linked live-work-recreate communities – so
       long as total employment capacity is maintained at or above current forecast levels.
       Also noted is that much of the demand for office as a component of commercial
       demand can be met with industrially zoned sites.
   •   Provide opportunity for large acreage, major employer campuses of up to 600+ acres
       consistent with national trends but not readily available regionally in Oregon. This is of
       pivotal importance nationally for semi-conductor and related tech employers,
       exemplified by Intel’s 2021 announced plans for two new fabrication plants in Chandler,
       Arizona on an approximately 700-acres “mega-factory” site, and by subsequent
       announcement for a nearly 1,000-acres multi-phase development in Ohio.
   •   Orient state and local incentive measures to support increased employment land
       utilization and redevelopment together with attraction and retention of target
       industries. This should include accounting for the potential of some albeit as yet

                   City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis ♦ Page 77
       uncertain permanent shift to work at home, especially for office workers – as well as for
       potential reduction in commercial brick-and-mortar commercial space needs, at least
       near-term. Also involved may be short- and long-term incentives for increased efficiency
       of employment land use including reduction of at-grade parking footprints when shown
       to be feasible.

While retention of Hillsboro’s leading tech manufacturing edge is not guaranteed, success will
be dependent on a more expansive land base than is currently available. Initial suggestions as
to how these implementation measures might be incorporated into Comprehensive Plan goals
and economic development policies are summarized with the concluding section to this EOA
Chapter and further detailed with Technical Appendix D.

Transportation & Utility Infrastructure
Transportation and utility infrastructure is critical to assuring development readiness for
industrial and other employment sites. DLCD Division 9 guidance calls for “policies, through
public facilities planning and transportation system planning, to provide necessary public
facilities and transportation facilities for the planning area.”

Transportation and utility Infrastructure of importance to Hillsboro-based business is provided
both by public and private entities. Compared to other locales regionally and nationally,
Hillsboro is better positioned competitively with respect to utility than transportation
infrastructure – though that may be changing in the wake of the COVID pandemic and potential
temporary or longer-term shift to more work from home.

Key implementation measure recommendations for consideration would be to:

   •   Target added local transport and utility infrastructure in conjunction with annexation
       to meet short-term employment land supply forecasts. Ideally, infrastructure should be
       provided in a phased manner ahead of or coterminous with prospective development,
       creating ready-to-build sites.
   •   Provide explicit policy support for a regional transportation system that effectively
       supports the movement of raw materials, manufactured goods and workforce to and
       through Hillsboro’s employment areas. This is a topic of growing significance not only
       regionally but more extensively due to supply chain and associated workforce issues
       impeding sustained economic recovery both nationally and globally.
   •   Increase policy emphasis on north-south access and reduction of work-force
       commutes (to maximize Hillsboro work-force commute-shed accessibility). Increasing
       regional congestion makes it more challenging for Hillsboro to draw substantial
       workforce from across the metro area; more of the local workforce is shifting to
       residence locations in Hillsboro or in communities to the north and south (as further
       documented with Appendix A to this EOA).
   •   Provide explicit policy support to further strengthen Hillsboro’s competitive
       advantage as a Pacific Northwest data hub for low latency, data intensive firms


                   City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis ♦ Page 78
       offering high “pull-through” potential. Building on Hillsboro’s existing position as a
       major west coast data hub, greater value add can be created by using data center
       investments to leverage higher employment uses increasingly reliant on data hub
       proximity especially with transition to data intensive research and applications as for AI,
       autonomous and EV vehicles.

Target & Supporting Industry Clusters
DLCD Division 9 guidance indicates that: “Plans may include policies to maintain existing
categories or levels of industrial and other employment uses including maintaining downtowns
or central business districts.” Unlike many jurisdictions across the state, Hillsboro’s
Comprehensive Plan clearly emphasizes the importance of traded-sector and associated target
industry retention, expansion and recruitment.

Continued prioritization of traded sector investment is warranted as a primary means for local
economic prosperity and wealth creation. However, the pandemic has disproportionately and
adversely affected local service businesses important to support the community’s traded sector
industry clusters. This suggests a bifurcated policy approach going forward – both for traded
sector industry and for supporting industry clusters.

Recommended with this EOA are four implementation policies – two focused on Hillsboro’s
traded sectors and two related to supporting business activities and non-traded sectors:

   •   Periodically modify and update Hillsboro’s current target industry listing to reflect and
       serve new or emerging traded sector industry opportunities in the years ahead. This
       will yield greater opportunity and flexibility to respond to changing market conditions
       together with local needs and opportunities beyond what is currently most readily
       foreseen. Along with Hillsboro, Metro and state economic development organizations
       are showing increased flexibility in adjusting target industry and business clustering
       priorities as the need arises – a practice that Hillsboro can also apply based on
       state/regional priorities balanced by Hillsboro’s own distinctive competitive attributes.
   •   Retain existing businesses including those at risk of displacement from pandemic
       and/or economic downturn. The goal is for a more resilient service sector economy,
       especially for retail, lodging and dining businesses that were disproportionately
       disadvantaged with the pandemic-related economic downturn.
   •   Add policy language to expand business opportunities for minority- and women-
       owned businesses. This can occur with programs that encourage small business
       investment and longer-term improvement of supplier linkages with tech employers.
   •   Add a policy priority for community amenities that support traded sector business
       investment, talent recruitment/retention and high wage job potential. This is of
       special importance for attracting and retaining younger workforce to Hillsboro as more
       of a full-service live-work-recreate community.




                   City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis ♦ Page 79
Workforce Readiness
While not explicitly called out by DLCD Division 9 administrative rules, workforce readiness is
clearly indicated as an economic development resource to be addressed in conjunction with
plan policies that may “emphasize the expansion of and increased productivity from existing
industries and firms as a means to facilitate local economic development.”

Workforce availability and skills (or readiness) is an issue of growing concern as documented by
stakeholders with a range of local industries. Key issues include continuing retirement of the
large baby boomer generation, workforce disruption by the pandemic (particularly as relates to
child-care), lack of a nationally recognized metro area research university, and needed skills
training for entry-level manufacturing workers.

Frequent mention with stakeholder interviews is made of the importance of partnering with
existing area institutions as with PCC, OHSU, PSU, OSU and Pacific University for apprenticeship
and technical training – also internships. In addition to these higher education resources, the
City of Hillsboro works with a range of local as well as state-level resource providers.

Due to pandemic related business curtailments coupled with other economic fallout, the
workers most adversely affected have been those in lower wage sectors including retail,
hospitality and dining. These sectors also often have higher proportions of women and
minorities – as employees and/or small business owners.

Suggested implementation measures are to:

   •   Include retraining emphasis for employees displaced in times of economic disruption
       and transition. Getting workers up to speed with rapidly changing work force skills will
       persist as a higher priority with continued economic recovery and to maintain
       Hillsboro’s long term competitive position for tech-adaptive existing and new
       employers.
   •   Add policy language to expand employment opportunities for under-represented
       members of the community including racial/ethnic minority groups, women and
       veterans. Attention to under-represented populations better addresses not only
       individual and community vitality objectives but also positions Hillsboro for greater
       diversity of talent going forward.
   •   Coordinate with Washington County to evaluate the most effective Workforce Board
       arrangements in support of community workforce needs. This could include
       partnership initiatives often utilizing existing resources as with the Hillsboro Advanced
       Manufacturing Work Group.
   •   Support efforts to create new workforce development programs meeting the needs of
       target and emerging industries. This suggests placing greater priority on reducing the
       time lag between industry-identified needs and workforce training delivery.
   •   Pursue designation as a Center of Innovation Excellence and Regional Technology Hub
       to support Hillsboro’s leadership role in research and development with expanded


                    City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis ♦ Page 80
       benefits to the community. Hillsboro provides a unique opportunity to advance a key
       strategic objective of Oregon’s 10-Year Innovation Plan completed in 2021 to “support
       centers of innovation excellence that leverage Oregon’s existing traded sector strengths
       and emerging market opportunities.”

Economic Development Incentives
DLCD Division 9 guidance addresses plan policies that “include additional approaches” in
support of economic development that cover but are not limited to such mechanisms as tax
incentives and disincentives, preferential tax assessments, and property acquisition techniques.
Also strongly encouraged are brownfield redevelopment strategies.

With an active in-house economic development department, the City of Hillsboro offers a
variety of state and local incentive programs aimed to reduce a firm’s cost of doing business.
Some of the most prominent are noted as including enterprise zones, a strategic investment
program, loan/guarantees/bonding program, vertical housing development zone, strategic
reserve fund, business expansion program, opportunity zones, storefront improvement grants,
and tenant improvement programs. 11

Bottom-line, targeted economic development incentives are recognized as having played an
important role in attracting industrial investment to Hillsboro. Some industry and economic
development stakeholders suggest that incentives be more narrowly targeted in the years
ahead – to businesses that can demonstrate some combination of strong employment, tax
revenue, and/or supplemental business leveraging benefits.

Suggested with this EOA is added policy language regarding implementation measures to:

   •   Provide a more prominent position for incentive mechanisms as integral to supporting
       or facilitating achievement of economic goals and policies. This can occur with active
       utilization of federal, state and regional programs together with publicized Hillsboro-
       specific economic development incentives.
   •   More specifically include incentives as a means to leverage increased density with
       uses that currently are associated with relatively low job per acre counts. Assumed is a
       long-term shift to more urbanized densities, transition from drive-alone commuting,
       potential for reduced at-grade parking footprint, and impetus for recycling of obsolete
       or redundant facilities – especially as current or prospective feasibility is demonstrated.
   •   Advance incentives focused on land readiness together with land aggregation as
       needed for industrial expansion and recruitment. A particular focus is on assuring
       capacity to serve expansion and attraction of major high-wage employers requiring
       large acreage sites.

Partnership Opportunities
This final topic is aimed to cover public-private partnerships and intergovernmental frameworks
as objectives to be addressed in local jurisdiction EOAs. Public-private and intergovernmental


                   City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis ♦ Page 81
partnerships have long been part of Hillsboro’s civic and economic development DNA. The best
opportunities going forward are to maintain and build on the partnerships already in place,
adapted to new challenges that have emerged with the pandemic and attendant economic
dislocation -- extending beyond to longer term recovery and resilience.

As implementation measures, two specific policy recommendations are noted to:

   •   Include urban renewal as a potential economic development funding tool within
       designated renewal districts. As has been demonstrated region-wide, broader
       application can extend use of this well-tested public/private investment tool beyond
       urban placemaking to also assist projects offering job-creating high wage employment.
   •   Add policy language to more explicitly encourage Metro and state-wide support for
       Hillsboro tech-focused economic development as an economic engine of significance
       and benefit regionally and statewide. Cited last but not least, obtaining support for
       tech-led Hillsboro investment may represent an increasingly pivotal commitment to
       raising the bar for economic vitality locally, regionally, and state-wide.
       Hillsboro’s economic significance regionally and statewide might be further documented
       as with economic impact analysis. Analysis of direct and indirect effects could serve to
       demonstrate the interconnectedness of the metro and state economy and the roles that
       Hillsboro’s leading edge tech industries play – not only for key traded sector industries
       but also with respect to region-wide housing location, transportation planning and
       related infrastructure investments.
       More recently, the impetus for statewide support for expanded semiconductor
       manufacturing is highlighted by recommendations of the Oregon Semiconductor
       Competitiveness Task Force in conjunction with federally authorized CHIPS and Science
       Act of 2022.

UPDATING COMPREHENSIVE PLAN GOALS & POLICIES
The approach taken with this 2021 Economic Opportunities Analysis EOA is to assure that
updated economic development goals and objectives are integrated into the framework of the
existing Comprehensive Plan rather than as a separate stand-alone objectives/policies
statement. Also assumed is an approach that may well involve refinement of the existing
Comprehensive Plan goal/policy framework, rather than a wholesale re-work.

Appendix D to this EOA provides more detail as to how recommended implementation
measures might be integrated into a refined, economically centered set of Comprehensive Plan
goals and policies together with vision-based Community Plan priority initiatives. Specific
revisions to text language are not provided at this time but are appropriate for consideration as
next steps with EOA adoption.

        City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis – Technical Appendices
APPENDIX A.
EMPLOYMENT TRENDS & OUTLOOK
This appendix provides background data and research utilized with the Chapter II EOA
discussion of employment trends and outlook. Topics covered by this appendix include
background and approach, employment trends and forecast scenarios, U.S. employment trends
and forecast, economic resilience with pandemic recovery, work commute considerations and a
detailed employment sector review .

BACKGROUND & APPROACH
In cooperation with the Oregon Employment Department (OED) for analysis conducted at the
outset of this EOA in 2019 and subsequently augmented by OED, it has been possible to
assemble consistent employment data over several years for the City of Hillsboro in comparison
to trends experienced for the 7-county Portland metro region. This appendix reviews the trend
data evaluated together with Metro’s regional forecast and resulting EOA implications.

Employment Definitions
Employment can be defined in a variety of ways, depending on the purpose of the data and
methodology for data compilation. Consequently, it is useful to briefly describe key
components of the data sources utilized – including limitations and adjustments made for this
2021 EOA update. Some of the factors noted may affect EOA results and so are important to
address in the event questions arise with EOA review. Of particular importance are the
following notes:

   •   Primarily reliance for trend data evaluated both for the City of Hillsboro and the 7-
       county Portland-Vancouver-Hillsboro metropolitan statistical area (MSA) is placed on
       Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW) data as compiled by the Oregon
       Employment Department (OED). This dataset is for jobs covered by unemployment
       insurance and so excludes some workers such as sole proprietors – most notably in the
       real estate sector. However, QCEW data is also consistent with monthly and annual
       results reported for the MSA by the U. S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS). At the time
       data was initially compiled in 2019, annual BLS data was readily available for specified
       years over the 2001-18 period.
   •   OED economist Christian Kaylor compiled data for the City of Hillsboro for 2007, 2010,
       2017 and 2018. For reasons described below, this analysis focuses on the 2007 and
       2018 datasets – both for Hillsboro and the Portland metro region.
   •   In compiling data specific to Hillsboro, OED has taken steps to assure that
       confidentiality provisions were not violated. This has necessitated a need to combine
       some employment categories. For direct apples-to-apples comparisons, the same
       combinations are reported for Hillsboro and the metro area (whenever possible).


         City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis – Technical Appendices ♦ Page 1
   •   As the Portland MSA straddles two states, employment data is compiled separately for
       the five counties of the Oregon side (Washington, Multnomah, Clackamas, Yamhill and
       Columbia) and from the two counties of the Washington side (Clark and Skamania). E. D.
       Hovee has combined these employment estimates, by sector, into a single 7-county
       dataset. Combined totals provided with this aggregation process match BLS
       employment estimates for the full 7-county metro region.
   •   OED/QCEW data is reported for the five Oregon counties of the MSA in two ways:
       a) with a composite total for all governmental employment; and b) with a narrower
       definition of NAICS 92 as being limited to public administration jobs only. The single
       biggest difference between the two methods is found in the allocation of education
       employees. As of 2018, 44% of all governmental workers were employed in education
       with another 7-8% in health care and social assistance. Smaller proportions are allocated
       to construction, transportation/warehousing, administrative, arts/entertainment/
       recreation and other service sectors.
   •   OED compiled Hillsboro data with this narrower NAICS 92 definition limited to Public
       Administration and with other governmental employees allocated to their actual
       employment sector. The two MSA counties of Washington state – Clark and Skamania –
       use the Governmental Sector figures only, so governmental employees are allocated to
       other sectors using the ratios applicable for the five counties of the Oregon side of the
       region. Metro also uses a governmental sector total only (albeit with a yet different
       dataset) – so similar adjustments have been made as a means to compare Hillsboro with
       metro-wide forecast results.
   •   For its regional forecasting process, Metro has relied on non-agricultural wage and
       salary employment information rather than QCEW datasets. This dataset is tracked by
       BLS and excludes some government workers, private households, proprietors and non-
       profit employees – based on both a monthly household and business establishment
       survey. There are some resulting differences in historical employment estimates. For
       example, as of 2010, the Metro non-ag estimate of 7-county age and salary jobs was
       979,140. This is 1.8% above the 961,710 covered jobs number indicated with QCEW
       data. Adjustments for these differences are made in this EOA with the comparison of
       updated Hillsboro forecast results with those of the prior 2017 Hillsboro EOA.
   •   Since the time of initial December 2021 EOA report preparation, OED has provided
       updated datasets for Hillsboro covering the 2003-20 period (albeit with 2021
       employment data not yet available). This data was provided to address DLCD questions
       regarding linear versus exponential employment change as described with the
       Employment Sector Review portion of this Appendix A. For purposes of employment
       forecasting, this EOA continues to rely on 2007-18 data as a primary source for the most
       recent economic cycle based on data as initially provided by OED in 2019. Future EOA
       updates may be of value as additional post-pandemic jobs data becomes available.

With this background methodological information in hand, this review now proceeds to
consider key components of the employment analysis and findings for Hillsboro, the metro
region and this EOA report.

         City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis – Technical Appendices ♦ Page 2
Forecast Approach
As a starting point for analysis, employment trends were reviewed for the period 2007-18,
starting with the onset of the Great Recession of 2007-09, with subsequent recovery through
2018, just ahead of local and regional job growth slowing in 2019, then followed by the onset of
the COVID-19 pandemic and economic downturn in 2020.

As of 2018, Hillsboro had a covered employment count of approximately 88,980 jobs. Hillsboro
accounts for 6.8% of the region’s QCEW employment. By comparison, with a population of
101,920 as of 2018, Hillsboro represents for 4.1% of the metro area’s population of nearly 2.5
million. From 2007-18, employment in Hillsboro increased by nearly 30%, almost double the
approximately 15% increase in regional-wide employment.

Recognizing that Hillsboro’s economy has been driven in large part by computer/electronics
traded sector activity which is dependent on market forces external to the Portland MSA, the
initial scenarios considered with this EOA have been to forecast the sector-by-sector growth
rates of the current economic cycle forward over the EOA time frame of 2020-40. Then
compare this growth with what has been projected for the region as a first test to assess
reasonableness of any Hillsboro forecast scenario.

Two scenarios for application of this extrapolation approach were initially prepared – involving
a comparison of straight-line with annually compounded growth rates. Both are reported in
QCEW covered employment terms, then also adjusted to provide for a meaningful apples-to-
applies comparison with the Metro-prepared regional non-agricultural employment forecast.
Subsequent to review of these initial scenarios, a third hybrid scenario was then prepared.

These two initial scenarios formulated as potentially plausible outcomes for future employment
growth are focused on the 20- year 2020-2040 time frame. The forecast scenarios represent
two contrasting perspectives on the extrapolation of past trends as a basis for future job
growth. The two initial contrasting forecast approaches considered are specified as follows:

   •   Scenario A Straight-Line Growth – assumes that employment for each of up to 18
       NAICS-based sectors will continue to increase (or decline) by the same average number
       of jobs gained or lost per year from 2007-18. The total 20-year job change equals the
       sum of the individual sectoral changes.
   •   Scenario B Exponential Growth – is based on the same 2007-18 experience but
       calculates growth in terms of a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) with each year’s
       new job increment greater than the last as the job base keeps getting larger over time.

As an added note, because 2018 was the last year for which detailed Hillsboro-specific QCEW
data was initially compiled, an estimate was made of potential 2020 conditions as a starting
point for the 20-year comparison. This forecast methodology and application was conducted in
advance of the 2020 pandemic and recession. Consequently, the resulting 20-year projections
assume the eventual recapture of jobs lost in 2020 in addition to the net gains anticipated over
the 2020-40 time horizon.


         City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis – Technical Appendices ♦ Page 3
EMPLOYMENT TRENDS & FORECAST SCENARIOS
The tables on the following pages provide results of this sector-by-sector analysis – separately
for two scenarios initially considered. For each sector, historical data is provided for Hillsboro
QCEW employment as of 2007 and 2018. The next column indicates the average annual change
per year from 2007-18. The next two columns in each table provide 2020 and 2040 forecast
employment estimates, with the last column indicating the numerical change from 2020-40.

The primary difference between the two approaches and resulting data table is with the change
per year column. Scenario A calculates the annual change as the average numerical change in
jobs each year from 2000-18 – a figure which is applied to each of the succeeding forecast
years. In contrast, Scenario B shows the average compound annual growth rate (CAGR)
experienced, a figure then multiplied by the employment in each prior year to arrive at each of
the succeeding years forecast employment. Results of these two initial contrasting scenario
approaches are provided as follows – then by consideration of a third hybrid scenario.

Scenario A – Straight-Line Growth
As noted, this first employment scenario provides a sector-by-sector straight-line extrapolation
of annual growth experienced from 2017-18 forward to 2040. As detailed by the following
chart, this scenario results in a 44% net increase of Hillsboro’s employment from 2020-40,
equating to a 1.8% CAGR over this 20-year period.

With this scenario, employment increases by 36,910 jobs over 20 years, from a projected
84,390 jobs in 2020 to 121,300 jobs by 2040. This equates to over 1,830 jobs added (on
average) in Hillsboro each year from 2018-40.

In terms of numerical increase, with this straight-line methodology health care and social
assistance would increase the most, by an estimated 7,980 jobs over 20 years – followed by
manufacturing at 6,200 added jobs.

Considered in terms of region-wide employment, Hillsboro would increase from just under 7%
of the region’s employment currently to about 8.5% in 2040. Manufacturing would increase
from 20-21% to just under 28% of the sector’s MSA count, information from 10-11% to 15%,
and health care/social assistance from 5-6% to nearly 8% of that sector’s regional job count.

Scenario B – Exponential Growth
Scenario B also is predicated on extrapolation of growth trends as experienced from 2007-18,
but extrapolated forward at compound annual growth rate (CAGR) rather than straight-line
average annual growth rates (AAGR). As detailed by the following chart, with Scenario B,
employment in Hillsboro conceivably could more than double over the next 20 years if sector-
specific compound annual growth rates of the 2007-18 period were to persist to 2040.

From 2007-18, Hillsboro’s employment increased at a CAGR of about 2.4% per year. Going
forward, the rate of employment increase is forecast to increase by 3.5% per year from 2018-40
(or 3.6% annually if calculated from 2020-40). A higher overall job growth rate in the years
ahead occurs as the effect of already large rapidly growing industry sectors outweighs the
lesser effects of smaller and/or slow growth/declining sectors.

With continued growth averaging 6.3% per year, health care and social assistance alone could
add 24,370 jobs over 20 years – with a total count of nearly 35,500 jobs and even exceeding
manufacturing’s total job count by 2040. Wholesale trade has been experiencing 6.7% per year
job growth since 2007. Extrapolated to 2040, this sector could see a net gain of as many as
9,650 jobs over 20 years.

Manufacturing would add an estimated 7,770 jobs – for about 25% more new jobs than with
Scenario A. The manufacturing job gains would be even greater if individual manufacturing
subsectors were to be accelerated independently, then aggregated. Substantial job growth in
the range of 5-7,000 jobs per sector could be experienced for the transportation/warehousing,
information, professional services, administrative, arts/education/recreation, and other
services sectors.

With Scenario B, Hillsboro would increase from about 7% currently to 12% of metro-wide most
likely employment by 2040. Within 20 years, Hillsboro could account for 30% of the
arts/entertainment/recreation, 29% of the manufacturing, 25% of the information, 22% of the
wholesale trade, 16% of the transportation/warehousing, and 15% of the health care/social
assistance jobs metro-wide.

Scenario C – Hybrid Growth
After review of Scenarios A and B and in consultation with City of Hillsboro Planning and
Community Development Departments, a third in-between forecast scenario was added,
predicated on consideration of Hillsboro target industry and associated sectors (or industry
clusters). The net effect of these applications is for an overall employment growth rate (CAGR)
averaging 2.7% per year from 2018-40 (or 2.8% annually from 2020-40).

Recognizing the changing and as-yet uncertain economic trajectory nationally and regionally
going forward, Scenario C involves a sector-by-sector analysis as a basis for determining
whether and to what extent to apply Scenario A or B outcomes to the Scenario C hybrid model.
This is consistent with the detailed and customized approach taken with this EOA that
incorporates qualitative as well as quantitative considerations as potentially consequential for
forecast outcomes.

Quantitative factors primarily reflect extrapolation of observed employment trends with
further sector-by-sector differentiation between straight-line and exponential growth.
Qualitative considerations are as detailed with Appendix B Community Economic Potential
discussion including stakeholder perspectives and policy priorities, for example, as represented
by Hillsboro’s adopted target industry priorities.


         City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis – Technical Appendices ♦ Page 6
This Scenario C Hybrid Growth model occurs via a 4-phase scenario selector or sector toggle
approach described as follows:

          0 – is applied to sectors for which employment decline was experienced from 2007-18.
          Rather than forecasting continued job loss, these sectors are assumed to experience no
          net change (None) in employment going forward to 2040.
          1 – is applied to sectors for which Scenario A straight-line (Linear) results are assumed
          as most applicable to the Scenario C hybrid, comprised of sectors not part of Hillsboro
          cluster industry targets.
          2 – is applied to sectors that are likely to be strongly influenced by exponential growth,
          though not expected to fully experience continued exponential growth going forward.
          These sectors are assigned mid-point (Mid) results by averaging outputs of Scenarios A
          and B.
          3- is applied to sectors that are most expected to experience continued exponential
          (Exp) growth going forward, particularly target industry sectors.

The outputs of this hybrid scenario are as detailed by the chart below.

By way of summary, with this hybrid scenario:

   •   Sectors of construction, manufacturing, transportation/warehousing, information, real
       estate and professional services are forecast for growth at continued exponential (exp)
       or historically observed CAGRs as experienced over the last economic cycle.
   •   Finance/insurance, health care/social assistance, accommodation and food services, and
       other services are assumed to experience results at a mid-point between the CAGR and
       straight-line extrapolation models.
   •   Wholesale, retail, administrative and arts/entertainment/recreation sectors are forecast
       experience linear (straight line) growth consistent with historically observed rates
       calculated on a straight-line basis.
   •   And employment sectors related to management, educational services and public
       administration which experienced net job loss in recent years are forecast to experience
       no further job loss (none) going forward.

Detailed sector-by-sector review of these Scenario C Hybrid Growth determinations is provided
as the last portion of this Appendix A document.

As with Scenario A, this hybrid or targeted job growth scenario would be led by health care with
an added 16,175 jobs over 20 years, followed by manufacturing at an added 7,770 jobs. Strong
job growth (in the range of 5-6,000 added jobs each) would be experienced by the information,
professional services and transportation/warehouse sectors.

These existing and potentially important traded sector activities provide economic multiplier
benefits above what can be expected from local consumer-oriented service functions. This is
because of added income flowing into Hillsboro and the metro region from customers nation-
wide and globally.

With Scenario C, Hillsboro would increase from about 7% to more than 10% of metro-wide
employment by 2040. Hillsboro would account for similar shares of the region’s employment
for sectors including manufacturing, information, and transportation/warehouse sectors as
with Scenario B. Hillsboro would increase from 5-6% to about 11-12% of the region’s
employment in health care and social services.




         City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis – Technical Appendices ♦ Page 8
Comparison to 2017 EOA
Hillsboro’s most recent 2017 EOA provided three alternative employment forecasts scenarios
covering a 20-year time period (from 2015-35):

   •   A safe harbor projection (based on an OED county-level regional forecast) – of an added
       28,906 Hillsboro jobs over 20 years.
   •   A Metro-based Transportation Area Zone (TAZ) forecast – of 34,281 added jobs.
   •   An alternative forecast based on Hillsboro’s then most-recent 5-year growth pattern
       (from 2010-15) – of 40,326 jobs over 20 years (at an average 2.0% growth rate).

As indicated by this summary, the safe harbor methodology resulted in an employment
projection that was well below that of other methodologies considered in 2017. The then
recommended and adopted 2017 approach of an alternative forecast was 40% above the
employment projection associated with the safe harbor forecast approach.

The 2017 EOA concluded that: “while either of the three forecast scenarios is supported by the
best available information and methodologies as required by OAR 660-024-0040(1), the
employment land forecast is based on the alternative employment forecast scenario” of an
added 40,326 jobs in 20 years.

By comparison, the two initial 20-year forecast scenarios as evaluated in this updated 2021 EOA
indicate a possible range of 36,910-87,800 net added covered jobs over the 20-year time period
of 2020-40. If adjustments are made for non-covered workers as was done with the 2017 EOA,
the range of this current 2021 EOA forecast update could be from 44,650-106,870 added jobs
over a new 20-year (2020-40) time horizon.1

The lower Scenario A straight-line forecast associated with this updated 2021 EOA comes
closest to the results of the prior 2017 EOA alternative forecast – albeit with a modified
methodology. The higher Scenario B compound sectoral growth approach yields a result that
potentially is well in excess of what was presented by any of the 2017 EOA alternatives then
considered. The Scenario C hybrid option (selected as a preferred or recommended EOA
scenario) is associated with employment outputs between those of Scenarios A and B.

With the current 2021 update process, an updated safe harbor projection initially was not
prepared. This was because prior results (from the 2017 EOA) came in below other alternatives
considered, not adequately reflecting Hillsboro’s historically observed increasing market share
of employment.

Also noted is that when the updated forecast scenarios (A and B) were initially prepared in
2019, a similarly updated TAZ zone forecast from Metro was not expected to be available in the
time frame anticipated for what was then anticipated to be a 2020 EOA update (subsequently
delayed due to the COVID pandemic).

SAFE HARBOR EMPLOYMENT PROJECTION
In review of the 2021 EOA analysis, staff representatives of the state Department of Land
Conservation and Development (DLCD) requested preparation of an updated safe harbor
projection for comparison with Scenarios A-C of this 2021 EOA. This appendix provides a safe
harbor update consistent with the methodology of the prior 2017 EOA report.

Safe Harbor Background
As background, it is useful to review state guidance regarding safe harbor provisions for
employment-based land use needs analysis. OAR 660-024-0040 states that an employment safe
harbor methodology “may be applied,” predicated on assuming that the current number of jobs
in the urban area will grow at a rate equal to either the county or regional job growth rate. The
OAR does not require a safe harbor projection but rather identifies this as an option to be
considered at local discretion.

As noted, the safe harbor projection prepared with the prior 2017 Hillsboro EOA resulted in an
employment forecast that was well below that of other methodologies considered in 2017. A
similar result is noted with this 2021 EOA update.

As documented by employment data compiled for this EOA update, Hillsboro is accounting for
an increasing share of county- and region-wide employment. Consequently, application of a
safe harbor methodology can be expected to result in an employment forecast that is below
that of other scenarios considered. In effect, the safe harbor option understates Hillsboro’s
actual recent historical employment experience and its continued opportunity over a 20-year
planning horizon.

Safe Harbor Projection
An updated 20-year Safe Harbor forecast is provided by the chart on the following page. As
noted, the approach with this update is similar to what was provided by Johnson Economics
with the 2017 EOA – applying a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) as has been utilized with
the current EOA exponential growth and hybrid growth scenarios.

In 2017, the OED region on which the Safe Harbor projection was made was for Washington
and Multnomah Counties. With more recent OED updates, the region now also includes
Clackamas County as the full tri-county area.

The time period covered by this safe harbor projection is 2020-2040, extrapolated from OED tri-
county projections (and associated CAGRs) for the shorter 10-year period of 2020-30. Baseline
2020 employment estimates represent QCEW job numbers as recently provided by OED.

per year.

This updated safe harbor projection comes in 19% below the current EOA straight-line (Scenario
A) forecast of an added 36,910 jobs (although calculated differently). It is further below the
additions of 87,800 and 61,895 jobs calculated over 20 years with the Scenario B exponential
growth and Scenario C hybrid scenarios, respectively.

Also noted is that the safe harbor projection is predicated on a 2020 starting point which
reflects an actual 2,331 employment reduction from 2019-20 due to the 2020 pandemic-related
recession. No assumption is made for job recovery other than as part of the 2030 and 2040
projections of incremental job increase. By comparison, the current EOA scenarios assume
recovery to normalized conditions plus forecast growth post-2020 consistent with the
methodologies applied for Scenarios A-C.

From 2000-20, employment nation-wide has increased at a compound annual growth rate
(CAGR) averaging 0.7% per year. Over the 2020-40 time period, the growth rate has been
forecast to decline slightly – to a rate of about 0.6% per year.

The most rapid job growth (in percentage terms) has been anticipated for professional
(including technical) services and for administrative sectors, each increasing at a 1.7% annual
growth rate – followed by construction at 1.6%. Modest job losses (of 0.1% per year) have been
forecast in manufacturing, with more rapid losses indicated for the wholesale trade, TWU,
management, education, and other service sectors.

While manufacturing has been anticipated for virtually no net job growth nationwide, there are
some differences between specific manufacturing sectors. Employment in electronics-related
manufacturing has been declining but expected to remain at about current levels over the next
20 years. However, employment across the U.S. in traditional sectors of wood products,
fabricated metals and machinery which were showing job loss have been forecast to experience
modest gains in employment going forward. Food products manufacturing also has been
anticipated to experience somewhat more rapid job gains in the years ahead.

While Metro’s regional forecast reflects many of these national changes, Hillsboro’s recent
employment experience and its future expectations clearly diverge from what is occurring
nationally and regionally. Hillsboro has been experiencing increases in manufacturing
employment – its major economic driver over the last economic cycle. Other industrial sectors –
notably TWU and wholesale trade – are also experiencing stronger growth, albeit on a smaller
base of existing activity to date.

An important caveat is that this national forecast which has served as a basis for current metro
employment forecasting with the Urban Growth Report (UGR) process pre-dates the current
pandemic and economic recession. Very possibly, future forecast revisions may reflect slowed
job growth relative to prior projections, at least to the point of full recovery and return to more
normalized conditions.

Also suggested by business activity through the pandemic has been the strength of industrial
development especially for warehouse-distribution (TWU) functions. How this recovery
potentially plays out for the Portland metro region and Hillsboro is further considered by
discussion in the next section of this Appendix.

In any event, when viewed in terms of community economic potentials, the combination of
these conditions (even when tempered) positions Hillsboro to continue along a high-wage
advanced manufacturing-led path. This includes opportunities for continued growth in what
have been historically small but now more important related sectors, possibly including freight-
intensive TWU and wholesale-distribution functions.

Looking forward, recent events including the COVID pandemic, subsequent supply chain issues,

ECONOMIC RESILIENCE WITH PANDEMIC RECOVERY
In the wake of pandemic and economic recession, this 2021 EOA places new emphasis on
prospects for metro area and Hillsboro economic recovery, also looking to opportunities for
improved resilience in the face of potentially similar unforeseen economic downturns in the
future. To assist in this analysis, data has been compiled to compare month-by-month
employment starting February 2020 (pre-layoffs) and extending to mid-2021 (as economic
recovery has been in progress over multiple subsequent months). Data is provided for the
Portland metro area in comparison with U.S. economic performance.

Information is compiled from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) current employment
survey (CES). Data is illustrated by graphs for all employment, then disaggregated for major
employment sectors, then to also include a more detailed focus on manufacturing sectors.

terms of seasonally adjusted and non-seasonally adjusted jobs – with unadjusted data
indicating more variation depending on time of year. Employment is survey-based as of the 12th
of each month. So, for example, the data indicated for Apr-21 is as of mid-April 2021.

As indicated by the graph, an initial modest employment decline of 16,000 (seasonally

         City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis – Technical Appendices ♦ Page 15
Partial job recovery was experienced in subsequent months, with the region re-employing
79,900 by November (recapturing 44% of the initial job loss). Heading into the winter, the
metro region experienced renewed employment reductions (losing another 10,400 seasonally
adjusted jobs through January 2021). Since that time there has been a pattern of steady job
recovery. Over the course of 2021, the region added back another 71,300 jobs, with a
remaining 41,200 employees (or 3.3%) below the pre-pandemic February 2020 peak of
1,243,100 total non-farm metro area jobs.

Metro Compared with Oregon & U.S. Pandemic Jobs Experience

Analysis of month-to-month job changes for the Portland metro region can be distinguished
between commercially oriented and industrial sectors of the economy. For metro areas of the
U.S., BLS reports sector specific data only on a not seasonally adjusted basis. Data is presented
starting with the change from February to March 2020, continuing through to June 2021.

Commercial Employment Change. Prior to the pandemic (as of 2018 QCEW data),
commercial uses accounted for 71% of PDX metro and 54% of Hillsboro employment. For the
metro region, commercial uses have borne the brunt of the economic recession of 2020,
accounting for 86% of all metro area jobs lost in April 2020, increasing to more than 100% of
remaining cumulative net job loss by year-end 2021 (as industrial jobs by then had more than
fully recovered to exceed pre-pandemic levels).

Hospitality (including dining and lodging) has experienced the most severe and uneven impacts.
An estimated 63,100 jobs were lost in the March-April time frame of 2020. A sharp but partial
bounce-back was experienced over the summer and into fall of 2020, followed by a second
round of layoffs by year end. The sector has since again added back employment but remained
13,800 jobs short of pre-pandemic employment as of year-end 2021.

Due to potential long-term dampened consumer for bricks-and-mortar building space,
components of both the retail and hospitality sectors have faced continuing issues, in large part
due to measures as for social distancing – albeit with retail faring better than hospitality
(especially for larger format retailers). With a lower concentration of jobs in these most at-risk
sectors than the rest of the metro region, Hillsboro has been better positioned for continued
recovery – due to greater concentration of its employment base in less vulnerable economic
sectors. This is evidenced by 2020 jobs data (based on OED updates then available).

One potential question mark relates to the previously rapidly expanding health care sector.
There may be more upside potential when health care rebalances to include the full suite of
traditional medical services with less set-aside for COVID-related care as the pandemic recedes.
Across this sector as with other lower paid commercial sectors, jobs data for 2020 and 2021
indicate increasing challenges with securing adequate workforce. As yet uncertain is the extent
to which this proves to be a temporary challenge or represents a longer-term structural shift.

Industrial Employment Change. Pre-pandemic, industrial uses accounted for 29% of PDX
metro and about 46% of Hillsboro employment. Industrial uses represented 14% of all metro
area jobs lost in April 2020, with overall full recovery experienced by October 2021.

Manufacturing experienced the greatest net loss metro-wide of the industrial grouping – laying
off 9,000 workers from February-May 2020 and remaining 2,800 jobs below pre-recession
levels as of year-end 2021. However, manufacturing experience has varied depending on the
specific sector as further detailed below.

Of the industrial sectors, transportation and warehousing activities proved to be the star
performer through the pandemic and recession, up by 6,200 jobs metro-wide over pre-
pandemic levels as of December 2020 and increasing to a net gain of 6,700 jobs as of December
2021. This sector benefitted from the new attention to supply chain management coupled with


            City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis – Technical Appendices ♦ Page 18
the Amazon effect of dramatically increased shipments to residences and newly created home
offices as well as to recovering industrial and commercial businesses.

With the exception of transportation and construction, other industrial sectors have
maintained relatively stable employment through the pandemic with minimal net job loss. After
an initial downturn early in the pandemic, construction employment had more than recovered
to 3,600 above pre-recession employment levels as of summer 2021.

Taken together and consistent with national experience, industrial-related employment has
proved to be more stable and in many cases a driver of new job potential for the PDX region.

Manufacturing Focus. With this EOA it is also useful to drill down a bit further and evaluate
changes in metro area manufacturing employment through the period of pandemic related
recession and then subsequent recovery. As of 2018, manufacturing uses accounted for 11% of
PDX metro and 32% of Hillsboro employment.

Manufacturing represented just 5% of all metro area jobs lost in April 2020, increasing to about
9% of remaining cumulative job loss over a year later, then ranging between 7-9% for most of
2021. As shown by the chart for monthly employment changes for manufacturing employment
covered by BLS-CES data, some manufacturing sectors clearly held up better than others.

As of 2018, computer and electronics manufacturing accounted for 85% of manufacturing
employment in Hillsboro. Metro-wide, this sector experienced a net job loss of only 200 jobs
from February to April 2020. Layoffs continued to a peak of 800 fewer employees by September
2020. As of August 2021, employment was back to 100% of pre-pandemic conditions, increasing
thereafter albeit with some drop-off during the last month of 2021.




           City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis – Technical Appendices ♦ Page 19
Other manufacturing sectors experiencing full job recovery as of mid-2021 have included food
products, lumber and wood products, and machinery manufacturing. Metals-related and other
manufacturing sectors remained below pre-pandemic job level as of year-end 2021.

This metro-wide experience indicates effective resilience through this period coupled with what
appear to be strong indicators for further growth ahead – including for semiconductors and
other advanced manufacturing. While 2021 jobs data was not yet available as of the date of the
2021 EOA update for geographies below the metro level, OED data for 2020 indicate that
Hillsboro fared much better than the metro region for manufacturing job retention in the initial
pandemic year of 2020. From 2019-2020, manufacturing employment declined by only 0.5% in
Hillsboro as compared to a 6.3% job loss metro-wide.

For Hillsboro and nationally, pandemic related demand has been strong in applications ranging
from cloud storage to notebook computers due to more at home office employment – as well
as for other end-user products as with the auto industry. There is anticipation of continued
strong demand growth due to current semiconductor shortages globally and for emerging new
technologies ranging from artificial intelligence (AI) to the internet of things (IoT).

Reshoring of manufacturing capacity to the U.S. has emerged as a clear governmental and
industry priority creating added opportunity for Hillsboro firms (led by Intel) provided that
Hillsboro remains competitive with other regions of the U.S. for yet further investment and
added employment potential.

Food/textile and machinery job levels (including firms with a Hillsboro presence) also held up
well through the pandemic across the metro region. Other manufacturing activities experienced
greater earlier job losses coupled with subsequent volatility of employment metro-wide, albeit
with limited Hillsboro presence.

To summarize, Hillsboro’s current and prospective employment mix including recent pandemic
experience appears to offer benefits both of economic resilience and long-term growth
potential:

   •   Hillsboro’s business and industry mix has demonstrated a path toward economic
       recovery and resilience beyond what has been achievable across the rest of the metro
       region.
   •   The community’s nurturing of technology industries aligns well with the best
       opportunities for economic growth regionally and nationally – in recent years, through
       the 2020 economic downturn and post-pandemic.

Bottom line, these demonstrated advantages position the community to be an even more
significant source of job stability and renewed growth for the PDX metro region and state of
Oregon in what may be considered as the new-new-economy of the years just ahead. This sets
the stage for sharing in the longer-term transition to a more resilient and sustainable global as
well as domestic U.S. economy.



         City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis – Technical Appendices ♦ Page 20
WORK COMMUTE CONSIDERATIONS
An issue of growing concern in recent years is reduced effective accessibility of work force to
jobs throughout the metro region. While metropolitan areas are defined, in part, on the basis of
commuter access to jobs throughout a metro region, this has become more challenging in
recent decades due to growing transport congestion.

For example, it is assumed that Hillsboro workers can be drawn from throughout the metro
area, including more distant locations such as Clark County. However, as the travel time of
these cross-metro commutes increases, this premise becomes more tenuous than previously.

While the COVID pandemic temporarily increased access due to fewer commuters on the
freeway system and associated thoroughfares, this is now being offset by an apparent growing
preference from workers for better live-work integration, with less tolerance for long
commutes than previously.

Concerns with the work commute to Hillsboro have repeatedly been identified by stakeholder
employers– both initially and with subsequent contacts conducted for this EOA update. The
question relates to the effect of regional traffic congestion on work commutes and resulting
effective labor-shed available to Hillsboro employers – both historically and going forward.

A synopsis of data compiled and associated observations pertinent to this updated EOA is
provided on the following pages.

Also of note are home locations by age of worker and earnings:

       although this is the predominant wage range for jobs going to Hillsboro residents as
       well.

To summarize, this data indicates that transportation corridors and congestion are re-shaping
the Hillsboro workforce commute-shed. While local employers draw workers from across the
region, some areas associated with difficult commutes are clearly under-represented.

Due to increasing congestion within the core of the metro region, a growing share of the
workforce is being drawn from the edges of and further beyond to outside the immediate
metro area – especially from urban as well as more rural communities to the south.

While improved workforce accessibility depends, in part, on regional transportation
improvements, of equal or perhaps greater significance going forward may be the need to
provide added and more varied housing product to support continued employment growth
within the more immediate Hillsboro community.

EMPLOYMENT SECTOR REVIEW
In review of the 2021 EOA, DLCD staff questioned how the EOA considered and applied
compound or CAGR (exponential) versus straight-line (linear) projections of employment
growth. This last portion of Appendix A is intended to provide a detailed review of the forecast
methodologies considered and applied to preparation of a recommended preferred
employment growth scenario. This review is consistent with historical experience and changing
opportunities in the aftermath of a global pandemic, economic downturn and as yet in-progress
economic recovery.

Approach to Sectoral Analysis
As employment forecasting has been conducted on a sector-by-sector basis, this analysis is
similarly driven by sector-specific considerations. As described by the primary 2021 EOA
document, work on an updated EOA was initiated in 2019, then subsequently revised to reflect
COVID-related experience and changed economic conditions.

Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW) trend data was provided by the Oregon
Employment Department (OED) in late 2019 with data specific to Hillsboro for 2007 and 2018.
This period covered a near full economic cycle with recession starting in 2007 to recovery and
then to near a 2019 peak – prior to the subsequent recession associated with the pandemic in
2020.

Process for Goal 9 Compliance. OAR 660-009-0015 for EOAs states that forecast demand
is to be based on what could “reasonably be expected to locate or expand in the planning area
based on information about national, state, regional, county or local trends.” While the OAR
does not stipulate the use of a specific methodology, the application of a compound annual
growth rate (CAGR) reflects typical practice for EOA employment and land needs analyses.

Most significantly for the Portland tri-county region, Metro’s Urban Growth Report (UGR) has
been framed in terms of annually compounded job growth rates (described as an APR – Annual
Percentage Rate in Metro terminology). This also has been the approach taken, for example,
with Portland’s EOA as earlier adopted by the City of Portland in 2016.

In communities experiencing relatively slow job growth, there may be relatively little difference
in extrapolation of straight-line or annually compounded growth (where each year’s growth is
built on a higher base from the previous year). Hillsboro presents a different situation as growth
rates have been relatively rapid across a number of employment sectors in recent years. In this
situation, there can be a more substantial difference in future growth potentials depending on
whether the job trend is forecast based on a straight line or CAGR methodology.

Recognizing the potential difference, Hillsboro’s EOA was framed around a comparison of
straight-line and exponential (CAGR-based) growth rate calculations by major employment
sector, described as Scenarios A and B, respectively. Two reference years of jobs data were
obtained with 2007 as the starting and 2018 as the end point of the historical data analysis.


         City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis – Technical Appendices ♦ Page 25
With just these two years providing beginning and end-point data, it is not statistically possible
to determine whether a straight-line versus exponential (non-linear) growth rate calculation is
more relevant to Hillsboro’s experience. Making this determination could occur either by
obtaining data for each calendar year in the historical dataset and/or by informed judgement
including policy and planning objectives of the City of Hillsboro.

As detailed year-by-year sub-county data is not readily available from OED (without geo-coded
special data runs), primary reliance was placed on an approach reliant on informed judgement
of City of Hillsboro Economic Development personnel. This led to preparation of a third forecast
Scenario C. This scenario was termed as “hybrid growth,” based on a more detailed sectoral
evaluation of whether each sector appeared to be as yet emergent suggesting exponential
annual growth rates ahead or maturing, suggesting a straight-line approach where the %
change in jobs actually declines each year of the forecast period, as compared to the year prior.

Most significantly for this EOA, sectors with continued strong growth potential include those
that align with continuation of Hillsboro’s target industry emphasis on tech-driven and traded
sector business and industry clusters. The determination of whether a sector’s prospects are
classified to reflect a straight-line, exponential or mid-point forecast allocation was made in
consultation with Economic Development input as best reflecting recent trends together with
City of Hillsboro opportunities and strategic priorities.

At the request of DLCD, more detailed year-by-year analysis was completed based on a
special supplemental 2022 data run generated by OED to provide year-by-year and industry
sector employment data specific to Hillsboro, including updates for the 2019-20 years of
QCEW jobs data as subsequently made available. The next section of this review covers both
the methodology and the results of this more detailed sector-by-sector analysis together with
observations as to the appropriateness of straight-line and/or exponential growth rates
utilized with the Hillsboro EOA employment forecast process.

Methodology to Differentiate Straight-Line vs Exponential Job Growth Trend. As a
starting point for this analysis, it is useful to describe how year-to-year employment changes
can be reviewed to assess whether job growth is occurring on a straight-line versus exponential
trajectory. This is illustrated by the two graphs on the next page – each assuming a starting
year hypothetical base of 10,000 jobs, increasing by 25% to 12,500 jobs within 10 years.

   •   The graph to the left illustrates a hypothetical straight-line scenario. The 2,500 added
       jobs in 10 year occurs in equal increments of 250 added jobs per year.
   •   In contrast, the graph to the right illustrates an exponential scenario. Applied to the
       base year count of an assumed 10,000 jobs, getting to a net 10-year gain of 2,500 is
       achieved at what calculates to be a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 2.26% per
       year. Employment increases by 226 jobs in year 1 (equal to 10,000 x .0226), adding 231
       jobs in year 2 (equal to 1,226 x .0226), and so on … with each year’s job growth greater
       than the year previous as base level employment continues to increase each successive
       year.


         City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis – Technical Appendices ♦ Page 26
        Yr-Yr Illustrative Job Change (Straight Line)                                                     Yr-Yr Illustrative Job Change (Exponential)
  300                                                                                               300

  275                                                                                               275

  250                                                                                               250

  225                                                                                               225

  200                                                                                               200

         Year 1   Year 2   Year 3   Year 4   Year 5   Year 6   Year 7   Year 8   Year 9   Year 10         Year 1   Year 2   Year 3   Year 4   Year 5   Year 6   Year 7   Year 8   Year 9   Year 10




Both approaches start with the same employment number (in this case 10,000 jobs) and end
with the same number (12,500 after 10 years). The straight-line approach assumes the same
number of net new jobs are added each year. The exponential approach gets to the same end-
year result, but with more jobs added each year than the last, with each year’s job number
increasing at a constant percentage rate above the prior year’s base of total employment.

For purposes of assessing whether employment growth has followed a straight-line versus
exponential trajectory, the difference lies in the shape (or slope) of the trend line. Straight line
growth occurs on a relatively flat-line horizontal trajectory (with no upward slope), whereas
exponential growth occurs on an upward-sloping path.

This is particularly important in real-world assessments where job change from one year to the
next may be uneven, up one year and down the next. The trend line is based on the trajectory
that achieves the “best fit” across the years considered. Straight-line growth is the trajectory
where the “best fit” trend (or regression) averages to roughly equivalent job changes each
year. Exponential growth is indicated where the trend-line is upward sloping. This is the
approach taken with the remainder of this analysis.

Hillsboro All Sectors Job Change. This methodological approach is now applied to actual
employment changes in Hillsboro – first with consideration of all sectors combined and then on
an industry sector-by-sector basis. Two sets of graphs are utilized for this review:

   •     Job change from 2008-18 – the time period consistent with the EOA dataset as provided
         by OED in 2019. Note that the year of change is for the year indicated on the graph as
         compared to the year prior. For example, a 2008 data point shows the numerical change
         in employment occurring from 2007-08. Actual results are shown by the solid blue line.
   •     Job change from 2004-19 – as a somewhat expanded time frame based on year-by-year
         data as recently provided in March 2022 by OED. Notes: This time period is based on
         years for which geo-coded data is available for OED; earlier year geo-coded data is not
         available. The year of change is for the year indicated on the graph as compared to the
         year prior. So, for example, a 2004 data point illustrates the numerical change in
         employment from 2003-04. Also noted is that 2004 Hillsboro job estimates are adjusted
         per consultation with OED.

pandemic and recession year is included, a different trending pattern is observed. However,
this represents an incomplete view as it covers two down cycles and only one up-cycle of
employment change.

Recognizing that inclusion of 2020 down-cycle data in the absence of subsequent economic
recovery may represent an unduly conservative view of long-term growth prospects, DLCD has
allowed for exclusion of this anomalous year from Goal 9 EOA reviews underway.

With the detailed sector-by-sector review that follows, this analysis utilizes the 2008-18 and
2004-19 time periods as the primary comparative focus for analysis. In effect, the “best fit”
analysis based on either time frame indicates an overall pattern of exponential growth for
Hillsboro in recent years. However, rather than apply this overall conclusion across the board to


            City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis – Technical Appendices ♦ Page 28
encompass all sectors, the approach taken with the 2021 EOA is industry sector-by-sector, each
considered on its own merits – and with both the shorter and longer-time periods reviewed.

Particular focus is placed on traded sector industries including key supporting sectors. In cases
where the data supports both linear and exponential growth (depending on the time frame
considered), additional discussion is provided together with a rationale for the selected forecast
approach as part of the preferred hybrid growth scenario (Scenario C).

While 2020 analysis is not relied on as determinative, in some cases this pandemic-related
experience is factored into the discussion – especially for sectors for which there is evidence
that the 2020 downturn may presage a longer secular term change rather than a temporary
downturn.

Sector Toggle Approach. As described at the outset of this appendix, a four-phase sector
toggle approach was used to determine the employment forecast outcomes that would be
applied to the Scenario C hybrid model:

   •   Employment sectors for which job loss was experienced from 2007-18 are assumed to
       experience no further net change employment to 2040.
   •   Sectors for which Scenario A straight-line experience appears most applicable and not
       comprising a Hillsboro cluster target are assumed to continue experiencing employment
       growth consistent with the straight-line trajectory of the most recent economic cycle.
   •   Sectors that have experienced job change consistent with Scenario B exponential
       growth including target industry or affiliated sectors are forecast to continue
       experiencing job growth consistent with the historically based CAGR trajectory.
   •   Finally, sectors that appear to have experienced or be influenced by exponential growth
       but for which the two time frames considered suggest both exponential and straight-
       line patterns may be assigned a mid-point result by taking the average of the numerical
       job growth calculations associated with Scenarios A and B.

This sector-by-sector analysis now follows, organized by the NAICS industry sectors for which
sector-specific employment forecast have been made. For each industry sector considered,
discussion includes a brief review of the sector’s relative local employment significance, the
year-to-year job change (with each of the two retrospective time frames considered), other
factors based on both quantitative and qualitative considerations addressed with this EOA, and
conclusion as to the approach taken for inclusion with the recommended Scenario C hybrid
growth forecast.

Sectors for which exponential growth is indicated or for which there may be countervailing
evidence receive the most detailed attention. Sectors for which straight-line growth is clearly
indicated or which have experienced net job loss over the last economic cycle are generally
addressed in a more summary fashion.

analysis in 2019, the 2007-18 job trend indicates some tendency toward exponential growth,
