cycle and even into the pandemic downturn of 2020. This determination is also consistent with
the distinct role that the industrial/commercial portion of the construction sector plays in
supporting growth in manufacturing and traded sector employment in Hillsboro.

With exponential growth, the compound annual growth rate (CAGR) utilized for the 2020-40
period equates to an average 2.7% increase in employment over the prior employment in the
previous year. The result is that Scenario C (exponential growth) extrapolation results in a
forecast net addition of 2,350 Hillsboro construction jobs from 2020-40 as compared to a net
increase of 1,470 jobs if a straight-line employment projection were to be applied.

The experience of the last economic cycle (to 2018) indicates support for an exponential

Key factors affecting retail both before and extending through the pandemic include aging of
the population (with reduced propensity to spent), shift to internet retail and expansion of
multi-channel large-format stores, often at the expense of independent brick-and-mortar
retailers. While recent experience indicates some at least temporary potential shift back to in-
person shopping, a more cautious overall approach is suggested going forward. As a result,
retail has been assumed to experience a pattern of straight-line growth over the 20-year EOA
forecast horizon.

With a CAGR of only 1.1% average annual job growth as experienced over the last economic
cycle, there is a limited difference between outputs associated with an exponential versus
straight-line forecast. Assuming straight-line growth with Scenario C, an estimated 1,490 in-city
retail jobs would be added from 2020-40. With an exponential growth, this job target is
increased by 21% for 1,810 net added retail jobs over the 20-year EOA planning horizon.

What might be termed as the “Amazon effect” has been replicated across a range of other

affecting customers for at-home delivery as well as multi-modal trade flows. For freight

of up to an added 5,290 added transportation and warehousing jobs from 2020-40, as
compared with 1,730 added jobs if a straight-line projection were to be applied.

To some extent and due to the complementary nature of respective business activities, there
may be trade-offs between job growth assigned to NAICS 42 wholesale trade (applying a
straight-line projection) vis-à-vis a more substantial NAICS 48-49 transportation and
warehousing CAGR-based forecast (as determined for Scenario C).

metro region’s employment in this sector as of 2018 to nearly 8% as of 2040. With Scenario B,
exponential growth, Hillsboro could increase to just over 15% of the metro-wide job count by
2040. In effect, Hillsboro’s share of regional health care jobs would be above its 12% share of
employment across all sectors of the metro region which appears as a less plausible outcome.

As a result, for this sector the Scenario C hybrid outcome reflects the mid-point of the Scenario
A and B projections – indicating an increase of 16,175 jobs for this sector from 2020-40. This
appears more realistic in terms of regional share considerations. With Scenario C, Hillsboro
would account for 11-12% of all jobs region-wide in this sector by 2040, comparable to the
city’s projected 10%+ share of employment across all job sectors metro-wide.

Summary Implications for EOA Employment Forecasts
Hillsboro’s updated 2021 EOA has been based on preparation of three alternative employment
scenarios:

   •   Scenario A – assuming a straight-line employment projection across all industry sectors
   •   Scenario B – predicated on exponential employment growth across all sectors
   •   Scenario C – as a hybrid approach predicated on evaluating employment trends, market
       prospects and policy priorities on a sector-by-sector basis

In response to DLCD comments, this sector-by-sector analysis has focused on the
appropriateness of the Scenario C hybrid approach – which has been recommended as the
preferred scenario of Hillsboro’s updated 2021 EOA. More specifically, this analysis addresses
the question of whether and under what conditions a straight-line versus exponential sector
projection is more consistent with prior experience.

While this retrospective analysis draws on more detailed and extensive employment data than
utilized with initial EOA preparation as of year-end 2021, it supports the reasonableness of
Scenario C projections provided with the EOA – even with anticipation of likely continued year-
to-year variations going forward.




         City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis – Technical Appendices ♦ Page 42
APPENDIX B.
COMMUNITY ECONOMIC POTENTIAL
This appendix provides detailed background and qualitative research summarized by Chapter III
of the 2021 EOA addressing community economic potential. Topics covered by this appendix
include background and approach, qualifying and then identifying factors affecting community
economic potential, Hillsboro’s competitive position, and target industry clusters.

A key source of information obtained for this review has involved qualitative research including
focus group and interview discussion with business and community stakeholders. This is an
extended version of the summary discussion provided with Chapter III of the Hillsboro EOA.

BACKGROUND & APPROACH
As initially conceived, the purpose of this this review of community economic potential has
been to serve as a bridge between the quantitative review of economic and subsequent
assessment of anticipated employment land needs together with recommended
implementation policies going forward. A major objective is to discuss factors consistent with
Oregon Goal 9 guidelines affecting community economic potential including: work force;
availability of transportation facilities for access and freight mobility; access to suppliers and
utilities; location, size, and buying power of markets; state and federal environmental
protection laws; and service infrastructure.

This work was initiated prior to and then was interrupted by the March-April 2020 recognition
of the profound health and economic effects of the global COVID-19 pandemic. Much of the
assessment was subsequently updated and revised to address pandemic and potential post-
pandemic opportunities for economic recovery and resilience.

From Pre-COVID to Post-Pandemic World
The most important change from initial EOA research conducted prior to 2020 is to address
reasonably foreseeable changes to community economic potential as a result of the COVID-19
pandemic, ensuing economic downturn and subsequent early phases of economic recovery.
When in the middle of sweeping change, it is challenging to reliably assess both short- and long-
term prospects for the global economy, let alone implications for any particular jurisdiction.
Consequently, greater flexibility in anticipating a wider range of outcomes may be warranted
than is typically the case with EOA documentation.

The pivotal question is: Will the economy re-stabilize to pre-COVID conditions, or is this new-
new normal to be fundamentally different from what has occurred over recent business cycles,
especially as experienced since the Great Recession of 2007-09?




         City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis – Technical Appendices ♦ Page 43
This assessment takes an approach that looks to the past as one potential guide to the future
while also considering the character and extent of potential transformative change that may
now be underway. In effect, the decision of a viable path to pursue involves a risk-reward
evaluation reflecting potential multiple economic scenarios.

The analysis and recommendations resulting from this assessment suggest a risk mitigation
strategy that might involve elements of both approaches – working to keep the best of the past
while being an early adapter of the post-pandemic changes most likely to endure.

QUALIFYING ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT POTENTIAL
Characterizing economic development potential to this point has been, in large part, driven by
the numbers. Addressing the statewiide land use planing Goal 9 Economic Development
requires quantification of potential employment change and associated land requirements.
However, understanding and preparing for the future is about more than numerical modeling.
Qualitative assessment is also important – especially when it comes to setting policies to
implement the plan in a way that also will meet broader community objectives.

OAR 660-009-0015 (5) provides guidance to the effect that:

       “Cities and counties are strongly encouraged to assess community economic
       development potential through a visioning or some other public input process in
       conjunction with state agencies.”

To assist with this qualitative assessment, focus group discussion and stakeholder interviews
were conducted with a range of local and regional business and economic development
interests. This input process is further augmented by a public hearing process before the City of
Hillsboro Planning Commission and City Council with EOA completion.

The stakeholder outreach process has occurred in two phases. An initial round of interviews
was conducted in early 2020 (pre-pandemic) with input organized around the following topics:

   •   Existing or emerging global to local trends that Hillsboro should pay attention to for
       economic development over the next 5, 20 and up to 50 years.
   •   Hillsboro’s greatest strengths versus weaknesses affecting business and economic
       vitality.
   •   Most promising opportunities short- and long-term – as compared with threats that
       might undermine realization of these opportunities.
   •   Short- and long-term needs for industrial and commercial land.
   •   Other public and private initiatives as might be considered to support Hillsboro’s best
       opportunities.

A second round of phone interviews was conducted over the summer of 2020, as initial steps
toward economic recovery were taking hold. In addition to the topics noted with the first


         City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis – Technical Appendices ♦ Page 44
round, the second round also involved asking participants to comment on two key items – the
near-term pace and timing for pandemic-related economic recovery together with implications
for sustained economic recovery and resiliency longer-term over the next 5-20 years.

Identifying and characterizing community economic development potential involves both
quantitative analysis and qualitative understanding of key economic players active in the
Hillsboro community.

Opportunities & Threats
Focus group and interview participants identified opportunities including continued tech-
focused manufacturing/products, broader industrial and commercial business diversification,
improved jobs/housing balance, and transport innovation. Also supported is the need to extend
Hillsboro’s economic development vision beyond the state-mandated 20-year planning horizon
to encompass a longer-term 50-year planning perspective.

Potential threats or barriers cited by those interviewed relate to the risk of losing Hillsboro’s
semiconductor-oriented and anchor firm competitive edge, issues with workforce
displacement, concerns with remaining a less than full-service community, transport gridlock,
and non-market regulation.

Working Through & Beyond the Pandemic
For virtually all stakeholders contacted over the summer of 2020, the world of work and
business has clearly become a different place than it was pre-pandemic. However, many of the
fundamental forces of change already at work globally and locally still appear to remain in
place. Existing trends for Hillsboro of disruptive technology and live-work connection have not
necessarily changed, but rather have dramatically accelerated.

As one industry source suggests, changes that would normally occur over a 5-year time horizon
have been compressed into five months. This theme of “executing faster” is one that is echoed
in various ways by business and community leaders across multiple sectors.

   •   Hillsboro’s tech-driven and related traded sector industries appear to have generally
       held their own – or in some cases performed even better as evidenced by industrial
       construction and plans for business expansion. The major exception noted is for local
       businesses linked to what has been a struggling global aerospace sector.
   •   Somewhat surprisingly, a recurring theme is the continuing if not intensified challenge
       of hiring and retaining qualified workforce. More mention in the second round of
       interviews was made of the importance of partnering with PCC, OHSU and OSU for
       apprenticeship and technical training – also internships.
   •   The pandemic also seems to have heightened interest in the need for improved
       transportation logistics. Partnering with the city, state, Port of Portland and UPS has
       resulted in major improvements as with the new UPS facility, extended Hillsboro airport
       runway and dedicated flight service.
   •   Service sectors ranging from retail to dining have been the most adversely affected.
       Small locally-based business bring “unique flavor and flair” important for community
       identity but are most at risk now and going forward. There is pressure on tenant
       capacity to pay rent with resulting implications for landlords and lenders. Capital
       availability will affect those who survive versus those who have or will close their doors.
   •   Health care providers also have been adversely affected – at least near-term – due to
       needed prioritization of COVID care over more routine care. The health crisis also is

     City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis – Technical Appendices ♦ Page 48
Industrial & Commercial Land Needs
Recognizing that a primary purpose of this EOA update is to define short- and long-term needs
for industrial and commercial land, an important question is: What employment land needs are
most important to address?

Two overall observations emerge from the stakeholder discussions:

   •   First, priority should be placed on assuring that shovel-ready land required to
       accommodate new employment will be there as demand warrants. Hillsboro has a
       strong track record of serving major employers with large sites – making possible
       development that otherwise likely would not have occurred in the metro region.
       Increasing demand for large sites to accommodate less employment intensive uses such
       as warehouse-distribution and data center uses can also be expected – as potentially
       important for tax base, also supporting some other business and consumer needs locally
       and regionally. Encouraging increased density with vertical development for land-
       extensive uses is appropriate to consider, though this opportunity may be constrained
       by still comparatively affordable land prices favoring lower density development – at
       least in the near-term.
       A stronger case needs to be made to understand the value of land banking for uses
       needing flexibility or anticipating major expansion in the years ahead. Bottom line, the
       suggestion is to “be prepared in advance – getting added reserves happens over
       multiple years, so start now.”
       In the wake of the pandemic, there is growing recognition that employment land needs
       may change in ways not previously expected – ranging from more work-at-home to
       office reconfiguration and retail downsizing to more large site demand for industrial and
       distribution functions led by major corporate investment. This suggests a need to be
       more flexible with land use planning and regulation than in the past, including
       consideration of mid-course adjustments as the character and extent of these emerging
       land demand changes become more apparent.
   •   Second, there is growing recognition of the need to accommodate both exclusive
       industrial zones and mixed-use development. Business requirements and priorities vary
       depending on the specific characteristics of different industrial and commercial uses. For
       large industrial users, multi-tenant business parks and some commercial uses with
       requirements as for extensive truck traffic, night operations and/or need for outside
       storage, it is important to provide a clear separation from residential development.
       For other smaller scale business uses, there have been clear and increasing benefits to
       locate as part of mixed-use projects – as at Orenco or in downtown Hillsboro. The
       opportunity to attract creative service and tech users to Hillsboro may be influenced by
       enhancement of these opportunities in areas offering good proximity to mixed-use
       development opportunities. With potential reduced commercial space demand,
       horizontal rather than vertical mixed-use may become the more pronounced market
       opportunity at least near-term.


        City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis – Technical Appendices ♦ Page 49
Other Public & Private Initiatives
A final topic of discussion has been on identifying other public and private initiatives that
should be considered with this EOA. These are initiatives that extend beyond but support the
City’s land use policies. Priorities suggested center on the following:

   •   Workforce training – expected to be more important due to rapidly changing
       technology and career trajectories, across the spectrum of K-12, higher education and
       on-going workforce training. Specifically referenced is the need for training tied to
       career and technical education (CTE) programs, linked more explicitly and with greater
       flexibility to meet employer needs. The desire for workforce training that is yet more
       customized to employer needs appears to have intensified even through the pandemic.
   •   Smart transport investment – tailored to different needs for internal versus external
       transport linkages. Connections within and between the city’s employment, residential
       and public/open space areas should emphasize greater walkability and opportunity to
       cycle, improved transit connections/ride sharing, and preparation for autonomous
       vehicles – all reducing the need for driving (and associated parking). To the extent and
       for the duration that COVID risk persists, regaining lost transit ridership will be
       challenged.
       External connections suggested are for a balanced mix of transit and major highway
       corridor improvements. Particular emphasis is needed for better freight mobility –
       especially for time sensitive products reliant on airborne transport. A related long-term
       objective may be for improvement of the Cornelius Pass connection – as an alternate
       route to the Portland International Airport (PDX) and the I-5 North freeway system.
   •   Long-term utility Investment – in the area’s electric, water, and wastewater systems.
       Adequate and reliable electric power is essential to major semiconductor firms plus a
       range of related high-tech industries. Hillsboro has benefitted from strategic, industry-
       supportive investments by Portland General Electric.
       Similarly, the City of Hillsboro is recognized for having made the right decision 50 years
       ago with water system investment -- “setting the table” for tech companies as well as
       overall development that has since occurred. From this perspective, it is again important
       to now prepare for the next 50 years; as a community, “we need to pay forward.”
   •   Targeted economic development incentives – are recognized as having played an
       important role in attracting industrial investment to Hillsboro. Some suggest that
       incentives be more narrowly targeted in the years ahead – to businesses that can
       demonstrate some combination of strong employment, tax revenue, and/or
       supplemental business leveraging benefits.




        City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis – Technical Appendices ♦ Page 50
FACTORS AFFECTING COMMUNITY ECONOMIC POTENTIAL
An element of the EOA process involves consideration of location or market factors affecting
where a particular type of industrial or other employment use may locate. Ad defined by OAR
660-009-0005, these locational factors “include but are not limited to, proximity to raw
materials, supplies, labor, services, markets, or educational institutions; access to
transportation and freight facilities such as rail, marine ports and airports, multimodal freight or
transshipment facilities, and major transportation routes; and workforce factors (e.g., skill level,
education, age distribution).”

Separately outlined by OAR 660-009-0015 (4) are potential advantages and disadvantages to be
considered with the assessment of community economic development potential that “may
include but are not limited to” items (a) to (h) as listed by the following chart. Due to the
overlap of the locational and market factors stipulated by OAR Definitions (0005) and Economic
Opportunities Analysis (0015), these factors are considered together but organized around
topics that have emerged as most germane to Hillsboro’s current and prospective community
economic potential.

With this EOA, 11 factors are identified as pivotal both now and going forward for economic
development in Hillsboro. The relationship of these Hillsboro-specific factors to those outlined
by OAR 660-009-0005 are as provided by the following chart.

Each of the 11 Hillsboro specific factors considered with this EOA is briefly described, in turn.
This is followed by a summary assessment of associated strengths, weaknesses, opportunities
and threats (or SWOT assessment).


          City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis – Technical Appendices ♦ Page 51
(1) Globalization/Localization
In recent decades, the supply chains of American businesses, especially multinational firms,
have become increasingly globalized. More recently, this has coincided with growing consumer
orientation to purchase via the internet rather than shop at local brick and mortar stores.

However, there are clear signs that this trend may be now headed in reverse, at least for
corporate traded sector firms and for the immediate future. A trend back to localized sourcing
is occurring for a variety of reasons including more populist governance both domestically and
globally, tariffs and related trade conflicts, national security and technology protection
concerns, rising wages in emerging markets, automation, desires to reduce corporate carbon
footprints, quicker response to changing consumer preferences, and most recently for
improved containment of potential pandemic risk.

Over the next several years and possibly beyond, the transition back from global to local may
significantly affect manufacturing decisions by re-shoring closer to a U.S. home base. With more
suppliers and customers of semiconductor and tech products locating and expanding in
Hillsboro, the community’s competitive position is further enhanced going forward. An
offsetting issue or weakness is the increasingly limited industrial land supply affecting both
large scale and smaller firms.

(2) Technology
Technology has been and will be a continued if not primary source of innovation – affecting
virtually every aspect of business and consumer choice. Markets have matured for computers
and now for smart phones, with new applications affecting both hardware manufacturing (or
product space), software/apps and creative services (or service space requiring added footprint
including for at-home work).

New manufacturing techniques as with 3D printing offer yet more innovation for customized
products benefitting both entrepreneurial and established businesses. Key growth sectors
include autonomous and electronic vehicles (AV/EVs), the internet of things (IoT), artificial
intelligence (AI), 5G wireless networks, and cloud computing.

Product space tends to require larger sites, typically in suburban or exurban locations. Over the
last 10-20 years, service space has gravitated more to urban areas to meet the
live/work/recreate preferences of a younger workforce. However, that is now changing in
response to COVID-safety concerns and as more millennials start families with some looking for
more traditional, larger and less expensive housing options – but with urban amenities close at
hand.

Hillsboro can capitalize on these multiple trends to the extent that the community offers
diversity of business and residential choice and capacity for adaption to future changes as yet
not readily foreseen.




         City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis – Technical Appendices ♦ Page 52
(3) Workforce
Workforce affects business location decisions in at least two key respects. First is the availability
of workers. With a large baby boom cohort now moving to retirement, there is a smaller
Generation X cohort with significant workforce experience coming in immediately behind.

This may create added advancement opportunity for the relatively large cohort of millennials,
especially in regions of the U.S. attractive to younger workers as has been the case for the
Portland metro area. However, the next Gen Z cohort now readying to enter the labor force will
again be somewhat smaller – placing an added potential premium on labor supply longer-term.

A second consideration relates to workforce skills and training. Despite absence of a nationally
recognized full-service research university, this metro region has done well to attract workers
with managerial and technical skills, including for those skill sets not as abundant with the
existing indigenous labor force. The metro area reportedly performs well with a solid base of
workers having experience in diverse manufacturing settings.

For stakeholders contacted most recently as the region was beginning its economic recovery,
there appears to be less emphasis by employers on four-year education options, offset by more
focus on K-12 workforce orientation to tech industries and, even more critically, to customized
community college or technical school options.

These appear to be interests shared across diverse high-tech fields ranging from
semiconductors to biotech, for example, with programs for clean room technology. City
leadership with encouragement of “gap year” internships is specifically cited and appreciated,
with strong support indicated for program continuation. On-going provision and adaptation of
workforce training capacity will be important over the planning horizon of this EOA.

(4) Vendor & Customer Networks
While not having the depth of established networks as in some larger metro areas (for example
as with the Seattle-Bellevue-Redmond tech cluster), Hillsboro and metro area businesses can
draw from other local businesses for key business-to-business relationships where the market is
large enough to support added local vendors – especially for larger firms such as Intel and Nike.
The end use customer base is not as well populated since major area firms (as with
semiconductors) ship a large portion of their output to customers outside the region for
product assembly, packaging, marketing and distribution.

Hillsboro’s growing base of tech-supportive industries represents greater competitive
advantage going forward. A challenge is regional transportation congestion and distance from
the Portland International Airport – offset in part by improvements to the Hillsboro airport and
attraction of transportation, wholesale and distribution firms to the Hillsboro area.




         City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis – Technical Appendices ♦ Page 53
(5) Incomes & Buying Power
Resident incomes are important for buying power at consumer-oriented retail, dining/
entertainment, and service businesses. While the metro area and state have lagged other major
west coast markets, Hillsboro workers are relatively well compensated – with wages that
average 46% more than the average wage across the entire metro area.

While high incomes are supportive of greater consumer expenditures, a growing share of
consumer expenditure need not occur locally. This is especially the case if the total market area
served is more readily accessed from other Washington County or metro area locations or via
the internet and associated e-commerce.

(6) Transportation
Transportation access is important to Hillsboro’s economic development potential in three key
respects. First is the business need for effective, reliable freight transportation via truck or
airport access. Rail and marine appear to be lesser considerations due to lack of significant rail
access to Hillsboro industries and lack of marine container shipment capacity until subsequently
re-introduced on a weekly basis from the Port of Portland.

Reasonable workforce commute access is important as a determinant of the effective labor
shed. Commute access is vulnerable due to regional road congestion and possible worker
unwillingness to commute long distances (especially for younger workers). This is further
documented by information provided with Appendix A.

Convenient transportation access is a consideration for retail and consumer service businesses
reliant on trip times competitive with alternative business locations. Hillsboro’s location
(especially for its downtown) at the edge of the metro area limits its total customer draw
relative to other parts of the metro area – as compared with Beaverton/Tigard serving the
greater Washington County market or central Portland as serving businesses dependent on a
metro-wide customer base. Disruptive technologies as with autonomous/electronic (AV/EV)
vehicles may well transform transportation in ways not yet readily foreseen – although timing
for regulatory and consumer acceptance remains uncertain.

(7) Utility Infrastructure
Infrastructure important to Hillsboro industry includes electric power (as for semiconductor and
other power intensive tech users), redundant fiber for telecommunications, water (as for
semiconductor and food processors), and wastewater treatment. The availability, quality and
cost of utility infrastructure has been a significant location consideration and draw for major
Hillsboro area employers. On-going investment is important to support further growth.

(8) Civic Infrastructure
Included in this category is critical community infrastructure as for City services, K-12 schools,
health care, parks/open spaces, and cultural attractions. By most accounts, Hillsboro is well


         City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis – Technical Appendices ♦ Page 54
regarded for the depth and quality of its community infrastructure. This is exemplified in recent
years by investments ranging from rapid expansion of local health care facilities to recruitment
of a minor league baseball franchise.

Due to the COVID pandemic, access to much of this civic infrastructure locally and nationally
was curtailed as a precaution to limit infection spread. Whether and how civic access and
engagement fares with effective vaccines and longer-term protocols is not yet fully clear but
will be important to re-establish sustained civic involvement and identity.

(9) Environmental Conservation
Conserving the environment yields both business benefits and costs. Protection of wetlands,
other critical areas and open spaces can be an amenity – drawing business facilities that value a
campus setting as has been the case in Hillsboro over a sustained period.

Conversely, environmental set asides reduce developable land area, contributing to the city’s
prospective employment land deficit. Permitting processes add time and cost to a development
project, especially constraining if viewed as more onerous relative to competitive locations
domestically and internationally. In Hillsboro, 5 significant portion of the vacant employment
land inventory is categorized as undevelopable due, in part, to wetland and other
environmental constraints.

(10) Housing
Due to regional traffic congestion and growing workforce interest in shorter commutes, job-
housing balance is of more significance than in the past when the labor shed was considered to
be the entire metro region plus adjoining non-urban counties. Affordability is also of growing
concern for this metro area as well as others nationwide – a concern of even more pronounced
significance through the pandemic and ramp-up of housing demand.

Greater diversity of housing product increasingly factors into the live-work equation. Younger
workers are often willing to trade off a large suburban home for smaller house and yard
offering immediate walkable access to urban amenities and public open space, albeit with more
of the home space allocated to work-related uses in the wake of the COVID pandemic.
Hillsboro’s competitive position for continued industrial investment depends, in part, on
providing the quantity, quality and diversity of housing expected by a changing workforce.

(11) Quality of Life
Quality of life is a largely subjective consideration that can mean different things to different
people in varied settings across the U.S. For Oregon residents, a significant part of the quality of
life equation is rooted in access to outdoor recreation – both active and passive – including
mountains, ocean areas and, more recently, to regional attractions ranging from internationally
recognized wineries to locally sourced foods. To attract the workforce of the next generation, it
appears important to provide more urban and placemaking amenities in a setting with better
integration of work and home then previously.


         City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis – Technical Appendices ♦ Page 55
HILLSBORO’S COMPETITIVE POSITION
OAR 660-009-0015 (4) stipulates that a community’s assessment of economic development
potential “must consider the planning area’s economic advantages and disadvantages.” This
EOA has taken a focused approach to identify and characterize economic advantages and
disadvantages from the perspective of the community’s competitive position for investment
and employment.

This approach is especially important for a city like Hillsboro which has an unusually high share
of traded sector activity – defined by ORS 2855.280 as “industries in which member firms sell
their goods or services into markets for which national or international competition exists.”

Economic advantages and disadvantages may be considered as a snapshot in time – specific to
the business mix and locational attributes of the community at the present time. This
competitive position assessment also identifies opportunities and threats – conditions
reasonably anticipated in the future and often driven or greatly affected by market forces
external to the local community.

The assessment of competitive position draws from both the quantitative and qualitative
perspectives as provided with this updated Hillsboro EOA. The chart below provides a summary
listing of strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats (or SWOT), followed by more
detailed discussion of each SWOT component.

       reputation for solution-oriented public-private partnership. As one interviewee notes,

       including provision of development incentives as with urban renewal and access to
       Enterprise Zone (EZ) and Strategic Investment Program (SIP) resources.

As observed by one stakeholder, “We have the second most manufacturing economy in the U.S.
and Hillsboro is the most important traded sector in Oregon.”

Weaknesses
Counterbalancing the strengths are weaknesses that will be important to address over the
current 20-year planning cycle. These weaknesses are noted as including:

   •   Overdependence on one anchor semiconductor firm – with Hillsboro’s economic
       prosperity reliant on the cyclical and long-term performance of a single industry, further
       compounded by primary reliance on the competitive fortunes of a single (albeit
       dominant) firm in that industry.
   •   Consumer services not fully meeting local needs – with Beaverton offering proximity
       more central to the full westside residential and business market. By contrast,
       downtown Hillsboro is situated to serve one side of the city somewhat removed from
       other major sources of in-city and westside population.
   •   Lack of nationally recognized research university – placing greater reliance on
       attracting non-local educated workforce for higher skilled and management positions.
       Interviewees cite a need to broaden the talent pool and address loss of talent as a large
       cohort of baby boomer workers reach retirement.
   •   Regional congestion affecting freight & workforce access – an issue of growing
       significance unless mitigated by regional highway, transit and future vehicle technology
       improvements together with added local workforce housing. With regional growth and
       congestion, more freight and distribution facilities are needed across the metro area.
   •   Availability and affordability of workforce housing – cited as an emerging “economic
       development issue” requiring new approaches as for a broader range of housing types
       and possibly company-sponsored housing development.
   •   Land inventory inadequate for forecast job growth – with the existing developable
       employment land base adequate to handle only 23%-55% of projected employment
       growth potential for Hillsboro over the next 20 years. In the wake of the pandemic,
       greater flexibility in land use planning will be needed in the years ahead. As one industry
       leader commented, the region “is too rigid in how it thinks about land.” Another notes
       that the land use process is simply “too slow,” not keeping up with the times. Yet
       another suggests a “what to do” guide to addressing regulatory requirements.
   •   Uncertain tax and regulatory environment – potentially affecting proposed and other
       future tax and incentive programs as may affect feasibility of Hillsboro investments,
       especially with capital intensive fab and related high-tech facilities.



        City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis – Technical Appendices ♦ Page 58
Opportunities
Going forward, key opportunities for realization over the next 5-20 years and perhaps beyond
to a 50-year time horizon may reasonably be expected to include:

   •   R&D with applied technology manufacturing – aimed to attract and foster creative and
       intellectual talent and capital indigenous to Portland as a globally recognized center
       more on par with Los Angeles, Silicon Valley, and the Puget Sound.
   •   Business diversification – focused on enhanced market presence for the City’s targeted
       industry clusters together with potential for other under-represented sectors that have
       demonstrated improved competitive position through this most recent economic cycle,
       then showing resilience through the subsequent pandemic and economic downturn.
   •   Jobs/housing balance – to assure housing opportunity accommodating the full range of
       local workforce residential needs and preferences. While Portland has been the draw in
       recent years, stakeholders suggest that the opportunity for live/work balance may now
       be shifting toward Washington County. Beaverton pops up as perhaps a prototype for a
       lower density but urban environment of the future, offering synergistic opportunities in
       combination with Hillsboro’s tech-forward manufacturing prowess.
   •   Transport innovation – supporting balanced public transportation options regionally
       and locally together with industry-driven AV/EV technology pioneered in Hillsboro and
       the Portland metro market.
   •   Market-driven 50-year urbanization – likely aimed at some employment densification
       together with more at-home work and reduced on-site parking need coupled with
       world-class technology and related education/workforce training leadership.

Threats
Potentially offsetting the opportunities are prospective threats or barriers that could serve to
undermine continuing and sustained economic vitality for the Hillsboro community, greater
Portland metro region and state, including:

   •   Risk of losing the anchor competitive edge – which could result for a variety of reasons,
       whether specific to Hillsboro’s largest firm or from external forces such as off-shore
       competition and threats to global supply chains. This concern is especially the case for
       firms that are local because they started local. As one locally grown business owner
       suggests: “We’re here because we live here. But with the new economy, we could be
       anywhere.”
   •   Workforce displacement – for reasons potentially related to automation, need for
       continuing adult education, reduced potential availability of workplace benefits as for
       health care, lack of employer-responsive job training and greater childcare issues
       through at least the duration of the COVID pandemic.
   •   Less than full-service community – with local residents and businesses forced or
       preferring to leave Hillsboro for a significant portion of their retail and service needs.


         City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis – Technical Appendices ♦ Page 59
   •   Transport gridlock – if out of step with competitive locations, resulting in lost local
       business investment and employment opportunity (particularly for high wage jobs).
   •   Non-market regulation – ranging from state-wide issues such as potential loss of tax
       incentives for high value manufacturing and placement of tariffs affecting pricing and
       competitiveness for local product manufacturing. As expressed by one stakeholder, a
       concern is that Oregon “may go the way of California.”

Transition to a New-New Normal
The aftermath of the 2007-09 Great Recession was focused on the transition to what was
termed as a new normal. With COVID and economic recession of 2020, the focus now shifts
perhaps even more dramatically to what might be considered as a new-new normal.

Historical economic data presents often useful guideposts of where the economy has been, but
not necessarily of where it is now going. Qualitative evidence from stakeholders provides useful
insights as to the transition now underway but not yet with a clear picture of where Hillsboro
will be five years from now, let alone over the next 20 or 50 years.

A clear message from business and community leaders is that this next round of a new normal
will be about more than economic recovery or a simple return to the business and economic
development practices of the last decade. In addition to accelerating trends of disruptive
technology and live-work connection, the next decade may well serve to define technologies
viewed as most pivotal and further shift current live-work boundaries. These transitions likely
will blur traditional distinctions between employment and residential land uses.

The realization of how vulnerable a community can be to external conditions that are well
beyond local control places increased emphasis toward better assuring resiliency in the face of
unexpected shocks to the local economy. This may mean prioritizing business sectors less
vulnerable to downturns or that offset one another – much as is expected with a diversified
stock and related investment portfolio. As one stakeholder interviewed during the summer of
2020 observes: “Improved resiliency requires increased diversification of the economic base.”

Even with a less than clearly discernable crystal ball, there are some features of this new-new
normal that can be outlined – at least in preliminary terms. This discussion can be divided
between Hillsboro’s expanding tech-driven traded sector industrial base and its resulting
service-based economy. Emphasis is placed on potential land use implications.

Tech Driven Traded Sector Industries
Considered are prospects for semiconductor, data center, biotech, software and supportive
industrial activity:

   •   Hillsboro tech has been driven by Intel as its anchor semiconductor firm and largest
       employer. As with others in the industry, Intel has experienced record-breaking sales
       with tech intensification through the pandemic, but future prospects are perhaps less
       certain due to rapid technological change, global competitive and policy initiatives.

   •   Other supportive industrial activity includes vendors to Hillsboro’s tech firms, logistics
       and transportation (including air freight) providers, distribution and fulfillment centers,
       and other diversified manufacturing (for example related to sportswear). Nationally,
       warehouse/distribution activity has recently performed as the nation’s top industrial
       market segment – but appears increasingly oriented to the nation’s largest metro areas
       (often of larger scale than the Portland metro region). While employment density can
       vary, catering to uses that support Hillsboro’s core traded sector competencies will best
       reinforce long-run economic recovery and on-going resiliency to future external shocks.

Service Sectors
Sectors covered are office space, retail/hospitality, health care, and workforce housing:

   •   As noted, prospective demand for office space is currently the most uncertain due to
       short- and long-term outcomes of the pandemic, dependent on whether and to what
       extent work-from-home becomes viewed as a viable long-term option. This transition is
       likely to play out as existing tenant leases come up for renewal. Existing office spaces
       may be reconfigured for greater flexibility including social distancing with priority to key
       corporate functions. If overall demand decreases, there may be the eventual need to
       repurpose some office spaces, especially in older facilities toward non-office uses.
   •   Even before the pandemic, retail/hospitality space demand had stalled due to more
       sales activity occurring via e-commerce. This trend subsequently accelerated, meaning
       further slowing in retail demand growth. The effect can be severe for small independent
       retail and dining establishments. Viable retail will involve more on-site pick up. As retail
       vacancies increase, existing developments as with older strip centers and potentially
       downtown retail uses may need to be repurposed for other uses, ranging from last mile
       fulfillment centers to residential use. Lodging demand will return albeit slowly with the
       long-term outlook also uncertain due to possible permanent reduction in business and
       meeting-related travel (replaced by virtual Zoom and related video conference options).
   •   While health care facilities have experienced financial issues during the pandemic, a
       return to normal can be expected as vaccine and therapeutic treatments prove
       effective. Latent demand for procedures foregone during the pandemic can re-emerge.
       Hillsboro’s growth and an aging population should support a return to a more rapid job
       growth trajectory for providers in the years ahead. However, locations of service may
       become more decentralized as with smaller store-front clinics and telemedicine.
   •   While not previously considered as an employment use (except for self-employed), the
       worker’s residence may become a significant (perhaps the fastest growing) workplace in
       the years ahead. Those working at home are already showing desire for increased
       allocation of distinct work area in the home and millennials are gravitating to ownership
       away from rentals where financially affordable. This could reverse the trend from multi-
       family rental occupancy back toward demand for single-family home ownership. If
       multi-family demand subsides, there still may be a need for larger rental units than have
       been developed in recent years. Over a 20-50 time horizon, it is possible that the home
       becomes a primary workplace of choice, potentially even for a majority of Americans.

         City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis – Technical Appendices ♦ Page 62
TARGET INDUSTRY CLUSTERS
Like many communities, Hillsboro has identified target industry clusters for which it is either
competitive now or has reason for aspiring to increased economic opportunity in the years
ahead. This assessment of community economic development potential involves comparison of
local target industry clusters with those of the metro region and the state – followed by
suggestion of potential target sector refinements resulting from this EOA.

Comparative Regional to State-Wide Target Industries
In addition to target industries defined for the City of Hillsboro’s economic development
program, those most relevant for added consideration are similar listings for the metro area as
articulated by Greater Portland Inc. (GPI) and statewide targets as defined by the state agency
Business Oregon. A summary comparison of current listings is provided by the following chart.

While the nomenclature of the three target industry listings varies, there is considerable overall
correspondence in terms of substantive content. All three organizations favor varied
combinations of tech-oriented and advanced manufacturing. More specifically, local and metro-
wide focus is also placed on computers, electronics and software.

Some differences are also noted:

   •   Unlike its counterpart organizations, Hillsboro includes bioscience and medical devices
       as a key industry.
   •   For the Portland metro area, GPI includes industry clusters not as strongly represented
       in Hillsboro – notably apparel and outdoor, metals and machinery, food and beverage,
       climate tech, and design and media.
   •   Business Oregon also provides attention to sectors important to metro and non-metro
       areas of the state but not necessarily represented strongly in Hillsboro – as with
       business services, outdoor gear and apparel, food and beverage, and forestry and wood
       products.


         City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis – Technical Appendices ♦ Page 63
Target Sector Refinements
Clearly for Hillsboro, it is advantageous to identify key industries based on existing comparative
and competitive advantages of the city’s existing business and industry mix – both as
complementary to and distinct from the metro region and state.

An added advantage and a challenge posed by target sector listings lies in their seeming
ambiguity. Historically defined in terms of readily measurable industry (as with NAICS)
categories, target sector listings now often intentionally reach across traditional industry
classifications. This approach recognizes the reality of the marketplace – especially where there
are opportunities for a particular industry to be supported by local vendors or customers within
a related business segment.

As in the past, Hillsboro may modify its industry clusters to reflect and serve new or emerging
industry opportunities in the years ahead. This would recognize the potential to step in
alongside and encourage sectors that currently may be relatively weakly represented in
Hillsboro but with growing competitive presence.

Listed below are examples of already identified emerging industry opportunities including:

   •   Increased computer chip manufacturing capacity
   •   Automotive & aerospace applications
   •   Energy storage
   •   Data centers
   •   Artificial intelligence research & deployment
   •   Supply chain on-shoring & management
   •   On-shoring national defense manufacturing
   •   Tangible hardware
   •   Bio-tech expansion
   •   Climate technology
   •   Digital security

The listing is intended to be illustrative and not to preclude other as yet unforeseen but future
potential prospects not yet on the horizon.

Priority consideration for business targeting might be provided to these emerging sectors (or
specific businesses) offering potential for strong employment, tax revenue, and/or
supplemental business leveraging (or “pull-through”) benefits. Hillsboro’s target industries also
represent traded sector functions with higher economic multipliers – creating more indirect
and induced added employment and income opportunities – above what are typically realized
from local consumer-oriented service sectors. Consistent with a hybrid development scenario,
an adaptive industry cluster approach can be positioned to address international, domestic and
regionally-driven opportunities.

EMPLOYMENT LAND NEEDS
This appendix comprises detailed background and tabular results associated with the Chapter
IV EOA discussion of employment land needs. Topics covered by this appendix include analysis
purpose and approach, description of Hillsboro’s employment buildable lands inventory (BLI),
employment and land demand forecast scenarios, and employment-driven land need.

ANALYSIS PURPOSE & APPROACH
The determination of needs for commercial and industrial employment lands draws on results
of the employment forecast scenarios coupled with the more qualitative perspectives
describing community economic potential. In effect, this portion of the EOA analysis compares
land supply with projected employment driven demand to assess site availability over 5- and
20-year planning horizons with alternate employment scenarios considered. Also included is
summary consideration of potential longer-term, 50-year potential employment land needs.

The land needs analysis is intended to identify and characterize the demand and supply for
industrial and commercial sites. Also described are the types of sites needed to accommodate
targeted growth industries and existing employers that could potentially expand – together
with opportunities for spin-off employers and entities that provide support for existing clusters.

The analysis aims to further identify specific site sizes, special site requirements or other
characteristics affecting the needed land supply. The readiness of the existing land supply for
industrial/manufacturing and other types of employment development is also addressed.

HILLSBORO’S EMPLOYMENT BLI
The City of Hillsboro has coordinated with Metro to evaluate the city’s supply of buildable lands
available for employment uses. The City has utilized Metro’s Buildable Land Inventory (BLI)
methodology to revise portions of the 2018 Draft Urban Growth Report (UGR) pertaining to
Hillsboro’s Urban Growth Boundary (and future growth areas).

BLI Approach & Methodology
Hillsboro’s employment BLI has been updated utilizing an approach similar to that of Metro.
However, the exact methodology applied for this update differs somewhat from Metro’s 2018
analysis since the City does not have direct access to the Metroscope model in-house. The
resulting supply focused BLI was prepared by the City of Hillsboro in late 2019. This
approximated the time period of data availability for employment as a driver of land demand.

The 2021 EOA was adopted in 2022 and was appealed to the Land Use Board of Appeals (LUBA)
by 1000 Friends of Oregon (Friends) and Metro. While Friends and Metro raised several


         City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis – Technical Appendices ♦ Page 65
assignments of error relating to employment growth forecasting and the Comprehensive Plan
status, most of these arguments were denied by LUBA. However, LUBA agreed with Friends
that the 2019 buildable lands inventory (BLI) for employment land that was included in the
2021 EOA did not apply the correct analysis for determining the redevelopment potential of
“developed lands.” LUBA thus remanded the decision to the City to address that issue.

Consequently, this 2021 EOA has been amended to incorporate an employment BLI based on
December 2020 data as prepared by the planning firm MIG in compliance with the terms of the
LUBA remand. The results of the amended BLI dated May 13, 2024 as provided by the planning
firm MIG are included as Appendix E.

Appendix E describes the methodology utilized for the amended employment BLI together with
quantitative land supply results. This Appendix C document focuses on the demand side of the
land needs analysis, specifically the conversion of employment forecasts associated with
alternative scenarios into associated building space and employment land needs. The combined
supply-demand outputs are brought together and summarized with Chapter IV of the main EOA
report document.

What now follows is a more detailed discussion of the process for translating forecast
employment growth into associated land needs.

EMPLOYMENT & LAND DEMAND FORECAST SCENARIOS
Three employment scenarios have been identified and quantified with this 2020 EOA – each
involving substantially different potential forecast outcomes per Chapter III of the EOA report:

   •   Scenario A Straight-Line Growth
       (forecast for a net addition of 36,910 Hillsboro jobs from 2020-40)
   •   Scenario B Exponential Growth
       (with net addition of as many as 87,800 net new jobs from 2020-40)
   •   Scenario C Hybrid Growth
       (focused on target industry sectors with 65,975 net new jobs from 2020-40)

The initial model alternatives formulated were Scenarios A and B. Scenario C was then
developed as a hybrid composite of Scenarios A and B. This Appendix focuses on detailed
quantification of the initial scenarios – A and B. Chapter IV of the full EOA compares and
contrasts summary outputs of all three scenarios.

For purposes of this EOA, forecast scenario results may be categorized in three separate ways –
by NAICS (or overall employment sector), by building type (a primary focus of this EOA) and by
overall Comprehensive Plan designation (as summarized in Chapter IV of the EOA report).




         City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis – Technical Appendices ♦ Page 66
NAICS Categories
The employment trends analysis has been based on employment categories of the North
American Industry Classification System (NAICS) – as this is the industry classification system
most used for defining employment uses locally, statewide and nationally.

Key differences between Scenarios A and B can be found in potential job growth associated
with sectors including health care/social assistance, wholesale trade, transportation and
warehousing, information, professional services, administrative, arts/entertainment/recreation,
and other services – as discussed with EOA Chapter II. These are all sectors for which recent job
growth has been particularly rapid post-recession. If extrapolated over the next 20 years with
Scenario B, net job growth is at least double that of Scenario A job outcomes.

Categorization of Employment by Building Type

type(s) of buildings that a particular employment sector typically inhabits. This categorization
system was first applied with Metro’s 2009 UGR as a means of translating employment growth
to building and associated land needs. This methodology also was applied with the most recent
2017 Hillsboro EOA.

EMPLOYMENT-DRIVEN LAND NEED
The next steps in this demand or needs analysis require the translation of employment growth
into associated employment land need. The analysis begins with discussion of the conversion
factors utilized, followed by presentation of resulting land need outputs for Scenarios A and B.

Conversion Factors
Translating employment growth to land demand involves three sets of conversion factors:

   •     Conversion of employment need to building space requirement – by applying typical
         ratios of building square footage per employee suitable to each building typology.
   •     Conversion of building space need to associated land demand – by applying a floor area
         ratio (FAR) factor specific to each building typology.
   •     Application of a market vacancy factor – recognizing space turnover at normalized
         occupancy typical for each building type.

As indicated by the following chart, a fourth line provides the resulting implied overall
employment density factors associated with each typology including adjustment for market
vacancy. Ratios applied are those previously used with Hillsboro’s 2017 EOA. These factors are
generally consistent with conversion factors first applied with Metro’s 2009 UGR (including sub-
regional variations), but with some modifications apparent with the city’s 2017 EOA – including
addition of market vacancy factors.

For industrial uses, employment densities range from 3.0 employees per acre with data center

from 18 jobs per acre for institutional to nearly 45 jobs per acre with institutional uses. These
conversion factors are applied to job forecasts with all scenarios considered.

Employment-Driven Land Needs by Scenario
With the straight-line growth forecast of Scenario A, close to 2,230 net acres of employment
land would be required from 2020-40. This is similar to the 2,336 acre 20-year need estimated
with the prior 2017 EOA. With a more robust compound growth rate (CAGR) applied based on
experience of the current economic cycle as shown by Scenario B, the employment land need
more than doubles to a net total of nearly 5,330 acres over the same 2020-40 time horizon.

building needs at 10-13% of net land need, with office and retail each at about 12%. Scenario C

When considered by NAICS employment sector (as detailed on the next page), the largest

wholesale trade (15%), information (11%), and transportation/warehousing (10%).

With Scenario B, the relative ordering of employment land needs changes somewhat – with
wholesale trade and health care and social assistance each accounting for as much as 20% of
total land need. Information and transportation would each account for 12% of land need with
manufacturing at 11%. The manufacturing land need does not change as much as for the other
significant employment land uses noted between Scenarios A and B.

APPENDIX D.
IMPLEMENTATION POLICIES
This Appendix provides a detailed review of the implementation framework for existing and
prospective City of Hillsboro policies affecting economic development implementation city-
wide. This review is conducted in support of the summarized recommendations as provided by
the Chapter V implementation policies discussion of the 2021 Hillsboro EOA. Topics covered by
this appendix are background and approach, current framework for Hillsboro economic
development, key drivers of economic development change, EOA recommended
implementation policies and measures, and updating of Comprehensive Plan goals and policies.

BACKGROUND & APPROACH
As stipulated by OAR 660-009-0020, these policies are to provide a statement of community
development objectives, commitment to provide a competitive short-term supply of land for
industrial and other employment uses, and a commitment to provide adequate sites and
facilities.

Related OAR provisions address strategies within a metro area to meet short-term supply
needs, maintain existing levels of industrial and other employment use, support expansion and
increased productivity of existing firms, include brownfield redevelopment and address prime
industrial land. Cities also are encouraged to adopt plan policies covering additional
implementation approaches including but not limited to tax incentives, land use controls,
preferential tax assessments, capital improvements, property acquisition techniques,
public/private partnerships and intergovernmental agreements.

CURRENT FRAMEWORK FOR HILLSBORO ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT
City policy related to economic development is covered primarily from two documents – a 2017
Economic Opportunities Analysis (EOA) and the subsequent updated Hillsboro Comprehensive
Plan (dated November 21, 2017 and effective as of January 2, 2018). Also of significance – albeit
with less specific land use detail – is the more recently completed Hillsboro 2035 Community
Plan.

2017 EOA
The most recent Hillsboro EOA dated February 7, 2017 did not include a direct statement of
community economic development objectives as stipulated by OAR 660-009-0020 but did
address a series of recommendations organized around three topics – capacity, business
environment and recruitment/retention. As stated by the EOA, provided was a “summary list of
implementation measures to encourage effective utilization of the City’s employment
capacity.” 2017 EOA recommended implementation measures are detailed by the listing on the
following page.

         City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis – Technical Appendices ♦ Page 73
                   2017 EOA Recommended Implementation Measures

   • Ongoing planning and infrastructure investments in the North Hillsboro Industrial
       Area
   •     Maintain and expand infrastructure necessary to support employers and realize the
         City’s development capacity
   •     Support additional investment in existing employment areas, including programs
         supporting adaptive re-use
   •     Review current zoning and entitlements to ensure they are supportive of desired
         development outcomes
   •     Evaluate parking management programs where appropriate to potentially free up
         additional property and/or allow for intensification of employment densities

   •     Monitor land consumption and usage patterns within the City over time, and

         City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis – Technical Appendices ♦ Page 74
2018 Hillsboro Comprehensive Plan
Chapter 11 of the Hillsboro Comprehensive Plan addresses “Building Economy & Infrastructure”
including five goals, each of which is supported by more specific and detailed policy measures.
The adopted five goals read as follows:

   •   Goal 1 – Competitive Advantage: Diversify and expand the economy to give Hillsboro,
       the region, and the state a competitive advantage.
   •   Goal 2 – Facilities, Utilities & Services: Catalyze economic development through high-
       quality public facilities, utilities and services.
   •   Goal 3 – Land Supply: Manage land supply to meet short and long-term economic
       development needs of Hillsboro, the region, and the state.
   •   Goal 4 – Equity: Promote economic development opportunities for individuals and small
       and emerging businesses to ensure equitable access to resources.
   •   Goal 5 – Livability: Develop and sustain a vibrant City to support economic
       development.

On the following two pages are provided the goals and associated economic development (ED)
policies of Hillsboro’s Comprehensive Plan as currently adopted.

Comparability of Implementation Listings
While the 2017 EOA and 2018 Comprehensive Plan listings are comparable in terms of overall
policy direction, there is little direct consistency in terms of topic organization or the details of
specific policies. The areas of greatest alignment appear to be with respect to themes as for
target industry prioritization, business recruitment/retention, employment land supply,
infrastructure support for economic development, and employee housing choice.

Overall, the Comprehensive Plan policies cover more topics and tend to be more detailed.
However, the prior EOA implementation recommendations also provide detail regarding such
items as infrastructure investments in the North Hillsboro Industrial area and encouragement
of parking management programs to free up additional property or increase employment
densities – items not as directly addressed with the Comprehensive Plan ED policies.

Neither the EOA nor the Comprehensive Plan provide much of a direct link to the City of
Hillsboro’s active economic development programs, specifically the application of development
incentives to assist in meeting the City’s goals for building economy and infrastructure. As an
added note, neither the EOA recommendations nor the Comprehensive Plan policies are
organized in a manner that provides ready comparability to the implementation policy
framework outlined as guidance by OAR 660-009-0020.

The approach taken through the rest of this implementation appendix follows what could be
considered as a three-step process to:

   •   Focus on key economic and local conditions that have changed in the recent years or
       remain as unmet challenges, meriting added attention with an update to Hillsboro’s
       economic development policies
   •   Address topics as outlined by the Division 9 LCDC guidance
   •   Place and arrange resulting recommended policies into the existing framework of the
       Chapter 11 portion of Hillsboro’s existing or updated Comprehensive Plan

While there undoubtedly are other approaches that might be considered to organize an
updated set of economic development implementation policies, this 2021 EOA aims both to
reinforce adopted City-wide planning priorities and identify new initiatives as appropriate.

KEY DRIVERS OF ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT CHANGE
This update reflects key drivers of economic development changes globally that have emerged
since the 2017 EOA, notably:

   •   The COVID pandemic and economic downturn which have accelerated temporary and
       likely lasting changes to work and shop from home at the expense of brick-and-mortar
       commercial office and retail space – but also creating demand for upsized housing.
   •   Resurgence of industrial space demand due to e-commerce distribution, accelerated
       technological change, data center needs, and re-shoring of traditional manufacturing.

         City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis – Technical Appendices ♦ Page 78
   •    Changing competitive advantage of tech leadership with semiconductors, to the recent
        disadvantage of American firms including Intel as Oregon’s largest private employer,
        albeit with additional planned investment as renewed corporate and national priorities.
   •    Governmental commitment to a reinvigorated semiconductor industry exemplified by
        passage of the federal CHIPS and Science Act of 2022 coupled with August 2022 findings
        and recommendations of the Oregon Semiconductor Competitiveness Task Force.

Hillsboro has great opportunity to capitalize on these emerging trends as Oregon’s economic
engine – to the extent that it maintains and builds on its core semiconductor technology
manufacturing prowess. But there is also new downside risk, dependent on the changing
fortunes and continued industry leadership of the community’s major employer. And on local
and regional capacity to better leverage the next waves of tech-forward investment.

Implementation policies are organized to cover topics stipulated by OAR 660-009-0020 to
reflect key issues and objectives associated with this 2021 EOA update. Topics covered are
employment land use, transportation and utility infrastructure, target and supporting industry
clusters, economic development incentives, workforce readiness, and partnership opportunity.
