Employment Land Use
Following the articulation of community economic development objectives, the first policies
identified by OAR 660-009 are to provide an adequate employment land inventory with priority
emphasis on short term supply defined as “suitable land that is ready for construction within
one year of an application.”

Attention is also needed to assure total land supply as determined to be “adequate to
accommodate industrial and other employment uses for a 20-year planning period.” Cities are
to provide at least 25% of the total land supply within their UGB as short-term supply – albeit
with exceptions noted for jurisdictions unable to meet this target. 3

2017 EOA. Hillsboro’s 2017 EOA forecast employment of 40,000 net new jobs over a 20-year
planning horizon. This resulted in a projected short-term need for 663 acres and long-term
need for 2,952 acres (including 195 acres on non-employment land). The reconciliation of
employment needs and available capacity indicated an adequate 20-year supply of industrial
land but an inadequate supply of land for commercial uses.

The EOA also indicated that vacant land alone was inadequate to meet 20-year needs. Assuring
adequate supply would mean that capacity from redevelopment and infill would need to
represent nearly half (46%) of all employment land capacity. Inclusion of redevelopment and
infill lands appeared adequate to provide capacity for less than 15 years of the 20-year planning
period. A further conclusion was that: “The heavy reliance upon redevelopment and infill to
meet employment needs represents a significant risk,” suggesting a need for ongoing land
inventory monitoring and refinements of employment capacities as better data becomes
available.

With regard to short-term needs, the 2017 EOA appears to be less definitive, albeit noting that
the “limited supply is indicative of short-term supply challenges and suggests that new urban
areas will be critical in maintaining a competitive land supply.” The report also noted that:
“Because potential infill land with existing urban services is a large share of short-term
inventory, this condition could be limiting Hillsboro’s ability to maintain a market ready
inventory of sites.” 4

2021 EOA. This updated EOA is based on employment forecast scenarios and an amended
employment buildable lands inventory (BLI) with data from December 2020 was prepared by
MIG as of March 2024. As amended, the BLI results in an estimate of 1,225 net buildable acres
on vacant lands together with portions of partially developed sites suitable for added
development. Of this, 91.3% is zoned for industrial, 2.2% for commercial and 6.5% for mixed
commercial and residential use. Of the net buildable acreage, 46% is currently outside the
Hillsboro city limits but within the community’s Urban Growth Boundary (UGB). Results of this
refined BLI have been compared with three alternative 20-year employment forecast scenarios:


         City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis – Technical Appendices ♦ Page 80
   •   Scenario A Straight-Line Growth – from a base of an estimated 84,390 jobs as of 2020,
       this scenario would involve an increase of an increase of 36,910 jobs over the 2020-40
       time period, resulting in 121,300 jobs by 2040. Scenario A results in a need for nearly
       2,230 acres over 20 years – with a resulting deficit of 1,004 acres (particularly for
       commercial lands).
   •   Scenario B Exponential Growth – extrapolating growth forward on an exponential basis
       could result in an increase of as many as 87,800 added jobs over 20 years, effectively
       doubling employment in Hillsboro by 2040 to 173,570 in-city jobs. If realized this
       scenario would result in a prospective need for as much as 5,330 acres over 20 years –
       with the total employment land deficit quadrupling to about 4,105 acres.
   •   Scenario C Hybrid Growth – resulting in an estimated 146,975 jobs in Hillsboro by 2040,
       based on assumption of compounding growth for industries associated with cluster
       targets versus lesser rates of growth for other sectors. Of the year 2040 estimate,
       61,895 net new jobs would be added over the two decades from 2020-40. Scenario C
       results in a need for just over 3,840 acres over 20 years – with a resulting deficit of 2,617
       acres.

With any of these scenarios, Hillsboro also would not be able to satisfy the short-term (5-year)
need with reliance on existing in-city lands only. As with the prior 2017 EOA, the greatest land
shortfall (in percentage terms) is for lands zoned for commercial or mixed-use – potentially
placing pressure for conversion of some industrial land to commercial development.

Implementation Options. With both the prior 2017 and 2021 EOAs, the clear indication is
that Hillsboro likely does not have adequate employment land capacity to accommodate either
short-term (5-year) or long-term (20-year) employment growth. Several mitigation options have
been outlined with this EOA – together with identification of associated advantages and
disadvantages -- as a potential means to better reconcile employment land demand and supply.
These might include any or some combination of the following:

   •   Reduce the EOA employment forecast to match current BLI capacity – essentially
       discarding Scenarios B/C and reducing the Scenario A jobs forecast by about 45%. This
       option may avoid the need to expand Hillsboro’s UGB and future annexations of land for
       industrial development – but at the expense of foregoing significant high-wage job
       potential for Hillsboro, the metro region and state in the years ahead.
   •   Focus EOA forecast reductions on the most land extensive sectors – likely resulting in
       reduced allocations for lower job density uses as for data centers, warehouse and some
       flex/business park uses. This option may reduce but not necessarily eliminate the
       impetus for added land outside of Hillsboro’s current city boundaries even from higher
       density major potential employers. Lack of property inventory for some land-extensive
       supply-chain uses may also dampen the appeal of Hillsboro for major tech employers.
   •   Adjust employment to land need conversion factors toward a more urban profile –
       emphasizing increased building FAR and job densities together with site redevelopment.
       factors. This option is associated with advantages and disadvantages similar to those


         City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis – Technical Appendices ♦ Page 81
       with focused on discouraging land extensive sectors (as noted above). Also possible
       would be to eliminate the market vacancy factor which is not explicitly included in some
       EOA analyses.
   •   Increase the planned BLI supply, especially for growth areas around Hillsboro – most
       notably with further annexation and urban service provision but also via mitigation
       measures to increase net to gross acreage use ratios – as a significant portion of the
       vacant and partially vacant employment land inventory is categorized as undevelopable
       due, in part, to wetland and other environmental constraints. This approach to
       increasing in-city land supply might be accomplished, for example, with off-site
       mitigation but would depend on significant and regional planning and regulatory review
       and approvals.
   •   Pursue Metro region and statewide recognition of Hillsboro’s strategic significance –
       for long-term competitiveness and high wage jobs as integral to long-term economic
       vitality, both metro and state-wide. Of the options considered, this is perhaps the most
       pivotal to ensuring the continued competitiveness of Hillsboro as Oregon’s center of
       high-tech investment but depends on broad recognition of current and prospective
       benefits for sustained community and economic vitality regionally and statewide.

As a result of the pandemic and changing work patterns, another option might be considered –
allocating more of employment growth (on an FTE equivalent basis) away from work to home
sites. There are two potential downsides with this option: a) no sustained experience as yet
post-pandemic to determine the extent of a permanent shift to work from home (primarily
affecting office workers); and b) uncertainty as to whether and how much space needs in
traditional single use employment settings may change per on-site employee (either decreasing
or increasing floor space requirements as from robotization and improved supply change
management), especially for manufacturing and warehouse/distribution uses.

Implementation Measures. On a preliminary basis the following measures are
recommended for consideration:

   •   As a minimum measure, adopt a 20-year jobs and land use forecast similar to Scenario
       C Hybrid Growth. This scenario best serves Hillsboro’s existing and prospective
       competitive advantages for sectors targeted to business-cluster growth opportunities.
   •   Annex and serve added employment land as needed to meet at least the 5-year
       Scenario A Straight-Line short-term supply requirement. While it is possible that a slow
       or delayed economic recovery may dampen demand near-term, this is less likely for
       industrial than commercial use. Having the full complement of shovel-ready site supply
       in place also better positions Hillsboro and the region from the mutual and reinforcing
       perspectives of economic recovery and resilience.
   •   Utilize the Scenario B forecast as an initial means to begin determination of longer-
       term needs for added industrial reserves and land capacity. This will help set the stage
       for 20-50 year UGB expansions – adjusted as needed to reflect actual experience with
       economic recovery and sustained economic vitality going forward.


        City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis – Technical Appendices ♦ Page 82
   •   Provide more opportunity to accommodate both exclusive industrial zones and mixed-
       use development. For large industrial users, it can be important to provide a clear
       separation or buffer from residential development and other non-industrial uses that
       would pose an unreasonable risk to public health or safety. For smaller scale uses as
       with creative and support service firms together with potential reduction in commercial
       space demand, horizontal rather than vertical mixed-use may become the more
       pronounced market opportunity for closely linked live-work-recreate communities – so
       long as total employment capacity is maintained at or above current forecast levels.
       Also noted is that much of the demand for office as a component of commercial
       demand can be met with industrially zoned sites.
   •   Provide opportunity for large acreage, major employer campuses of up to 600+ acres
       consistent with national trends but not readily available regionally in Oregon. This is of
       pivotal importance and a national priority for semi-conductor and related tech
       employers, exemplified by recently publicized plans of Intel for additional manufacturing
       facilities both domestically and internationally.
       Within the U.S., Intel in 2021 announced plans for two new fabrication plants in
       Chandler, Arizona. Situated on an approximately 700 acre “mega-factory” site, the
       campus is planned to be Intel’s largest manufacturing complex globally. Subsequently, in
       January 2022, Intel announced plans for construction of two leading-edge chip factories
       on a nearly 1,000-acre site near Columbus, Ohio as the “largest single private-sector
       investment in Ohio history.” The site will provide capacity for up to eight fab facilities at
       eventual full build-out planned over the next decade. 5
   •   Orient state and local incentive measures to support increased employment land
       utilization and redevelopment together with attraction and retention of target
       industries. This may include accounting for the potential of as yet unknown permanent
       shift to work at home, especially for office workers – as well as for potential reduction in
       commercial brick-and-mortar commercial space needs, at least near-term. Also involved
       may be short- and long-term incentives for increased efficiency of employment land use
       including reduction of at-grade parking footprints when shown to be feasible.

While retention of Hillsboro’s leading tech manufacturing edge is not guaranteed, success will
be dependent on a more expansive land base than is currently available. Initial suggestions as
to how these implementation measures might be incorporated into Comprehensive Plan goals
and economic development policies are outlined as the last section to this EOA appendix.

Transportation & Utility Infrastructure
Transportation and utility infrastructure is critical to assuring development readiness of
industrial and other employment sites. DLCD Division 9 guidance calls for “policies, through
public facilities planning and transportation system planning, to provide necessary public
facilities and transportation facilities for the planning area.”

Transportation and utility Infrastructure of importance to Hillsboro-based business is provided
both by public and private entities. Compared to other locales regionally and nationally,


         City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis – Technical Appendices ♦ Page 83
Hillsboro is better positioned competitively with respect to utility than transportation
infrastructure – though that may be changing in the wake of the COVID pandemic and potential
temporary or longer-term shift to more work from home.

Transportation Infrastructure. Key elements of Hillsboro’s transport infrastructure can be
described as comprising:

   •   Interstate/Highway Access – U.S. Highway 26 provides the major freeway access
       directly to Hillsboro, notably for the city’s major industrial firms situated in close
       proximity. U.S. 26 feeds directly into Interstate freeways I-405, I-5 and I-84
       approximately 18 miles east (as well as to the 217 freeway which runs south through
       Beaverton, then connecting with I-5 south).
   •   Air Travel – Portland International Airport (PDX) provides regularly scheduled domestic
       and international commercial air service about 30 miles east of Hillsboro. Local
       businesses also are served by Hillsboro’s own general aviation airport – Oregon’s 2nd
       busiest after PDX. Due to freight shipping concerns at congested periods across the
       metro region, a new air cargo service now connects Hillsboro airport to PDX every day
       for business customers shipping by air. The Hillsboro Airport also includes a U.S.
       Customs and Border Protection office for international flights and has three fixed-base
       operators.
   •   Public Transit – The regional transit agency Tri-Met serves Hillsboro with bus and light-
       rail options including the MAX Blue Line. Bus service includes the North Hillsboro Link, a
       shuttle providing employee transportation to the North Hillsboro Industrial Area.

Looking ahead, smart transport investment can be expected to be increasingly customized to
different needs for internal versus external transport linkages. Connections within and between
the city’s employment, residential and public/open space areas could emphasize greater
walkability and opportunity to cycle, improved transit connections/ride sharing, and
preparation for autonomous vehicles – all reducing the need for driving (and associated
employee parking). In the near term, while COVID risk persists, regaining lost transit ridership
will be challenged.

Suggested is a balanced mix of transit and major highway corridor improvements. Special
emphasis is needed for better freight mobility – especially for time sensitive products reliant on
air transport. A related long-term objective may be for improvement of the Cornelius Pass
connection – as an alternate or reliever route to the Portland International Airport (PDX) and
the I-5 North freeway system.

Utility Infrastructure. The strong role that public-private partnerships and intergovernmental
arrangements have played is clearly evidenced with key elements of Hillsboro’s existing and
planned infrastructure for local business and industry:

   •   Water - The City of Hillsboro Water Department provides water west of Cornelius Pass
       Road and south of Highway 26. The Tualatin Valley Water District (TVWD) provides


         City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis – Technical Appendices ♦ Page 84
       water east of Cornelius Pass Road and north of Highway 26. The Joint Water
       Commission operated by the City and TVWD is the largest conventional water treatment
       plant in Oregon, capable of treating up to 75 million gallons per day. Of specific note are
       steps that the City and TVWD are taking to build infrastructure necessary for improved
       water supply reliability and system resiliency over the next 50 years.
   •   Wastewater – Clean Water Services cleans and recycles wastewater, provides industrial
       pre-treatment, and manages surface and storm water systems.
   •   Electric Power – As the largest investor-owned utility in Oregon, Portland General
       Electric (PGE) provides electrical service to the region with three high-reliability
       substations to serve tech and other industries in Hillsboro’s industrial district. PGE offers
       multiple clean energy options, including renewables of hydroelectric, wind and solar
       energy.
   •   Natural Gas – As the largest independent natural gas utility in the Pacific Northwest,
       Northwest Natural serves Hillsboro’s natural gas needs.
   •   Digital Infrastructure – Hillsboro has the most dense network of international (trans-
       Pacific) and domestic cable service in the Pacific Northwest, with low latency data
       capacity a major reason for attraction of data centers as well as with finance, media,
       health care, e-commerce and IT users to the area. The City and area business are well-
       served by multiple national “last mile” telecommunications carriers providing fiber optic
       data, voice and wireless internet service. 6

Both short- and long-term, utility investment has been and will need to be continued with the
area’s electric, water, and wastewater systems. Adequate and reliable electric power is
essential to major semiconductor firms plus a range of related high-tech industries. Hillsboro
has benefitted from strategic, industry-supportive investments by Portland General Electric.

Similarly, the City of Hillsboro is recognized for having made the right decision 50 years ago with
water system investment – “setting the table” for tech companies as well as overall
development that has since occurred. From this perspective, it is important to again prepare for
the next 50 years; as a community we “need to pay forward.”

Implementation Measures. Key implementation measure recommendations for
consideration would be to:

   •   Target added local transport and utility infrastructure in conjunction with annexation
       to meet short-term employment land supply forecasts. Ideally, infrastructure should be
       provided in a phased manner ahead of or coterminous with prospective development,
       creating ready-to-build sites.
   •   Provide explicit policy support for a regional transportation system that effectively
       supports the movement of raw materials, manufactured goods and workforce to and
       through Hillsboro’s employment areas. This is a topic of growing significance not only
       regionally but more extensively due to supply chain and associated workforce issues
       impeding sustained economic recovery both nationally and globally.


         City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis – Technical Appendices ♦ Page 85
   •    Increase policy emphasis on north-south access and reduction of work-force
        commutes (to maximize Hillsboro work-force commute-shed accessibility). Increasing
        regional congestion makes it more challenging for Hillsboro to draw substantial work-
        force from across the metro area; more of the local workforce is shifting to residence
        locations in Hillsboro or in communities to the north and south.
   •    Provide explicit policy support to further strengthen Hillsboro’s competitive
        advantage as a Pacific Northwest data hub for low latency, data intensive firms
        offering high “pull-through” potential. Building on Hillsboro’s existing position as a
        major west coast data hub, greater value add can be created by using data center
        investments to leverage higher employment uses increasingly reliant on data hub
        proximity especially with transition to data intensive research and applications as for AI,
        autonomous and EV vehicles.

Target & Supporting Industry Clusters
DLCD Division 9 guidance indicates that: “Plans may include policies to maintain existing
categories or levels of industrial and other employment uses including maintaining downtowns
or central business districts.” Unlike many jurisdictions across the state, Hillsboro’s
Comprehensive Plan clearly emphasizes the importance of traded-sector and associated target
industry retention, expansion and recruitment.

Continued prioritization of traded sector investment is warranted as a primary means for local
economic prosperity and wealth creation. However, the pandemic has disproportionately and
adversely affected local service businesses important to support the community’s traded sector
industry clusters. This suggests a bifurcated policy approach going forward – both for traded
sector industry and for supporting industry clusters.

Traded Sector Target Industry Clusters. As in most communities, industry sectors targeted
for business expansion and recruitment tend to change over time based on market dynamics –
often in conjunction with public policy and/or incentive preferences. As shown by the following
chart, Hillsboro’s current key industry list is different and more streamlined than what was
envisioned with the 2017 EOA.

                      Comparative Hillsboro Target Industry Clusters
       2017 EOA Target Industry Clusters                         Current Key Industries
  • Computers & electronics manufacturing
  • Software & media                                   • Computers & electronics
  • Health sciences & technology                       • Software & information technology
  • Health services                                    • Advanced manufacturing
  • Data centers                                       • Bioscience & medical devices
  • Amenity retail, recreation & hospitality
                               Sources: 2017 EOA and City of Hillsboro website:
        https://www.hillsboro-oregon.gov/our-city/departments/economic-development/key-industries


         City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis – Technical Appendices ♦ Page 86
As in the past, Hillsboro may modify its priority industry clusters to reflect and serve new or
emerging industry opportunities in the years ahead. This is similar to the approach that has
been taken by Greater Portland, Inc. which also includes a key sector category for emerging
industries.

For Hillsboro, this would recognize the potential to step in alongside and encourage sectors that
are currently relatively weakly represented in Hillsboro but showing or with the potential to
demonstrate growing competitive presence. Examples as identified by the employment trends
analysis include the manufacturing sectors of food/textile, wood, chemical/plastic and non-
metallic mineral manufacturing.

Priority consideration for business targeting might be provided to those emerging traded sector
industries (or specific businesses) offering potential for strong employment, tax revenue,
and/or supplemental business leveraging (or “pull-through” benefits).

Supporting Industry Clusters. Non-manufacturing sectors that have been under-
represented but with growing local presence are construction, wholesale trade,
transportation/warehousing, FIRE, professional, health/social and arts/entertainment/
recreation services. While many of these non-manufacturing firms serve primarily local
markets, firms or industry segments that have a strong traded sector orientation to North
American and/or global markets may be well positioned also to receive priority assistance.

Service sectors ranging from retail to dining have been most adversely affected throughout the
pandemic and economic downturn. Small locally based business bring “unique flavor and flair”
important for community identity but are most at risk now and going forward. There is pressure
on tenant capacity to pay rent with resulting implications for landlords and lenders. Through
the pandemic and now economic recovery, capital availability may affect those who survive
versus those who have or will close their doors.

Implementation Measures. Recommended with this EOA are four implementation policies:

   •   Periodically modify and update Hillsboro’s current target industry listing to reflect and
       serve new or emerging traded sector industry opportunities in the years ahead. This
       will yield greater opportunity and flexibility to respond to changing market conditions
       together with local needs and opportunities beyond what is currently most readily
       foreseen. Along with Hillsboro, Metro and state economic development organizations
       are showing increased flexibility in adjusting target industry and business clustering
       priorities as the need arises – a practice that Hillsboro can also apply based on
       state/regional priorities balanced by Hillsboro’s own distinctive competitive attributes.
   •   Retain existing businesses including those at risk of displacement from pandemic
       and/or economic downturn. The goal is for a more resilient service sector economy,
       especially for retail, lodging and dining businesses that were disproportionately
       disadvantaged with the pandemic-related economic downturn.



         City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis – Technical Appendices ♦ Page 87
   •   Add policy language to expand business opportunities for minority- and women-
       owned businesses. This can occur via programs that encourage small business
       investment and longer-term improvement of supplier linkages with tech employers.
   •   Add a policy priority for community amenities that support traded sector business
       investment, talent recruitment/retention and high wage job potential. This is of
       special importance for attracting and retaining younger workforce to Hillsboro as more
       of a full-service live-work-recreate community.

Workforce Readiness
While not explicitly called out by DLCD Division 9 administrative rules, workforce readiness is
clearly indicated as an economic development resource to be addressed in conjunction with
plan policies that may “emphasize the expansion of an increased productivity from existing
industries and firms as a means to facilitate local economic development.”

Workforce availability and skills (or readiness) is an issue of growing concern as documented by
stakeholders with a range of local industries. Key issues include continuing retirement of the
large baby boomer generation, workforce disruption by the pandemic (particularly as relates to
child-care), lack of a nationally recognized metro area research university, and needed skills
training for entry-level manufacturing workers.

In interviews with a range of business and community leaders, a recurring theme is the
continuing if not intensified challenge of hiring and retaining qualified workforce. Despite these
limitations, Hillsboro has the highest labor force participation rate in the metro area – including
quality skill sets for bioscience, clean tech, information technology, and manufacturing
industries.

Workforce training is expected to be increasingly important due to rapidly changing technology
and career trajectories across the spectrum of K-12, higher education and on-going workforce
development. Specifically referenced is the need for training tied to career and technical
education (CTE) programs, linked more explicitly and with greater flexibility to meet employer-
specified needs. This desire for workforce training that is ever more customized to employer
needs appears to have intensified even through the pandemic.

Frequent mention with stakeholder interviews is made of the importance of partnering with
interested institutions such as PCC, OHSU, PSU, OSU and Pacific University for apprenticeship
and technical training – also internships. In addition to these higher education resources, the
City of Hillsboro works with a range of local as well as state-level resource providers, including:

   •   WorkSource Oregon, sponsored by the Oregon Employment Department offers a one-
       stop solution to businesses for finding and retaining qualified employment candidates.
   •   Worksystems, Inc. designs and coordinates workforce development programs and
       services through a network of local partners – including employers, labor groups,
       community colleges, high schools and community-based and economic development
       organizations.

         City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis – Technical Appendices ♦ Page 88
   •   Enterprise Zone Workforce Development Program – offers classroom and on the job
       training for groups of employees available through businesses located within Hillsboro’s
       Enterprise Zone.
   •   Prosperidad Economic Empowerment Center – represents an alliance of community
       partners focused on employment and self-employment strategies.

Implementation Measures. Due to pandemic related business curtailments coupled with
other economic fallout, the workers most adversely affected have been those in lower wage
sectors including retail, hospitality and dining. These sectors also often have higher proportions
of women and minorities – as employees and/or as small business owners. Key suggested
implementation measures are to:

   •   Include retraining emphasis for employees displaced in times of economic disruption
       and transition. Getting workers up to speed with rapidly changing work force skills will
       persist as a higher priority with continued economic recovery and to maintain
       Hillsboro’s long term competitive position for tech-adaptive existing and new
       employers.
   •   Add policy language to expand employment opportunities for under-represented
       members of the community including racial/ethnic minority groups, women and
       veterans. Attention to under-represented populations better addresses not only
       individual and community vitality objectives but also positions Hillsboro for greater
       diversity of talent going forward.
   •   Coordinate with Washington County to evaluate the most effective Workforce Board
       arrangements in support of community workforce needs. This could include
       partnership initiatives often utilizing existing resources as with the Hillsboro Advanced
       Manufacturing Work Group.
   •   Support efforts to create new workforce development programs meeting the needs of
       target and emerging industries. This suggests placing greater priority on reducing the
       time lag between industry-identified needs and workforce training delivery.
   •   Pursue designation as a Center of Innovation Excellence and Regional Technology Hub
       to support Hillsboro’s leadership role in research and development with expanded
       benefits to the community. Hillsboro provides a unique opportunity to advance a key
       strategic objective of Oregon’s 10-Year Innovation Plan completed in 2021 to “support
       centers of innovation excellence that leverage Oregon’s existing traded sector strengths
       and emerging market opportunities.”

Economic Development Incentives
DLCD Division 9 guidance addresses plan policies that “include additional approaches” in
support of economic development that cover but are not limited to such mechanisms as tax
incentives and disincentives, preferential tax assessments, and property acquisition techniques.
Also strongly encouraged are brownfield redevelopment strategies.



         City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis – Technical Appendices ♦ Page 89
With an active in-house economic and community development department, the City of
Hillsboro offers a variety of state and local incentive programs aimed to reduce a firm’s cost of
doing business. Some of the most prominent are noted as including: 7

   •   Enterprise Zone – providing 100% property tax abatement for eligible businesses on
       new qualified capital assets (not currently on the tax rolls) within the designated
       enterprise zone for a three- to five-year period.
   •   Strategic Investment Program - exempting a portion of large new capital investments
       by traded sector businesses from property taxes for 15 years. A community service fee is
       paid each year to the local jurisdiction equal to 25 percent of the tax savings, up to a
       maximum of $2 million per year. 8
   •   Loan, Loan Guarantees and Bond Programs – administered by Business Oregon and
       usually backed by Oregon Lottery funds.
   •   Vertical Housing Development Zone - offering a partial property tax exemption to
       mixed-use residential development within City-specified zones and extending larger tax
       incentives for development that includes affordable housing. Administered by the State
       until the end of 2017, the City has developed its program in concordance with Senate
       Bill 310, passed during the 2017 legislative session, giving control of the program to local
       jurisdictions.
   •   Strategic Reserve Fund – A discretionary Business Oregon incentive program focused on
       job creation/retention.
   •   Business Expansion Program – another Business Oregon resource available to existing
       companies expanding their operations in Oregon or new companies coming to the state.
       The program is cash based, usually in the form of a “forgivable loan” tied to the
       estimated increase in income tax revenue from new hiring associated with the project.
   •   Opportunity Zones – a federal program for properties within designated zones allowing
       investors to receive a capital gains benefit for investments made into historically
       impoverished areas.
   •   Storefront Improvement Grants – Grants administered and issued by Hillsboro using
       Downtown Urban Renewal dollars to match owner investment up to a maximum
       amount for storefront and building façade improvements.
   •   Tenant Improvement Grants – A matching fund grant administered by the City for
       tenant improvements involving existing food services businesses.

In addition to these direct tax and other funding incentive programs, the City of Hillsboro is
actively engaged in or supporting other programs offering business and industry support – most
notably for workforce and training, power utilities benefits, and large water user SDC
deferrals/financing.

The role and the capacity of the public sector to effectively support economic recovery has
been called into question across a variety of fronts. Issues cited by stakeholders include
concerns with land availability and cost together with regulatory and tax issues.


         City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis – Technical Appendices ♦ Page 90
Needs for a stable tax structure and funding for economic development incentives are noted as
being of importance for business retention and recruitment going forward. The City of Hillsboro
is complimented for its role in reaching out through the pandemic, “doing the right thing.”

Bottom-line, targeted economic development incentives are recognized as having played an
important role in attracting industrial investment to Hillsboro. Some industry and economic
development stakeholders suggest that incentives be more narrowly targeted in the years
ahead – to businesses that can demonstrate some combination of strong employment, tax
revenue, and/or supplemental business leveraging benefits.

Implementation Measures. Suggested with this EOA is added policy language regarding
implementation measures to:

   •   Provide a more prominent position for incentive mechanisms as integral to supporting
       or facilitating achievement of economic goals and policies. This can occur with active
       utilization of federal, state and regional programs together with publicized Hillsboro-
       specific economic development incentives.
   •   More specifically include incentives as a means to leverage increased density with
       uses that currently are associated with relatively low job per acre counts. Assumed is a
       long-term shift to more urbanized densities, transition from drive-alone commuting,
       potential for reduced at-grade parking footprint, and impetus for recycling of obsolete
       or redundant facilities – especially as current or prospective feasibility is demonstrated.
   •   Advance incentives focused on land readiness together with land aggregation as
       needed for industrial expansion and recruitment. A particular focus is on assuring
       capacity to serve expansion and attraction of major high-wage employers requiring
       large acreage sites.

Partnership Opportunities
This final topic is aimed to cover public-private partnerships and intergovernmental frameworks
as objectives to be addressed in local jurisdiction EOAs. Public-private and intergovernmental
partnerships have long been part of Hillsboro’s civic and economic development DNA. The best
opportunities going forward are to maintain and build on the partnerships already in place,
adapted to new challenges that have emerged with the pandemic and attendant economic
dislocation – extending beyond to longer term recovery and resilience.

Implementation Measures. As implementation measures, policy recommendations are to:

   •   Include urban renewal as a potential economic development funding tool within
       designated renewal districts. As has been demonstrated region-wide, broader
       application can extend use of this well-tested public/private investment tool beyond
       urban placemaking to also assist projects offering job-creating high wage employment.




        City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis – Technical Appendices ♦ Page 91
   •   Add policy language to more explicitly encourage Metro and state-wide support for
       Hillsboro tech-focused economic development as an economic engine of significance
       and benefit regionally and statewide. Cited last but not least, obtaining support for
       tech-led Hillsboro investment may represent an increasingly pivotal commitment to
       raising the bar for economic vitality locally, regionally, and state-wide.
       Hillsboro’s economic significance regionally and statewide might be further documented
       as with economic impact analysis. Analysis of direct and indirect effects could serve to
       demonstrate the interconnectedness of the metro and state economy and the roles that
       Hillsboro’s leading edge tech industries play – not only for key traded sector industries
       but also with respect to region-wide housing location, transportation planning and
       related infrastructure investments.
       More recently, the impetus for statewide support for expanded semiconductor
       manufacturing is highlighted by recommendations of the Oregon Semiconductor
       Competitiveness Task Force in conjunction with federally authorized CHIPS and Science
       Act of 2022.

and objectives are integrated into the framework of the existing Comprehensive Plan rather
than as separate stand-alone objectives/policies statements. Also assumed is an approach that
may well involve refinement of the existing Comprehensive Plan goal/policy framework, rather
than a wholesale re-work.

EMPLOYMENT BUILDABLE
LANDS INVENTORY
As described in the 2021 EOA report and by Appendix C to this appendices document, and in
response to the LUBA remand related to redevelopment potential with “developed lands,” the
City of Hillsboro retained the planning firm MIG to prepare an amended employment Buildable
Lands Inventory (BLI). The following memorandum of May 13, 2024 describes the methodology
and resulting outputs of this amended inventory.

The amended BLI reflects employment BLI conditions as of December 2020. This is consistent
with the 2020-40 time frame considered as the 20-year forecast planning horizon for Hillsboro’s
2021 Economic Opportunities Analysis.

Outputs of this amended BLI have been incorporated as the supply determinations included
with the Chapter IV EOA evaluation of Employment Land Needs.




        City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis – Technical Appendices ♦ Page 96
HILLSBORO EMPLOYMENT
BUILDABLE LANDS
INVENTORY
Memorandum
May 13, 2024




Introduction
This memorandum describes the methodology and draft results of the Employment Buildable Lands
Inventory (Employment BLI) for the City of Hillsboro conducted in 2023/2024 to support the City’s
long-range planning for employment lands. This information will inform an update of the City’s 2021
Economic Opportunities Analysis (EOA), prepared by E.D. Hovee & Company, LLC.

Generally, this methodology is based on the approach used in the 2018 Metro Buildable Lands
Inventory1 with updates as noted.

The BLI is conducted in the following steps:

      •   Step 1: Land classification. This step identifies the land in the City that is available for
          employment uses.
      •   Step 2: Constraints to Development. This step identifies constraints such as natural
          resources, steep slopes, and utility easements that limit development.
      •   Step 3: Development Status. This step assigns a “Development Status” of vacant, partially
          vacant, or developed to tax lots in the inventory.
      •   Step 4: Net Buildable Area. This step removes land for future rights-of-way and other land
          needs to provide a net number of acres for each City zoning designation.
      •   Step 5: Redevelopment. This analysis includes an assessment of potentially redevelopable
          sites in the City and adjacent growth areas.

    https://www.oregonmetro.gov/sites/default/files/2018/07/03/UGR_Appendix2_Buildable_Lands_Inventory.pdf

        City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis – Technical Appendices ♦ Page 104
Employment Land
Employment land includes the sub-categories of Commercial Land and Industrial Land, described
below.

Commercial Land
Commercial land is identified as land within the C comprehensive plan designation or zoning
designations of C-G or C-N. This land is intended to provide for retail, service, and office commercial
developments.

Industrial Land
Industrial land is identified as land within the IN designation, intended to provide for all types of
research and development, manufacturing, warehouse, and wholesale industrial uses.


Mixed Use Land
Mixed Use land can be developed to meet the City’s residential and employment needs – sometimes
within the same structure. It includes land within the SCPA, MU, MU-UR, MU-UC, MU-UE, MU-I
designations, unless it meets the criteria for “Public/Other” land. Mixed-use land is assumed to be
partially available for employment uses as described in later steps.


Non-Employment Land
Non-employment land includes land designated for residential uses, land that is owned by a public
or semi-public entity and not set aside for employment uses, and certain other categories as follows.

Residential Land
Residential land has a comprehensive plan of RL, RM, RH, and RMR designations. Residential land is
assumed to be unavailable for employment uses.

Publicly Owned/Other
This category of land includes the PF and OS designations, as well as land in the following categories:

    •   Land in another Comprehensive Plan designation under City, County, State, Federal, or
        Special District Ownership
    •   Land commonly held in HOA ownership, such as required open space.
    •   Private driveways and ROW

Parcels in this category may be included in other classifications if information is available to suggest
development capacity for residential or employment uses.

restrictive constraint applies.

Step 3: Development Status
Each parcel in the study area is categorized as Vacant, Developed, or Partially Vacant.

Vacant parcels (including parcels with low-value structures) are assumed to have development
capacity equal to the area unconstrained by natural resources, minus additional set-asides for
future Right-of-Way and infrastructure.

Developed parcels are subject to further screening for redevelopment potential, described below
and in Step 5.

Partially Vacant parcels have existing development but some portion of the site is available for
future employment uses.

These parcels are identified as follows:

    •     Industrial Zones: Site has greater than 1 acre of unconstrained vacant land, as visible on
          aerial photo
    •     Commercial Zones: Site has greater than ½ acre of vacant land, as visible on aerial photo
    •     Mixed Use Zones: Site has greater than ½ acre of vacant land, as visible on aerial photo
    •     Jackson East Area: This portion of the city has many existing rural homes, which are
          generally excluded from the developable area.

Additionally, “Developed” parcels received two screens to determine whether a portion of the site
would support additional employment area, in which case the parcel was recategorized as "Partially
Vacant.”

    •     Parcels were compared to the Metro Regional Land Inventory System (RLIS) inventory of
          vacant land, and tax lots intersecting vacant areas (as identified by GIS polygons) were
          recategorized as "Partially Vacant."
    •     Aerial Photo Review. Employment parcels were reviewed based on aerial photography. Land
          with remaining developable acreage categorized as "Partially Vacant" and capacity was
          estimated on a case-by-case basis.

Estimates of developable area have been created on these parcels using aerial photo review,
comparison to Metro Vacant Land Inventory, and City staff input.

Approximating Development Status of December 2020
This Employment BLI was prepared by MIG with input from the City of Hillsboro in 2023 using data
from 2023. In order to be consistent with employment forecasts and other information in the 2021
EOA, the City of Hillsboro updated the inventory to reflect the development status of parcels as of
December 2020, as follows:

Inputs:

    •     2023 EBLI (prepared by MIG, see Step 1 through Step 3 in this methodology)
    •     December 2020 UGB (reproduced from Metro RLIS UGB History data set)
    •     December 2020 Hillsboro city limits (provided by City of Hillsboro)


           City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis – Technical Appendices ♦ Page 108
   •   November 2020 tax lots (provided by Metro)
   •   December 2020–February 2021 aerial image (provided by Metro)
   •   Aerial imagery:
           o   December 2020–February 2021 aerial image (provided by Metro)
           o   July 2020 aerial image (provided by City of Hillsboro)
           o   July 2021 aerial image (provided by City of Hillsboro)
           o   June 2023 aerial image (provided by City of Hillsboro)
   •   Report of issued permits for which Transportation Development Tax (TDT) was assessed in
       North Hillsboro between January 1, 2019 and December 31, 2020 (provided by City of
       Hillsboro)
   •   Hillsboro Airport’s Runway Protection Zone (provided by City of Hillsboro)


Methodology to update Development Status:

   1. Imported 2023 EBLI, December 2020 UGB, December 2020 Hillsboro city limits, November
       2020 tax lots, aerial imagery, and Hillsboro Airport’s Runway Protection Zone.
   2. Isolated November 2020 tax lots within the December 2020 Hillsboro city limits and within
       expansion areas inside the December 2020 UGB.
   3. Added 2020 development status field to November 2020 tax lots.
   4. Applied 2023 development statuses to November 2020 tax lots.
   5. Updated 2020 development status field to reflect changes both visible in aerial imagery and
       from November 2020 tax lot building values (e.g., development of previously vacant tax lots,
       demolition of structures on previously developed tax lots, etc.).
   6. Updated 2020 development status field to reflect vacant or partially developed tax lots that
       received permits between January 1, 2019 and December 31, 2020.
   7. Updated 2020 development status field to “Public/Other” for tax lots significantly
       constrained by the Hillsboro Airport Runway Protection Zone.

Step 5: Redevelopment
This Employment BLI evaluates the redevelopment potential of employment parcels categorized as
“Developed.” This test is an estimate commonly used to evaluate redevelopment potential at a high
level, though there are many factors that will ultimately determine the redevelopment of a given
parcel.

   1. Strike Price Analysis. The “strike price” is a value per square foot at which a developer can
      afford to purchase the property and theoretically redevelop profitably. The 2018 Metro
      Urban Growth Report's BLI estimated strike prices for various land uses and locations
      throughout the region. Strike prices used for this analysis are greater than those identified
      for suburban jurisdictions in the 2018 report to account for inflation of land values between
      2018 and 2020. Acreage thresholds remain the same; industrial land less than 1 acre and
      commercial land less than .25 acres is excluded. Mixed use land is assumed to develop
      partially with residential uses as described in Table 2. Redeveloping parcels are not assumed
      to have further takeouts for right-of-way and other infrastructure.

       The results of the strike price analysis are summarized in Table 4. There are a total of 65
       taxlots that meet the size and strike price, encompassing an estimated 143 acres of


        City of Hillsboro ♦ Economic Opportunities Analysis – Technical Appendices ♦ Page 111
       employment land in the study area. Roughly 85% of the redevelopable land in this analysis is
       in industrial categories.

Summary and Use of Redevelopment Information

There are many variables that determine whether an individual site will redevelop, including
property owner willingness, the availability of other suitable sites, and macroeconomic factors. This
analysis has identified roughly 143 gross acres of land on which redevelopment for employment
uses may be economically viable, based on available data. The EOA report discusses the extent to
which this redevelopment information can be relied upon to accommodate future employment
needs for the City.




Summary
The results of this inventory are described in the following tables. Key points include:

    •   The study area contains a total of 1,225 acres of net employment acreage, accounting for
        constrained areas, lots with remaining capacity, and future rights-of-way and infrastructure
        needs. This amount does not include the 143 acres of potentially redevelopable land from
        Table 5.
    •   Over 90% of this land is in industrial designations, and about half of this land is outside
        the 2020 City Limits.
    •   Over half of the net employment acreage is on lots with a gross area of 20 acres or
        greater.

I.    BACKGROUND INFORMATION

      These findings are associated with Case File No.: HCP-003-22, 2021 Economic
      Opportunities Analysis (EOA), which proposes a text amendment to the Hillsboro
      Comprehensive Plan (HCP), Ordinance No. 6249, as amended. The text amendment,
      attached as Exhibit A modifies the HCP to replace the 2016 EOA, referenced in the HCP
      and hereto as “2017 EOA” and provides an updated reference to the 2021 EOA as
      supplemented in May 2024.

      This decision comes before the City on remand from the State of Oregon Land Use Board
      of Appeals (LUBA) following an appeal by 1000 Friends of Oregon (Friends) and Metro
      of City Council approval of HCP-003-22 and adoption of Ordinance No. 6420. While
      Friends and Metro raised several assignments of error relating to employment growth
      forecasting and the Comprehensive Plan status, most of these arguments were denied by
      LUBA. In their final opinion, LUBA affirmed the City’s decision in adoption of Ordinance
      No. 6420 in every respect except two and these findings are limited to those. The issues
      now under consideration are limited to compliance with the Hillsboro Community
      Development Code (CDC) Section 12.80.164 – Comprehensive Plan Minor Text
      Amendment and the standards in State law for the buildable lands inventory, Oregon
      Statewide Planning Goal 9 – Economy, and OAR 660-009-0015 (3). LUBA agreed with
      Friends that the 2019 Buildable Lands Inventory (BLI) for employment land that was
      included in the 2021 EOA did not apply the correct analysis for determining the
      redevelopment potential of “developed lands.”

      These findings are limited to and demonstrate compliance with:

      •      Hillsboro Community Development Code (CDC) Section 12.80.164
      •      Oregon Statewide Planning Goal 9, Economy, and OAR 660-009-0015 (3)

      The 2019 BLI was initiated because the City witnessed a noticeable increase in industrial
      property absorption as suppliers to Hillsboro’s Computer and Electronics, Advanced
      Manufacturing, and other target sectors including Software and Information Technologies,
      expanded with strong growth in all these sectors and more. Additional demand increases
      have also been noted in sectors such as freight and distribution, and bio-technology leading
      to a reduced short-term supply of land, as well as, rapid absorption of total land supply. To
      better understand what the City was witnessing and to best position its programs, policies,
      and land supply to compete for these significant changes in economic development
      opportunities, the City began this 2021 EOA review to update the 2017 EOA, which was
      adopted with the 2018 Hillsboro Comprehensive Plan.

      completed in March 2024 and based on December 2020 data prepared by the planning firm

      In the remand order, LUBA found that the 2019 BLI was “not supported by an adequate
      factual basis,” with respect to the redevelopment potential of “developed lands.” The
      definition of “vacant land” at OAR 660-009-0005(14) includes (1) any lot or parcel larger
      than one-half acre that is completely undeveloped, and (2) any lot or parcel larger than five
      acres with at least four and one-half acres undeveloped. “Developed lands” is defined as
      “non-vacant land that is likely to be redeveloped during the planning period.” OAR 660-
      009-0005(1). The 2020 BLI evaluates the redevelopment potential of “developed lands”
      consistent with the rule’s definition and in compliance with the standards in State law,
      including whether the developed portions of lots and parcels is “likely to be redeveloped”.
      These changes are further described in the findings below.

II.   PROCEDURAL REQUIREMENTS

      This minor amendment to the Hillsboro Comprehensive Plan (HCP) Ordinance No. 6249,
      as amended, classified as a legislative amendment as defined by the Hillsboro Community
      Development Code (CDC) Section 12.070.060 (B) and 12.70.020-1.


Page 3 of 24
Exhibit D
Ordinance No. 6474

      This proposed amendment is a Comprehensive Plan Minor Text Amendment because it
      only involves a text amendment to replace the “2017” EOA with the “2021” EOA in the
      Comprehensive Plan Section 23.4 “Economic Opportunities Analysis/Buildable Lands
      Inventory – Employment.” The CDC, Section 12.80.164, provides in relevant part:

      A. Purpose. A Comprehensive Plan Minor Text Amendment provides a process to
         consider small-scale legislative amendments to the text of the Comprehensive Plan
         whenever the evidence of the need for such a revision is documented, and the
         amendment does not have significant effect beyond an immediate site or area. Such
         amendments may be necessary to reflect changing community conditions, needs, and
         desires; to fulfill regional obligations; or to address changes in State law.

      D. Approval Criteria. To approve a Comprehensive Plan Minor Text Amendment, the
         Review Authority shall make findings of fact, based on the evidence provided, that the
         following criteria are satisfied:

         1. This proposed Comprehensive Plan Minor Text Amendment is necessary to reflect
            changing community conditions, needs, and desires, to fulfill regional obligations,
            and to address changes in State law.

         2. The proposed text supports the goals and policies of the Comprehensive Plan.

      A comprehensive plan “minor” amendment is distinguished from a “major” amendment.
      According to CDC Section 12.80.166, a Comprehensive Plan Major Amendment is either
      a Major Amendment-Significant Change or a Major Amendment-Plan Revision:

      B. Major Amendment-Significant Change. ...A “significant change” is one that amends or
         refines both the Plan text and map, affects a large geographic area and is likely to have
         significant environmental, energy, economic and social consequences.

      C. Major Amendment-Plan Revision. …A “Plan Revision” means a revision(s) to the
         entire Comprehensive Plan text or map initiated; (1) under a Periodic Review Program
         pursuant to ORS 197.628; (2) to implement an adopted Regional Framework Plan or
         Metro Functional Plan; or (3) as part of a comprehensive evaluation of the
         Comprehensive Plan.

      A Major Amendment-Significant Change proposes a significant change that amends or
      refines both the Comprehensive Plan text and map, affects a large geographic area and is
      likely to have significant environmental, energy, economic and social consequences. A
      significant change includes but is not limited to Plan amendments that incorporate
      community plans as part of the Comprehensive Plan or incorporate portions of a public
      facility plan as part of the Comprehensive Plan in accordance with State statute and
      regulations implementing Statewide Planning Goal 11. A Major Amendment-Plan
      Revision proposes a revision(s) to the entire Comprehensive Plan text or map.
Page 4 of 24
Exhibit D
Ordinance No. 6474
City Council
      Here, the proposed amendment does not amend the plan map, and does not have significant
      environmental, energy, economic and social consequences. It simply replaces the 2017
      EOA with the 2021 EOA. Therefore, it is not a Major Amendment-Significant Change. In
      addition, it does not revise the entire comprehensive plan, is not proposed as part of
      periodic review, does not implement Metro’s functional plan or framework plan, and is not
      part of an overall evaluation of the comprehensive plan. Thus, it also is not a Major
      Amendment-Plan Revision.

      A Comprehensive Plan Minor Text Amendment application is reviewed using the Type IV
      procedure described in CDC Section 12.70.060. The proposed amendment was initiated
      through approval of the Planning Commission Order No. 8370 on May 11, 2022,
      acknowledging that due to changes in land use activity, growth projections, future
      employment needs, and other “changing community conditions, needs, and desires,” an
      update of the EOA through a Minor Comprehensive Plan Text Amendment application
      process was appropriate to maintain the Comprehensive Plan land use inventories. These
      changes are further described in the findings below.

III.      APPLICABLE APPROVAL CRITERIA

       1. Hillsboro Community Development Code Section 12.80.164

          In order to adopt the proposed amendments, the City must demonstrate that the
          amendments are consistent with CDC Section 12.80.164.D, which specifies the approval
          criteria for a proposed Comprehensive Plan Minor Text Amendment as follows:

          D. Approval Criteria. To approve a Comprehensive Plan Minor Text Amendment, the
             Review Authority shall make findings of fact, based on evidence provided, that the
             following criteria are satisfied:

             1. The proposed text is necessary to reflect changing community conditions, needs,
                and desires, to fulfill regional obligations, or to address changes in State law.

          Finding: The HCP minor text amendment proposes to replace the reference to the 2017
          EOA with an updated EOA. There are several reasons the City initiated an update on the
          EOA. First has been the continued growth of Hillsboro’s population and employment base,
          which continue to grow more quickly than the region. Hillsboro’s population increased
          from 88,300 in 2007 to 108,800 residents in 2021, an increase of approximately 20%.
          During that same 14-year period, employment in Hillsboro has grown from 62,430 to
          81,000, approximately 30%, double the 15% for the region. Since the initiation of an
          updated EOA, the City has continued to see increased population and employment growth,
          especially in multiple manufacturing areas, including but not limited to the Computer,
          Electronics, Bioscience, and Advance Manufacturing sectors. These policy changes, drive
          a substantial change in the economic opportunities of the City and warranted an amending
          of the Comprehensive Plan.

          In addition to the rapid population and employment increases, vacant employment land has
          seen quick absorption. The City has seen approximately 800 acres of employment land
          absorbed in the North Hillsboro Community Plan area in the past ten years due to the
          success of the North Hillsboro Industrial Park and Industrial Renewal District.

          Further changes to the City’s economic landscape include emerging federal policy and
          work trends, including automation, onshoring of logistics and suppliers, and remote work.

          The national economic policy was changing before the COVID-19 pandemic, with Federal
          regulatory tariffs incentivizing manufacturers, and suppliers, to reshore to the United
          States. Efforts to accelerate the re-shoring of critical national security traded-sector
          manufacturing and particular high-tech manufacturing leverages the City’s existing
Page 6 of 24
Exhibit D
Ordinance No. 6474
City Council
      strength in this employment area. With the passage of the federal CHIPS ACT in August
      2022, it is likely that because the Portland region has the largest concentration of
      semiconductor industry workers in the U.S., and Hillsboro has the largest concentration of
      firms and employees in the Portland region that more investments will occur, and at a
      higher trend then seen over the past 20 years. Taken separately and when viewed together,
      these initiatives are consistent with the robust strategy of the Hillsboro EOA for continued
      rapid tech industry investment and jobs.

      All these changes necessitated the City to initiate an updated EOA to provide updated
      information for City decision-makers to understand strengths, weaknesses, opportunities,
      and threats while considering possible policy implementation choices. Considering all
      these changes and to address the requirements of State Land-use Goal 9, Economy, and to
      help inform Hillsboro’s discussions with Metro’s Urban Growth Report (UGR) in 2023,
      the City has completed an update of the City’s EOA.

      Additionally, the City has witnessed various work trends since initiating the 2021 EOA
      due to the COVID-19 pandemic. The first is that many manufacturing workers do not work
      from home and must still be physically present on the job site. The managers of
      manufacturing facilities need to be close to their jobs for on-site problem-solving. Suppliers
      also increasingly need to be located close to customers as supply chain disruptions and
      leading edge innovations occur. There has also been an acceleration in e-commerce leading
      to a rapid absorption of existing industrial buildings driving Hillsboro Industrial vacancies
      to approximately 2% based on CoStar July 2022 along with increased development of
      warehouse and distribution facilities on vacant land. Additionally, the Hillsboro
      community continues to grow in population as workers seek homes with more indoor space
      for offices and more outdoor space to ensure social distancing as necessary. The ongoing
      population growth locally with more residents working from home, positively impacts the
      demand for local service sector jobs, with employers following their employees from
      Central City or creating small satellite offices.

      Staff find that this criterion is met.

      Finding: There are three foundational documents required by state law to establish and
      accommodate land needs for a range of population and employment growth within the
      Hillsboro plan area; these documents include a Buildable Lands Inventory (BLI), EOA,
      and a Housing Needs Analysis (HNA). The 2020 BLI and the 2021 EOA are the first two
      steps in updating all three reference documents consistent with the HCP.

      The EOA is required by OAR 660-009-0015(2) to conduct an analysis and identify required
      site types by the number that can be expected to be needed to accommodate the expected
      employment growth based upon typically expected uses. This analysis is found in 2021
      EOA Section 4 (Exhibit B), with supporting documentation in the 2021 EOA Technical
      Appendices (Exhibit C). These findings support both Policy’s UR 1.3, Infill, and UR 1.7,
      by maintaining a complete understanding of the economic need for both large and small
      lot sites to maintain a strong and diverse economy for the City.

      To complete the updated EOA, the staff conducted a new BLI. This data, combined with
      other quantitative and qualitative trends data, was used to complete the 2021 EOA and
      provide a refreshed understanding of Hillsboro’s current and future economy from the
      previous 2017 EOA. Completion and adoption of the 2021 EOA into the HCP supports
      Policy UR 1.8 by providing City policy and decision-makers with the current supply of
      developable land in all employment categories, including industrial, commercial, office,
      and mixed-use. The EOA finds and describes that if current trends were to continue, the
      City does not have a 20-year land supply as required by State Goal 9, Economic
      Development and implementing OARs.

      The 2021 EOA was developed consistent with OAR 660-009 and the four specific
      components required by OAR 660-009-0015 (1-4). Hillsboro staff, working with the
      project consultant, initially evaluated two scenarios, prepared just prior to the pandemic.

      The first, “Scenario A,” was established using the growth rate of the most recent economic
      cycle (2007-2018), based on the addition of 18,570 jobs over this 11-year period. This
      equates to an annual percentage employment growth rate of 1.9%.

      A second scenario, “Scenario B,” was developed based on a combination of national and
      local data. Hillsboro has experienced an increasing pace of land absorption and
      development combined with the opportunities seen by Hillsboro Economic Development
      Staff for targeted traded sector industries that correspond with national and industry trends,
      making reasonable the evaluation of an exponential growth opportunity scenario, forecast

Page 9 of 24
Exhibit D
Ordinance No. 6474
City Council
      separately for each of 17 employment sectors. The resulting overall growth rate used for
      Scenario B was a Compound Annual Growth Rate (CAGR) of 3.5%.

      Hillsboro staff and the project consultant then developed a third “Scenario C,” which is a
      hybrid of CAGR, and straight-line average growth and corresponding land factor
      conversions based on the “reasonably be expected to locate or expand within the planning
      area based on national, state, regional, county or local trends.” Scenario C used a “toggle
      switch” forecast methodology (explanation on EOA page 29) based on a detailed
      evaluation of historic employment experience from approach to determine whether job
      growth for each sector reflected a straight-line or exponential employment growth pattern,
      using detailed data extending back to 2003 (the earliest date available) as provided by the
      Oregon Employment Department (OED).

      OAR 660-0024 allows but does not require a “safe harbor” employment projection and
      based on a local employment growth trend; Hillsboro chose a 1.9% as its baseline growth
      rate (or minimal expectation) based on the most recent 11-year growth cycle pattern rather
      than the regional safe harbor growth rate of 1.6%. Because Hillsboro job growth has
      consistently been able to outperform the region, using the safe harbor approach would
      understate the employment opportunities.

      Using a CAGR is common practice in creating EOAs throughout the state and is especially
      pertinent when job growth rates are accelerating or demonstrated to be above the
      surrounding county or region for a specific City. As Eric Hovee, who has prepared EOAs
      across Oregon for over 40 years described at the September 14, 2022, Planning
      Commission hearing, CAGR calculations have been used by Metro’s UGR but are
      commonly referenced as “Annual Percentage Rate” (APR). The City of Portland used this
      approach in its 2016 EOA in a similar methodology. Often it is a matter of terms between
      CAGR, Annual Percentage Growth Rate (APGR), or Annual Percentage Growth Rate
      (APGR), but the math remains the same as each year builds on the previous year.

      The exponential employment and land forecast are based more on the possibility of all-
      sector compounding growth. Thus, using the CAGR and Exponential forecasts are
      reference points, a Hybrid forecast was developed by combining the Exponential forecast
      with a sector-by-sector analysis. The sector-by-sector analysis is explained on page 30 of
      the 2021 EOA. On page 31 of the EOA, there is a summary table that describes which
      forecast was used by employment sector and why that aligns with Hillsboro’s experience
      and with existing and targeted industrial employment policies to determine the preferred
      path toward continued realization of Hillsboro’s economic opportunities. The EOA
      Technical appendix pages 25 through 42 provide additional detail how the “four-phase”
      sector toggle approach using OED year to year review of employment for each sector.

      The results of the 2021 EOA are similar to the previous 2009 Hillsboro EOA conducted by
      Johnson Reid Land-use Economist in preparation for the Metro Urban / Rural Reserve
      process and the 2017 EOA prepared by Johnson Economics for the 2017 HCP update.

      Finding: As required by State Land-use Goal 9 and consistent with OAR 660-009, the
      2021 EOA’s primary purpose is to evaluate the existing employment BLI and City policies
      to create a 20-year forecast for employment land needs.

      The 2021 EOA is based upon the 2020 BLI that was created consistent with the Metro BLI
      used for the 2018 UGR, to provide a 20-year land forecast that includes an evaluation of
      existing parcel size and the importance of maintaining large sites to attract traded-sector
      industries seeking campus-style development. The 2021 EOA identifies the need to
      maintain a supply of diverse size employment land and Prime Industrial Land to ensure
      that firms of all sizes have opportunities to locate in Hillsboro and to fill unmet needs and
      expand as businesses grow. The 2020 BLI provides an analysis consistent with the
      standards called out in OAR 660-009 and OAR 660-24.

      The 2021 EOA’s identification of land needs is consistent with the City’s ongoing efforts
      to support and locate high-density employment nodes in Hillsboro’s
      Tanasbourne/AmberGlen Regional and Downtown Hillsboro Regional Centers that have
      access to regional transit. The 2021 EOA also recognizes that many traded sector industries,
      especially manufacturing, are often limited in how high density they can be due to
      operational specifics, spacing requirements, and site logistical needs. Hillsboro has seen
      many traded sector entities and manufacturers develop at 1 to 3 stories, but facilities at
      higher densities are not currently achievable and requirements for this type of development
      form will negatively impact the locational considerations and realization of these industries
      in the planned industrial areas.

      The 2021 EOA identifies the ongoing strength of employment growth in the health care
      sector in Hillsboro. The City’s support of both the OHSU / Pacific Health and Education
      District in Downtown Hillsboro, Kaiser Westside Medical Campus, OHSU West Campus
      and the Vaccine and Gene Therapy Institute, and private medical device manufactures are
      demonstration of the City’s commitment to this policy. Additionally, the City actively
      supports the ongoing growth of the bio-pharma employment cluster along with the
      retention and expansion of existing medical device manufacturers.

      The proposed HCP text amendments support and are consistent with the purpose of the

      information from which to evaluate future policy choices.

      The EOA is required by OAR 660-009-0015(2) to conduct an analysis and identify required
      site types by a number that can be expected to be needed to accommodate the expected
      employment growth based upon typically expected uses. This analysis is found in 2021
      EOA Section 4 (Exhibit B), with supporting documentation found in the 2021 EOA
      Technical Appendices (Exhibit C). These findings support both Policy’s UR 1.3, Infill, and
      UR 1.7 by maintaining a full understanding of the economic need for both large and small
      lot sites to maintain a strong and diverse economy for the City. The BLI and EOA further
      emphasize the need for effective and efficient use of all parcels, large and small, and the
      available capacity being serviceable overtime to capture market opportunities.

      To complete the update for the EOA, the staff completed an updated BLI. This data,
      combined with other quantitative and qualitative trend data completes the 2021 EOA and
      provides a refreshed understanding of Hillsboro’s current and future economy from the
      2017 EOA. Completion and adoption of the 2021 EOA by reference to the Comprehensive
      Plan supports Policy UR 1.8 for City policy and decision-makers regarding the current
      supply of developable land in all employment categories, including industrial, commercial,
      office, and mixed-use. The EOA describes that if current trends were to continue, the City
      does not have an adequate 20-year land supply as required by State Goal 9, Economic
      Development and implementing OARs.

      The 2021 EOA provides consistency with the Metro 2040 Plan by providing information
      that is necessary to fully understand the policy choices by local and regional decision-
      makers. The EOA further supports, as discussed in greater detail, the critical need for
      supporting and protecting employment lands of all types but particularly around traded
      sector employment.

      sections of the HCP including employment-related policies by providing updated data from

      Policy LU 2.11 Regular review. Regularly review and modify the Comprehensive
