      Finding: The proposed HCP text amendment supports and is consistent with the purpose
      of the project to provide decision-makers with the most up-to-date information from which
      to evaluate existing and future policies and have informed policy discussions with the
      Metro and State officials. The 2021 EOA is one of three foundational documents that the
      City uses to direct land use policy decisions.

      The 2021 EOA provides an updated analysis of the national, state, regional, and local trends
      for industrial, office, and commercial employment consistent with OAR 660-009
      methodology, including an updated BLI, that provides a basis a refreshed analysis and
      inventory of the land needed to support the policies and goals of the Hillsboro
      Comprehensive Plan and target industries.

      The City completed the 2020 BLI in compliance with the terms of the LUBA remand, using
      the Metro UGR BLI. As with the initial 2019 BLI, the amended 2020 BLI based on data
      from December 2020, utilizes GIS analysis based on Washington County tax parcel data
      (limited to the City of Hillsboro and associated future growth areas). The 2020 BLI focuses
      on parcels for which some form of employment use is permitted, differentiated between

Page 16 of 24
Exhibit D
Ordinance No. 6474
City Council
      COM commercial, IND Industrial, and MUR mixed use residential and commercially
      zoned properties (with employment capacity varied to reflect allocations differentiated by
      mixed use zoning designation). Both the initial and amended BLI inventories reflect land
      use conditions as of 2019-20 consistent with the baseline year for forecasting of
      employment growth over the ensuing 2020-40 time period. As noted, the amended BLI
      reflects employment land inventory conditions as of December 2020.

      The 2020 BLI (included in full as Appendix E of Exhibit C) is summarized as part of a
      five-step process. Step 1 Land Classification identifies the land in the City that is available
      for employment uses. Step 2 Constraints to Development identifies constraints such as
      natural resources, steep slopes, and utility easements that limit development. Step 3:
      Development Status assigns a “Development Status” of vacant, partially vacant, or
      developed to tax lots in the inventory. Step 4 Net Buildable Area removes land for future
      rights-of-way and other land needs to provide a net number of buildable acres for each City
      zoning designation. Step 5: Redevelopment screens developed parcels for redevelopment
      potential.
      Parcels in the inventory are categorized based on their Comprehensive Plan designations,
      zoning designations, property ownership, and other characteristics. Employment
      classifications include designation of lands with Comprehensive Plan designation as
      industrial, commercial and as a portion of mixed use land. Residential as well as publicly
      owned and other uses not consistent with employment activity are excluded from the
      employment BLI.
      Employment land that is constrained from development is excluded from net buildable
      acreage based on constraints including steep slopes, water bodies, FEMA floodway, FEMA
      100 Year floodplain, significant wetlands, significant forest resources, the City’s significant
      natural resources overlay (SNRO), BPA easements, and Hillsboro Airport’s runway
      protection area. Unconstrained or buildable areas of parcels are defined as vacant or
      partially vacant sites minus constrained acreage.
      To calculate net developable acreage for each parcel, an overall 25% reduction was applied
      to commercial, industrial and mixed use zones for roads, infrastructure, open space and
      other needs. Parcels in mixed use zones were further reduced based on the proportions of
      land area expected to occur as employment uses (with varied deductions applied specific
      to each of 16 applicable mixed use zones).

      Each parcel in the study area is categorized as vacant, partially vacant, or developed. Vacant
      parcels (including parcels with low-value structures) are assumed to have development
      capacity equal to the area unconstrained by natural resources, minus additional set-asides
      for future Right-of-Way and infrastructure. Partially vacant parcels have existing
      development but with some portion of the site identified as potentially available for future
      development subject to minimum site or use requirements for development suitability (as
Page 17 of 24
Exhibit D
Ordinance No. 6474
City Council
       specific to industrial, commercial and mixed use zones). Developed parcels are subject to
       further screening for redevelopment potential, using the “Strike-Price analysis. The “strike
       price” is a value per square foot at which a developer can afford to purchase the property
       and theoretically redevelop profitably. The 2018 Metro Urban Growth Report's BLI
       estimated strike prices for various land uses and locations throughout the region. This test
       is an estimate commonly used to evaluate redevelopment potential at a high level, though
       there are many factors that will ultimately determine the redevelopment of a given parcel.

       The City project consultant combined that baseline information with national, state,
       regional, and local trend data and local business qualitative information to arrive at the
       projected employment growth and land need for the 2021 EOA.

       Staff find that the 2021 EOA is consistent with policy LU 2.7 and 2.11.

   2. Oregon Statewide Planning Goal 9 - Economic Development

       Goal 9 outlines the importance of coordinated Comprehensive Plan policies to create a
       stable and healthy economy. The goal directs that City’s maintain a working inventory of
       employment land for industrial and commercial development. The rule also directs that
       economic land planning consider a 20-year land supply for employment uses that the
       community is targeting based on a reasonable likelihood that these uses could locate in the
       community.

       Finding: The update of the Hillsboro EOA was developed consistently with State Goal 9,
       Economic Development, and OAR 660-009 and specifically as outlined below in OAR

Exhibit D

City Council
      660-009-0015 (3) as it relates to the buildable land inventory. The proposed HCP
      amendment is to update Chapter 14 – Section 23.4 by replacing the reference to the
      previous 2017 EOA with the 2021 EOA.

      A) OAR 660-009-0015 (3)

         (3) Inventory of Industrial and Other Employment Lands. Comprehensive plans for
             all areas within urban growth boundaries must include an inventory of vacant
             and developed lands within the planning area designated for industrial or other
             employment use.

         (a) For sites inventoried under this section, plans must provide the following
             information:
             (A) The description, including site characteristics, of vacant or developed sites
                 within each plan or zoning district;
             (B) A description of any development constraints or infrastructure needs that
                 affect the buildable area of sites in the inventory; and
             (C) For cities and counties within a Metropolitan Planning Organization, the
                 inventory must also include the approximate total acreage and percentage of
                 sites within each plan or zoning district that comprise the short-term supply of
                 land.

          (b) When comparing current land supply to the projected demand, cities and
             counties may inventory contiguous lots or parcels together that are within a
             discrete plan or zoning district.

          (c)Cities and counties that adopt objectives or policies providing for prime
             industrial land pursuant to OAR 660-009-0020 (Industrial and Other Employment
             Development Policies)(6) and 660-009-0025 (Designation of Lands for Industrial
             and Other Employment Uses)(8) must identify and inventory any vacant or
             developed prime industrial land according to section (3)(a) of this rule.

      Finding: Hillsboro must “review and as necessary, amend” our comprehensive plan to
      provide an Economic Opportunities Analysis contained in OAR 660-009-0015 (1-4). OAR
      660-009-0015 (3) requires an EOA to “include and inventory of vacant and developed lands
      within the planning area designated for industrial or other employment use, which we refer
      to as a Buildable Lands Inventory (BLI).

      Further analysis is required of the inventory of developable land is required including
      descriptions of vacant and developed land within each zoning district; a description of
      development site constraints and infrastructure needs; and, for those cities within a

Page 19 of 24
Exhibit D
Ordinance No. 6474
City Council
       Metropolitan Planning Organization (MPO), the inventory must include the approximate
       total acreage and percentage of sites within a discrete plan or zoning district.

       Hillsboro’s 2020 BLI pre-recession comprises a total of just under 6,210 gross acres. Of
       this, over 3,753 acres (60%) are already developed – leaving 2,457 acres (40%) as not yet
       developed. Of the undeveloped acreage, the City’s BLI model indicates that approximately
       1,232 acres (20% of the inventory) represent unbuildable portions of vacant and partially
       vacant sites due to constraints and future infrastructure set-asides. This includes lands that are
       environmentally constrained and/or allocated for rights-of-way and utilitarian functions.
       The remaining 1,225 acres comprise Hillsboro’s remaining buildable area for employment
       use. Further additional detailed analysis is contained in both the 2021 EOA and 2021 EOA
       Technical Appendix.

       The 3,753 acres of developed land was further screened for redevelopment potential using
       the “strike price” analysis. A total of 65 parcels meet the size and strike price for potential
       redevelopment. Taken together, these parcels account for an estimated 143 acres of
       potentially redevelopable employment land.            Roughly 85% of this potentially
       redevelopable land is zoned for industrial use. If redevelopment of these 143 acres were
       to occur, it would increase Hillsboro’s buildable acreage (or net employment land) by up
       to about 12%. Given the numerous variables that determine whether an individual site will
       redevelop, including property owner willingness, the availability of other suitable sites,
       and macroeconomic factors, the 143 acres of potentially redevelopable land was not
       included in the 1,225 acres of Hillsboro’s remaining buildable area for employment use.

       Out of more than 6,210 acres of gross employment designated land area, more than 2,456
       acres (40% of the total) consist of tax parcels that are vacant or partially vacant with
       potential for some amounts of added employment development (before environmental,
       infrastructure, and other set-asides are taken into consideration). An estimated 128 parcels
       are considered partially vacant. Taken together, these partially vacant properties account
       for an estimated 1,203 acres. Of this amount 398 acres are viewed as potentially
       developable with 805 considered unbuildable. Overall average parcel size for these parcels
       that are partially vacant is about 9.4 acres. A total of 361 vacant land parcels comprises
       1,253 acres with average parcel size of just 3.5 acres. Of this, approximately 826 acres are
       estimated as net buildable with 427 acres classified as unbuildable. In effect, while
       Hillsboro’s vacant inventory is comprised of relatively small parcels, a higher proportion
       of this vacant lot inventory is assumed to be ultimately developable than with remaining
       partially vacant sites. Industrial lands identified as suitable for future employment use
       average about eight acres per remaining land parcels for which development potential is
       noted as compared with only 1.2-1.6 acres per lot for the average commercial/ mixed uses
       sites, respectively.

       This chart from the EOA illustrates a significant Hillsboro land supply shortage across all
       three employment growth scenarios considered. This supply gap affects Hillsboro’s future
       capacity to attract continued investment, especially from major employers requiring

         •   Forecast land demand over 20 years is 1.8 times existing BLI land supply with

         •   With the limited supply of BLI capacity comprised primarily of industrially
             designated land, not only is supply inadequate for potential industrial use but there
             may be pressure – including the potential to realize higher land values – with the
             conversion of some industrial land to commercial development as well as added
             redevelopment incentive.
         •   The commercial development that does occur on non-industrial lands is more likely
             to occur with Mixed-Use and Commercial designated sites.

IV.     TESTIMONY FROM PARTIES

        The City received a total of two letters of testimony. These two letters were from Friends
        regarding the proposed HCP amendment to update the 2017 EOA reference to the 2021
        EOA, as supplemented May 2024.

        1. Friends submitted a letter dated May 7, 2024. In this letter, Friends requested that the
           May 8th public hearing be continued to May 22, 2024 to allow more time to review the
           materials and that they be added to the mailing list to receive all materials related to
           this item.

        Finding: At the May 8th public hearing, the Planning Commission granted staff’s request
        to continue the hearing to May 22, 2024. After mailing the materials for the May 8th hearing
        to Friends, staff was made aware that the mailing address and contact information on file
        with the City for Friends was out of date. Staff updated the mailing information for Friends
        and provided the revised documents to Friends in advance of the continued public hearing
        on May 22, 2024.

        2. Friends submitted a letter dated May 22, 2024. This letter highlighted three specific
           areas of concern: 1) The City erred by failing to review the proposed amendment as a
Page 22 of 24
Exhibit D
Ordinance No. 6474
City Council
         major amendment; 2) The City proposed planning horizon is too long, growth
         assumptions unrealistic, and not based in fact; and 3) The City’s Buildable Lands
         Inventory (BLI) is inadequate.

      Finding: Friends argues that the City erred by failing to review the proposed amendment
      as a major amendment. Friends asserts that the decision to replace the 2017 EOA with the
      2021 EOA does not qualify as a minor amendment to the comprehensive plan and should
      instead be processed as a major amendment. This was raised in their argument against
      adoption of the 2021 EOA at the Land Use Board of Appeals (LUBA) hearing. The 2021
      EOA was remanded in part on this issue. Staff has compiled findings attached to this staff
      report (Exhibit D) that clarify why the proposed amendment is considered “minor” and not
      a “major” amendment and demonstrate compliance with CDC Section 12.80.164 – Minor
      Text Amendment.

      In order to be a major text amendment, the proposed change must amend or refine both the
      Plan text and map. This amendment does not amend both, and therefore is a minor
      amendment. Further, the City has discretion in interpreting its own code, and in this case,
      the City is simply replacing the 2017 EOA with the 2021 EOA, which the City does not
      believe has significant environmental, energy, economic, or social consequences.

      Additionally, Friends argues that the City’s proposed planning horizon is too long, and
      growth assumptions are unrealistic and not based in fact. Friends argues that the City may
      not plan beyond a 20-year projection and that the use of a compounded annual growth rate
      (CAGR) to determine anticipated land needs in Scenarios B & C has no factual basis. It is
      well established by case law that Friends cannot bring a new issue that is beyond the scope
      of the remand and could have been raised previously at a different stage of this proceeding.
      Therefore, Friends may not make this argument before the Planning Commission.
      Alternatively, Friends fails to cite any law when making this argument, instead relying on
      its own personal opinions. It is in the nature of planning to look ahead, and without citing
      a specific law or regulation, this argument is not valid.

      Finally, Friends believes the City’s BLI to be inadequate. Friends makes three arguments
      to this point.

      a) The City fails to evaluate development and redevelopment potential of developed land.
         This is a conclusory statement, not an argument. Friends is simply restating 1 of 2 of
         LUBA’s conclusions that resulted in this remand that the City is addressing with the
         amended Buildable Lands Inventory and EOA. Staff and the City’s consultant have
         supplemented the 2021 EOA and 2021 EOA Technical Appendices with additional
         Employment Buildable Lands Inventory (BLI) analysis and language regarding the
         redevelopment potential of developed lands. Additionally, staff has compiled findings
         that demonstrate compliance Oregon Statewide Planning Goal 9, Economy, and OAR
         660-009-0015 (3) as it relates to the Employment BLI and the redevelopment potential
         of developed lands.
Page 23 of 24
Exhibit D
Ordinance No. 6474
City Council
      b) The City fails to correctly consider certain types of land in its employment assessment.
         Friends argues that the City should have included residential land and land for other
         uses not consistent with employment activity in the land needs analysis. This argument
         is beyond the scope of this remand and, like in point 2 above, should have been raised
         by Friends at a different stage of these proceedings. LUBA concludes that the City must
         evaluate in the BLI whether the developed portions of lots and parcels are likely to
         redevelop on remand. However, LUBA does not open the door to a full re-evaluation
         of other elements or aspects of the BLI. Therefore, Friends may not make this argument
         before the Planning Commission. Alternatively, the BLI is an inventory of lands within
         the planning area designated for industrial or other employment use. Schools are not
         designated as an industrial or employment use, they are a civic use. In addition, schools
         practically would have a nominal effect on the BLI. Therefore, the City still fulfilled
         its obligations under OAR 660-009-0015(3) because it considered all lands designated
         for industrial or employment uses.


      c) City failed to account for high-tech companies’ growth on developed land. Friends
         argues that the City did not account for the growth and investments tech companies
         have been making on their existing developed land as part of investments approved
         under the recent CHIPS act funding. Like mentioned above, this argument is beyond
         the scope of remand (as provided above) and also beyond the scope of this matter before
         the decision-makers. The Planning Commission is deciding whether the BLI complies
         with relevant administrative rules (OAR 660-009-0015(3) by inventorying designated
         industrial and employment lands within the planning area. It is beyond the scope of this
         decision to look at how other counties are approaching the CHIPs act’s impact on
         buildable lands or UGBs, or whether this may affect the City’s UGB. This will be
         handled in subsequent decision-making processes.

      COMMENTARY



    How Many Jobs Do Data Centers Create? It Depends
    Data centers create jobs, but how many? We examine the variables affecting employment numbers and
    why the impact varies dramatically across different facilities.

                   Christopher Tozzi, Technology Analyst
                   August 28, 2025

        4 Min Read




    Data centers create varying levels of employment depending on facility type, location, and operational
    needs – from construction jobs to technical roles. IMAGE: ALAMY




https://www.datacenterknowledge.com/operations-and-management/how-many-jobs-do-data-centers-create-it-depends          1/8
9/24/26, 1:52 PM                                            How Many Jobs Do Data Centers Create? It Depends

    Data centers have frequently been criticized for creating few permanent jobs in relation to
    their footprint – and this criticism might not be entirely unfounded. In general, data centers
    generate relatively few jobs compared to the cost of building and operating a typical facility
    or the amount of land it occupies.

    On the other hand, the number of jobs resulting from data centers can vary widely depending
    on factors like facility type and location. It’s a little narrow-minded to conclude that data
    centers are always total busts when it comes to job creation.

    To understand why, let’s look at the extent to which data centers do or don’t spawn new
    employment opportunities.

    How Do Data Centers Create Jobs?
    Data centers can generate jobs in two primary ways:

        Temporary, contracted employment opportunities during data center construction. A
        large facility might keep thousands of construction workers busy, at least for the year or
        two that it takes to build.
        Permanent jobs for staff inside data centers. Once a data center is up and running, it
        usually requires some on-site technicians to handle tasks like setting up and managing IT
        equipment. Typically, however, the total data center staff number is only several dozen.

    Related: Leadership Updates: Key Data Center & Cloud Appointments (Q3 2026)

    So, while data centers may create many jobs in the short term, most result in relatively few
    permanent jobs – hence why critics tend to highlight the generous tax abatements that data
    centers often receive. They tend to argue that local communities receive few economic
    benefits from becoming home to a new data center.




https://www.datacenterknowledge.com/operations-and-management/how-many-jobs-do-data-centers-create-it-depends   2/8
9/24/26, 1:52 PM                                            How Many Jobs Do Data Centers Create? It Depends




    Job creation from data centers extends beyond direct employment, supporting broader
    economic growth through digital infrastructure for countless businesses. Image: Alamy

    Variables in Data Center Job Creation
    However, it would be inaccurate to conclude that meaningful employment opportunities
    spawned by data centers are always negligible. The actual relationship between data centers
    and job creation can vary widely depending on factors like the following.

    Data Center Density
    Areas that are home to a large and growing number of data centers stand to benefit more
    from data center job creation. In places where new data centers are always going up, workers
    employed in constructing facilities are more likely to find ongoing employment opportunities.

    In contrast, if a region hosts just one data center, the temporary jobs created by building the
    facility will disappear forever once it’s up and running.

    Dedicated vs. Colocation Data Centers



https://www.datacenterknowledge.com/operations-and-management/how-many-jobs-do-data-centers-create-it-depends   3/8
9/24/26, 1:52 PM                                            How Many Jobs Do Data Centers Create? It Depends

    In general, a dedicated data center owned and used by just one company will generate fewer
    permanent jobs than a shared colocation facility. In the latter type of data center, multiple
    companies can deploy servers, and each of those companies will need a way to manage its
    hardware. Hiring local technicians is one way to meet this challenge.

    Related: Colocation vs. Public Cloud: Cost, Performance, and How to Choose

    In addition, even if a company that rents space in a colocation facility outsources equipment
    management to a third-party provider, it’s still helping to support jobs at the provider.

    Bare-Metal Data Centers
    Data centers that are home to a large number of bare-metal workloads may also contribute to
    more permanent job growth. Bare-metal servers are more likely to require technicians to be
    physically present to maintain equipment, deploy applications and so on.

    Modern data center automation solutions make it possible to perform many tasks remotely or
    automatically, even when working with bare-metal hardware. Still, having “boots on the
    ground” tends to be more important when deploying applications on bare metal than when
    working with software-defined virtual infrastructure.

    Maintenance Needs
    The age and complexity of the physical infrastructure inside a data center play a role in how
    many permanent jobs it creates. For example, a facility with dated HVAC systems may require
    more technicians on-site to maintain components and address failures, although this may
    produce only a handful of additional jobs relative to a facility that requires minimal
    maintenance.

    Related: Will AI Agents Push Enforcement Back into the Database?

    Data Centers Do Create Jobs – Just Not Always at Scale
    It would be wrong to say that data centers are massive engines of job creation. The typical
    data center results in an almost negligible number of permanent jobs relative to its scale.



https://www.datacenterknowledge.com/operations-and-management/how-many-jobs-do-data-centers-create-it-depends   4/8
9/24/26, 1:52 PM                                            How Many Jobs Do Data Centers Create? It Depends

    But it’s also wrong to conclude that data centers never create a meaningful number of jobs.
    Under the right circumstances, data centers can contribute a fair number of employment
    opportunities to local communities. A single facility won’t put thousands of people to work
    forever, but ongoing data center construction, along with data centers that require especially
    high numbers of staff, can result in large-scale ongoing employment.

    Importantly, while this article focused on direct employment within data centers, we should
    also consider their broader economic impact. Data centers power countless businesses,
    organizations, and essential services. From this perspective, data centers support jobs
    across the entire economy – from small local businesses to major enterprises – by providing
    the digital infrastructure they need to operate in today’s world.

I.      EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

In order to support Clackamas County’s economic development efforts, Mackenzie reviewed, analyzed,
and mapped employment lands throughout the county through several different tasks. This document
includes three chapters, one with findings from each task. Some of the tasks build off of one another while
others are discrete and separate tasks, but all are summarized here together in one large report.

Chapter 1: Vacant Industrial Parcel Analysis

For the first task of this project, Mackenzie performed a desktop analysis of vacant and/or redevelopable
industrially zoned parcels greater than 5 acres in unincorporated Clackamas County to better understand
land availability and potential for future industrial development in the County. The analysis identified a
total of 23 parcels that fit into one of four categories for development potential (Development-ready,
Developable with constraints, Unlikely to develop due to constraints, and Active business use present).
These parcels add up to approximately 457 acres.

Approximately 90% of all inventoried parcel acreage (19 out of 23 parcels) are in Category 4: Active
business use present. Additionally, 43% of parcels (10 of the 23 parcels inventoried) are impacted by
environmental constraints such as steep terrain, wetlands, and flood hazard zones. There are two parcels
in the most promising category (Category 1: Development-ready), both owned by Clackamas County
Development Agency (parcels 1 and 2). Mackenzie put additional consideration into development
potential for these two parcels, including re-grouping the bisected and disconnected parcel segments and
aggregating the parcel segments with adjacent smaller parcels under the same ownership to create two
potential development-ready parcels.

Chapter 2: Economic Opportunity Analysis (EOA) Summary

For the second task of this project, Mackenzie reviewed Economic Opportunity Analyses (EOAs) for ten
incorporated cities within Clackamas County: Estacada, Lake Oswego, Milwaukie, Canby, Happy Valley,
Molalla, Sandy, Tualatin, West Linn, and Wilsonville (EOAs completed between 2011 and 2025). Findings
from each city’s Buildable Land Inventory (BLI) were extracted to compare and aggregate the buildable
land available for industrial and commercial uses (vacant and redevelopable), as well as the forecasted
land demand in the EOAs, and the resulting surplus or deficit for each city. This analysis illustrates that
there is a wide range of forecasted land scenarios for cities within Clackamas County, with some cities
forecasted to have surpluses of hundreds of acres, and other cities forecasted to have deficits of hundreds
of acres.

Mackenzie tabulated the total buildable employment land for both commercial and industrial land for all
these cities within Clackamas County, resulting in a total of 2,051 acres (AC) of buildable industrial land
and 627 AC of buildable commercial land. After accounting for the three cities that are in Clackamas
County but are also a part of another county (Lake Oswego, Tualatin, and Wilsonville), the adjusted total
by share of cities’ area within Clackamas County is 1,404 AC of buildable industrial land, and 601 AC of
buildable commercial land. (The methodology for accounting for multi-county cities is detailed in
Appendix 5.)

Combining the forecasted needs for each of the cities highlighted overall deficits for both industrial and
commercial land: a deficit of 194 AC of industrial land and a deficit of 169 AC of commercial land across




                                                                                                         5
the cities within Clackamas County.1 After accounting for multi-county cities, the adjusted overall deficits
by share of cities’ area within Clackamas County are a deficit of 841 AC of industrial land, and a deficit of
196 AC of commercial land.

Chapter 3: BLI Mapping and Analysis

After summarizing these ten EOAs in task 2, Mackenzie analyzed and mapped the Buildable Land Inventory
(BLI) for Canby, Estacada, Gladstone, Happy Valley, Johnson City2, Lake Oswego, Milwaukie, Molalla,
Oregon City, Sandy, Tualatin2, West Linn, and Wilsonville.3 This analysis involved identifying the status of
the buildable employment land as vacant, partially vacant/infill, or redevelopable based on 2024 data
from Metro and data from the jurisdictions outside of Metro (from various years between 2019 and 2025).
Important attributes such as parcel size and zoning classification were recorded. Additionally, to highlight
potential impact of parcel aggregation, Mackenzie identified parcels which may be suitable candidates for
aggregation based on shared property boundaries in order to create larger development sites.

Mackenzie found that the analyzed jurisdictions have approximately 930 parcels of buildable employment
land (commercial, industrial, and mixed use). Approximately 68% of the identified parcels are smaller than
one (1) acre in size and another 22% are in the 1-4.99-acre size range, meaning fewer than 10% of the
analyzed parcels are larger than 5 acres. Importantly, this analysis is a snapshot in time, using the best
available data, and may not be reflective of current conditions.

The analysis and technical findings are detailed in the following report and in the appendices, which
include the map packages, spreadsheet deliverables, and in-depth methodologies.




1
  Goal 9 does not have a required method for employment forecasting. Each city has different approaches to
forecasting demand scenarios, creating difficulty in direct comparison. Professional judgement was used to select
the most similar forecast for each city for this analysis, selecting the forecasts based on OED employment growth
trends and industry trends, or whatever forecast was available when only one was provided. The process for
selecting comparable scenarios is detailed in Appendix 5.

II.        CHAPTER 1: VACANT INDUSTRIAL PARCEL ANALYSIS

Purpose

To support Clackamas County’s economic development effort, Mackenzie performed a desktop analysis
of vacant and/or redevelopable industrially zoned parcels greater than 5 acres in unincorporated
Clackamas County. This analysis can help County staff better understand land availability and potential for
future industrial development in the region.

Findings Summary

The analysis identified a total of 23 parcels that fit into one of four categories for development potential.
These parcels add up to approximately 457 acres. Approximately 90% of all inventoried parcel acreage (19
out of 23 parcels) are in Category 4: Active business use present and have a lower likelihood of
redevelopment. Additionally, 43% of parcels (10 of the 23 parcels inventoried) are impacted by
environmental constraints such as steep terrain, wetlands, and flood hazard zones. There are two parcels
in the most promising category (Category 1: Development-ready), both owned by Clackamas County
Development Agency (parcels 1 and 2). Mackenzie put additional consideration into development
potential for these two parcels, including re-grouping the bisected and disconnected parcel segments and
aggregating the parcel segments with adjacent smaller parcels under the same ownership to create two
potential development-ready parcels.

The following section shares a summary of the methodology and findings of this analysis. More technical
information and findings, along with the maps, can be found in the below appendices:

▪          Appendix 1 – Spreadsheet summary of inventoried parcels
▪          Appendix 2 – Map package of inventoried parcels
▪          Appendix 3 – County wide map of inventoried parcels

Methodology Summary

To complete this analysis, Mackenzie utilized Geographic Information System (GIS) data from Clackamas
County and Metro Regional Land Information System (RLIS). Clackamas County provided a dataset with
all industrially zoned parcels of 5 acres or larger in the unincorporated areas of the County, which was
created by County staff in the summer of 2025. There were 108 total parcels in this dataset, totaling 1,404
AC. Mackenzie reviewed each of these parcels to identify the parcels that were entirely vacant or were
partially vacant but have at least 5 acres of contiguous vacant land. Parcels that were already fully in use
were removed from analysis.

Additional spatial layers were added to the analysis, including Flood Hazard Zones, wetlands, and streams,
which revealed significant development constraints on some parcels.4 Mackenzie also assembled
additional details for each parcel, including identifying existing operations through internet searches and
incorporating ownership (taxpayer) information and aerial photography. Discussions with Clackamas
County staff about parcel context, surrounding uses, and (re)development potential helped further refine
the list of parcels.

Based on this analysis, all parcels were placed into one of four categories:


4
    Flood hazard zone data provided by FEMA. Wetland and stream data provided by Metro RLIS.

                                                                                                           7
Category 1. Development-ready

▪       Vacant parcel, zoned for industrial development, without constraints (wetlands, floodplain,
        topography, etc.).
▪       Parcels in this category present no significant development constraints, have infrastructure at or
        near the property boundary, and entitlements are already in place or can be easily obtained.

Category 2. Developable with constraints

▪       Vacant parcel, zoned for industrial development, with some constraints (wetlands, floodplain,
        topography, etc.) that may or may not need to be mitigated prior to development.
▪       Parcels in this category could become viable for development within approximately three years,
        contingent upon addressing reasonable development constraints, securing necessary
        entitlements, and/or extending required public infrastructure.

Category 3. Unlikely to develop due to constraints

▪       Vacant parcel, zoned for industrial development, with significant constraints (wetlands,
        floodplain, topography, etc.), covering the majority of the parcels.
▪       Parcels in this category are significantly constrained, face challenges in obtaining entitlements, or
        are landlocked from viable public infrastructure. Examples include parcels with steep slopes,
        former quarry sites, or riverside locations with significant development restrictions.

Category 4. Active business use present

▪       Vacant or partially in use parcel owned by an existing business. Property may be partially in use
        by existing business or vacant but being held for future business needs/expansion.

Technical Analysis Findings

The analysis identified 23 industrially zoned parcels greater than 5 acres that are vacant, partially vacant,
or have opportunity for expansion of nearby business operations. See Table 1 for a summary of results.

Further Analysis of Category 1 Parcels

The two parcels that are in Category 1 (development-ready) are owned by the Clackamas County
Development Agency. These two parcels are made up of irregular and disconnected segments which are
also bisected by Highway 224. To better understand development potential for this area, Mackenzie
examined what would happen if parts of the parcels were re-grouped, creating two parcels: Parcel 1 could
be made up of the parcel segments on the east side of Highway 224 and Parcel 2 could be made up of the
parcel segments on the west side of Highway 224. Next, Mackenzie examined aggregating the parcels with
additional adjacent industrially zoned parcels with shared ownership that had not been included in the
previous analysis because they are smaller than 5 acres. With the addition of these smaller parcels, the
approximate size of hypothetical Parcel 1 is 9.38 AC and the approximate size of hypothetical Parcel 2 is
12.66 AC. Property line adjustments are necessary to deliver these as graphically shown.

The parcel aggregation of each new potential aggregated site is detailed in Table 4 and 5 and graphically
depicted in Appendix 2.

Conclusion

After reviewing approximately 1,404 AC of industrially zoned parcels greater than 5 acres throughout
unincorporated Clackamas County, Mackenzie identified 20.39 AC of development-ready land (Category
1), representing approximately 1.45% of all land studied. These 20.39 AC of developable land are all
located on two nearby parcels (Parcel 1 and Parcel 2), both owned by Clackamas County Development
Agency.

More detailed analysis of these Category 1 parcels led Mackenzie to examine aggregating the parcels with
adjacent parcels under shared ownership that were less than 5 acres (and therefore not included in
original inventory analysis). This aggregation could add approximately 1.66 AC, for a total of 22.05 AC of
development-ready land (Category 1), representing approximately 1.57% of studied land.

III.    CHAPTER 2: ECONOMIC OPPORTUNITY ANALYSIS (EOA) SUMMARY

Purpose

Mackenzie’s review of industrially zoned parcels greater than 5 acres in unincorporated Clackamas County
yielded limited opportunities for industrial development. Given these findings in unincorporated
Clackamas County, the next phase of this work was to investigate employment lands in incorporated
Clackamas County.

To do this, Mackenzie reviewed Economic Opportunity Analyses (EOAs) for 10 cities within Clackamas
County: Estacada; Lake Oswego; Milwaukie; Canby; Happy Valley; Molalla; Sandy; Tualatin; West Linn; and
Wilsonville. Findings from each city’s Buildable Land Inventory (BLI) were extracted to compare and
aggregate the buildable land available for industrial and commercial uses (vacant and redevelopable), as
well as the forecasted land demand in the EOAs, and the resulting surplus or deficit for each city.

The following section discusses the findings of this analysis along with data visualizations of these findings.
More technical information on the methodology and findings can be found in the appendices:

▪       Appendix 4 – EOA Summary and Analysis Matrix
▪       Appendix 5 – EOA Summary Methodology and Assumptions

Findings

This analysis illustrates that there is a wide range of forecasted land needs for cities within Clackamas
County, with some cities forecasted to have surpluses of hundreds of acres (e.g., Estacada), and other
cities forecasted to have deficits of hundreds of acres (e.g., Milwaukie and Canby).

Countywide Analysis

Mackenzie summed up the total buildable land for both commercial and industrial land for all the cities
within Clackamas County, resulting in a total of 2,051 acres (AC) of buildable industrial land and 627 AC of
buildable commercial land. After accounting for the three cities that are in Clackamas County but are also
a part of another county, the adjusted total by share of cities’ area within Clackamas County is 1,404 AC
of buildable industrial land, and 601 AC of buildable commercial land. (The methodology for accounting
for multi-county cities is detailed in Appendix 5.)

Combining the forecasted needs for each of the cities resulted in overall deficits for both industrial and
commercial land: a deficit of 194 AC of industrial land and a deficit of 169 AC of commercial land across
the cities within Clackamas County.5 After accounting for multi-county cities, the adjusted overall deficits
by share of cities’ area within Clackamas County are a deficit of 841 AC of industrial land, and a deficit of
196 AC of commercial land.

The findings are summarized in Table 6 below, and the full analysis can be found in Appendix 2.

IV.     CHAPTER 3: BUILDABLE LAND INVENTORY (BLI) MAPPING AND ANALYSIS

Purpose

After reviewing and analyzing the Economic Opportunity Analysis (EOAs) for ten cities within Clackamas
County and summing up the supply, demand, and surplus/deficit of employment land throughout these
ten cities, Mackenzie mapped the Buildable Land Inventories (BLI’s) to further analyze and illustrate the
buildable employment land. The purpose of this analysis is to further the economic development
objectives of Clackamas County through providing an analysis of buildable employment land within Canby,
Estacada, Gladstone, Happy Valley, Johnson City6, Lake Oswego, Milwaukie, Molalla, Oregon City, Sandy,
Tualatin, West Linn, and Wilsonville. Only the portions of Lake Oswego, Tualatin, and Wilsonville within
Clackamas County have been studied in this analysis.

To do so, Mackenzie identified the status of buildable employment land as vacant, partially vacant/infill,
and redevelopable based on data from Metro and the jurisdictions outside Metro. Important attributes
such as parcel size and zoning classification were recorded. Additionally, to highlight potential impact of
parcel aggregation, Mackenzie identified parcels which may be suitable candidates for aggregation based
on shared property boundaries in order to create larger development sites.

Importantly, the land in the Buildable Employment Land (BLI) datasets includes industrial, commercial,
and mixed use and is considered “buildable,” but not necessarily “development-ready.” “Buildable Land”
may have one, or more barriers to development (e.g. infrastructure availability). This should be taken into
account when considering site suitability and development feasibility.

Additionally, this analysis does not include land in unincorporated Clackamas County, because the County
does not have an Economic Opportunity Analysis (EOA), however, Metro’s Buildable Land Inventory (BLI)
does include urban and unincorporated areas within Metro’s jurisdiction. See the first chapter of this
report for an analysis of available industrially zoned parcels over 5 acres in unincorporated Clackamas
County. The second chapter of this report analyzed the EOAs for jurisdictions within Clackamas County,
taking into account forecasted needs and subsequent deficits and surpluses. Due to the lack of a County
EOA, a next project phase may include an investigation of commercial and mixed use inventory in
unincorporated Clackamas County, which would be a more robust county-wide perspective of available
and buildable land inventories.

The following section shares both a summary of the key findings and a more detailed discussion of the
technical findings along with recommended next steps. The map package and more technical information
on the methodology can be found in the below appendices:

▪       Appendix 6 – Map package of BLI by jurisdiction
▪       Appendix 7 – BLI Mapping Methodology and Assumptions

Findings Summary

▪       The analyzed jurisdictions have approximately 930 parcels of buildable employment land
        (commercial, industrial, and mixed use).

         in the 1-4.99-acre size range, meaning fewer than 10% of the analyzed parcels are larger than 5
         acres. These 5 acres and larger parcels (89 total) make up more than 1,000 acres of the 1,700
         acres identified in this report.
▪        As shown in Figure 11, below, approximately 66% of the identified buildable employment land is

         buildable employment land, with most parcels, 276 out of 373 (74%), smaller than 1 acre.

▪        Of the 5,800 acres of employment land identified by Metro in the 2024 Urban Growth Report,
         approximately 1,300 acres (22%) are within the Clackamas County Metro jurisdictions.

Data and Methodology Considerations

▪        For the jurisdictions in Metro, much of the employment land is impacted by one or more
         environmental constraints, including slope, wetlands, or floodplain. However, the acreage figures
         in this analysis are the net unconstrained acres after removal of the constrained areas.
▪        Many jurisdictions use different criteria to classify land as vacant, partially vacant/infill, or
         redevelopable. This presents a challenge when comparing jurisdictions evenly. These
         classifications are explained in the methodology appendix (Appendix 7) as reference.
▪        This analysis is a snapshot in time, with source data from different years, ranging from 2019 to
         2025. Therefore, the status of parcels may be outdated and not reflective of current parcel status,
         due to the age of the best available data used in this report.

Technical Analysis Findings

Mackenzie analyzed employment land supply data for 13 jurisdictions to provide detailed findings
regarding the inventory of buildable lands for the incorporated jurisdictions in Clackamas County. The
source of the buildable employment land data for Gladstone, Happy Valley, Johnson City8, Lake Oswego,
Milwaukie, Oregon City, Tualatin, West Linn, and Wilsonville was the 2024 Metro Buildable Lands
Inventory, provided by Metro. The source of buildable employment land data for Canby (2023), Estacada
(2019), Molalla (2025), and Sandy (2024), was each City’s respective Buildable Land Inventory (dates
provided in parentheticals), provided by Clackamas County. Refer to Appendix 7 for further details on
methodology and assumptions.

The initial step in the analysis was to filter Geographic Information System (GIS) data to identify parcel
status as vacant, partially vacant/infill, and redevelopable. This analysis focused on parcels with
employment zoning designations, including mixed use since office development is allowed in most mixed-
use zones.

Once parcel status was analyzed, Mackenzie tabulated the acreage by zone classification and parcel size.
Additionally, in situations where a parcel had a shared property line of over approximately 100' with
another parcel, these parcels were aggregated into sites to illustrate how parcel aggregation could impact


8
  No buildable employment land parcels were identified by Metro in Johnson City and Tualatin (the portion of the
City within Clackamas County). Therefore, these two jurisdictions have not been included in further steps of this
study.

                                                                                                              23
the supply of employment lands. Parcel aggregation did not take into consideration ownership, access, or
infrastructure, or other development related requirements.

Technical findings are summarized in charts and detailed in the tables and figures below. Additionally,
Appendix 6 contains a series of maps and tables showing the vacant, partially vacant/infill, and
redevelopable sites in the studied jurisdictions.

Parcel and Site Size Distribution

To provide a more complete picture of the County’s buildable employment land’s development potential,
Mackenzie sorted the identified parcels and sites into the following acreage size ranges to see the
distribution of parcel and site size:

▪       Smaller than 1 acre.
▪       1-4.99 acres.
▪       5-9.99 acres.
▪       10-19.99 acres.
▪       Larger than 20 acres.

Key Takeaways:

▪       As shown in Table 10, the analyzed jurisdictions have 933 parcels of buildable employment land
        (commercial, industrial, and mixed use) which can be aggregated into 484 sites.
▪       Approximately 68% of the identified parcels are smaller than 1 acre in size and another 22% are
        in the 1-4.99-acre size range, meaning fewer than 10% of the parcels are larger than 5 acres.
▪       There are several jurisdictions where most employment acreage (both parcels and sites) is in the
        1 acre and smaller category (Gladstone, Lake Oswego, Milwaukie, and West Linn).
▪       This analysis found 17 parcels (fewer than 2%) within the incorporated cities of Clackamas County
        that are larger than 20 acres. Parcel aggregation could increase that number to 25.
▪       Often, mid-size parcels (5-9.99 and 10-19.99 acres) can be aggregated to achieve sites larger than
        20 acres. Though this aggregation creates larger sites, it can lead to a reduction in the number of
        mid-size parcels.


                                                                                                        25
▪          When aggregating adjacent parcels, more large sites were able to be created in only one category:
           20 acres and larger (25 compared to 17). In the other acreage categories, site aggregation resulted
           in fewer sites compared to parcels as small parcels were aggregated with other smaller parcels,
           and barely resulting in a larger aggregated site. The aggregated sites were reduced by nearly 50%
           compared to individual parcels (484 versus 933). While this was expected, the difference in some
           jurisdictions is very large (Happy Valley, Oregon City, Wilsonville, Canby, Estacada, Molalla, and
           Sandy), meaning that property aggregation will be key to providing larger development sites.
▪          The average parcel size of all identified parcels is 1.7 acres, and the median parcel size is 0.25
           acres. The largest parcel of all identified parcels is approximately 50 acres, and the largest site
           (after aggregating parcels) is approximately 94 acres. Both the largest parcel and largest site are
           located in Estacada (notably, these parcels are not impacted by the 2023 rezone).
▪          The share of buildable parcels that is smaller than 1 acre is higher for jurisdictions within Metro
           (between 70% to 100%) than for jurisdictions outside of Metro (between 51% to 62%).
▪          In jurisdictions where site aggregation yielded a large reduction in the number sites (compared to
           individual parcels), this indicates the jurisdiction has a highly parcelized employment land base.
           Accordingly, parcel aggregation may have more impact in these jurisdictions.

County Wide Maps:

To provide a visualization of this analysis, Mackenzie prepared a series of maps showing the vacant,
partially vacant/infill, and redevelopable parcels by zoning classification in the analyzed jurisdictions.
These maps are included as Appendix 6. These maps are intended to assist staff and decision makers to
understand where employment land acreage is clustered and allow for a more streamlined update
process where parcels can be removed by staff as they are developed or conditions change.

Please note that although the entirety of the partially vacant/infill parcels are shown on the map, only a
portion of those parcels are considered “buildable” due to existing development. Additionally, though the
maps do not show the constraints that were considered in the underlying datasets, the removal of
constrained area is accounted in the acreage tabulations presented in this analysis.

Each jurisdiction map in Appendix 6 also contains two (2) tables: Employment Size Distribution and
Employment Acreage. The Employment Size Distribution table details the size of parcels and sites within
each jurisdiction. The Employment Acreage table tabulates the acreage by development classification
(vacant, partially vacant/infill, and redevelopable). These tables show that as parcels are aggregated,
there is potential for creation of larger sites.

Recommended Next Steps

The analysis was completed in May 2026 and utilized information from Metro’s BLI from June 2024 and
individual jurisdiction EOA data, some dating back to 2019. The findings in this report are based on the
best available information provided to Mackenzie to use in this report as of May 2026. Since this inventory
responds to the commercial real estate market, it is expected to change regularly as properties transact,
are rezoned, and/or get developed. Factors impacting this change will include:

▪       New or better information.
▪       Site development (resulting in sites coming off of the inventories).
▪       New properties coming on the market (Resulting in new sites added to the inventories).
▪       Properties in the inventory coming off the market due to transactions (resulting in parcels/sites
        coming off of the inventories).
▪       Other related issues (for example, rezones, annexations, etc.).

Due to this inventory fluctuation, it is recommended that county staff coordinate with jurisdictions to
periodically update this inventory to ground truth the data presented in this report for a more accurate
real-time inventory and consistent data age.

As a progression of this analysis, the County should consider conducting a study to identify sites for target
industries based on the Business Oregon Industrial Competitiveness Matrix, to see how the County’s land
supply matches up with what industries require for development. As part of that future study, it would be
beneficial to investigate infrastructure improvements which could move sites toward development
readiness.

Additionally, as a next phase to this project, staff should discuss whether further investigating the
identified parcels in this report to analyze how development read the sites are and identify any necessary
infrastructure improvements and analyze how the identified parcels match with County economic
development goals and target industries.


                                                                                                          31
Staff should also pursue the next phase of extending the Industrial Site Readiness Study already performed
(Chapter 1), to add commercial and mixed use properties in unincorporated Clackamas County. This would
provide a more holistic view that is more in line with the EOA summary and analysis. Once this analysis is
complete, the charts and graphs should be revised to include unincorporated Clackamas County as a
jurisdiction in order to analyze and review all buildable employment land in a single report.

Finally, staff should also track Metro’s Industrial Land Inventory project, taking place in 2026, and
encourage County participation and engagement with Metro staff through the process.

APPENDIX 5
EOA SUMMARY
METHODOLOGY AND
ASSUMPTIONS
APPENDIX 5 – EOA SUMMARY METHODOLOGY AND ASSUMPTIONS

Approach to Variation Across Cities

Scenario Forecasting

Statewide Planning Goal 9, which requires cities to consider future land needs for economic activities,
does not have a required method for forecasting employment change and land demand. As such, each
city has different approaches to developing forecast scenarios. This means it is difficult to accurately
project countywide land demand and the resulting countywide land surpluses or deficits because each
city has a different methodology for forecasting these needs, so the analysis is not comparing apples to
apples. However, if this countywide projection is taken with this caveat, it can still act as a useful
reference.

In order to aggregate the land demand projections from each city, the following process was undertaken
to select which forecast scenario was used in this EOA Summary and Analysis:

▪       Some cities’ EOAs only provide land demand figures for one scenario forecast. These cities are
        Molalla, Sandy, Tualatin, and Wilsonville. In the case of these cities, this forecast was chosen for
        the EOA Summary and Analysis due to no other data being available.
▪       For cities’ EOAs that provide land demand figures for multiple forecasts, the scenario that was
        most similar to meeting the following characteristics was chosen:
        ▫     Uses employment growth rate and projections provided by the Oregon Employment
              Department (OED)
        ▫     Considers industry trends

See Table 1 for the scenario that was selected for this EOA Summary and Analysis.

Though this process was imperfect, it allows for comparison across cities and allows for the cities’ land
demand and resulting land surplus or deficit to be aggregated for a countywide view of approximate
needs.

Redevelopable Assumptions

Like forecast scenarios, there is not a standard required methodology for how BLI’s should consider
redevelopment potential or how they define land as “redevelopable.” As such, each city approaches
redevelopment potential differently.

Some cities do not provide separate acreage figures for redevelopable, and instead only provide a total
“Vacant” land acreage figure. These cities include Canby, Happy Valley, Molalla and Sandy. Some of the
EOAs explain that some degree of redevelopment potential is already included in their Vacant land
category (like Molalla).

Other cities separate redevelopable and vacant land and use a variety of methodologies for determining
redevelopable land, including improvement to land value ratio or Real Market Value per square foot.

See Table 1 for how each city defines and calculates redevelopable.
  Multi-County Cities

  Three cities in Clackamas County also fall within another county: Lake Oswego (Multnomah County),
  Tualatin (Washington County) and Wilsonville (Washington County).

  The EOA’s for these three cities are city-wide, meaning they include buildable land across the entire city,
  which could include land in other counties. Including these cities’ entire buildable land could distort the
  countywide summary and projections because it could include land that is not within Clackamas County’s
  jurisdiction.

  In order to account for this, the percentage share of area (land mass) within Clackamas County was
  calculated for these three cities:

  ▪        Lake Oswego: 95% of City’s area is within Clackamas County.
  ▪        Tualatin: 9% of City’s area is within Clackamas County.
  ▪        Wilsonville: 89% of City’s area is within Clackamas County.

  An additional layer of analysis summarized and analyzed the buildable land in all the cities by share of
  area within Clackamas County. This alters the cumulative buildable land countywide, particularly for
  industrial land, given that the city of Tualatin had over 650 AC of buildable industrial land, but only 9% of
  Tualatin’s area is within Clackamas County.

  Though this is an imperfect method for accounting for buildable land in multi-county cities, it takes into
  consideration that these cities’ BLI’s are not accurately representative of Countywide land.

  EOA Completion Year and Forecast Year

  There is also variation across the cities for when the Economic Opportunity Analysis was completed,
  ranging from 2011 (Happy Valley) to 2025 (Wilsonville and Molalla). (Milwaukie’s EOA was completed in
  2017 but re-ran their BLI methodology to produce updated data in 2026.) As a result, the forecast year for
  each of these cities varied and the employment forecast scenarios vary based on different economic
  conditions in those time periods. For example, EOAs completed before the COVID-19 pandemic consider
  different economic conditions than those completed after.

  This EOA Summary and Analysis did not account for these temporal differences.

APPENDIX 7
BLI MAPPING
METHODOLOGY AND
ASSUMPTIONS
APPENDIX 7 – BLI MAPPING METHODOLOGY AND ASSUMPTIONS

To support the economic development activities of Clackamas County, Mackenzie conducted a systematic
review of the 2024 Metro Buildable Lands Inventory (BLI) and publicly available Economic Opportunity
Analysis (EOA) reports from incorporated cities within Clackamas County. This section provides
explanations of the methodology utilized in this project and the nuances and differences and similarities
between the datasets used in this report.

Metro Jurisdictions

For incorporated jurisdictions within the Metro Urban Growth Boundary (UGB), this analysis used the
Buildable Lands Inventory (BLI) from the 2024 Metro Urban Growth Report, provided by Metro. These
jurisdictions are Gladstone, Happy Valley, Johnson City, Lake Oswego, Milwaukie, Oregon City, Tualatin,
West Linn, and Wilsonville. Metro classified parcels as Vacant, Partially Vacant/Infill, Redevelopable. Refer
to the Metro Urban Growth Report, Appendix 2, for further details of Metro’s BLI methodology.

Once the GIS BLI dataset from Metro was obtained, the study area was isolated to the area of the above
listed jurisdictions within Clackamas County. Then, the GIS data was filtered to identify parcels designated
as Industrial, Commercial, and Mixed Use Residential per Metro’s land use classification. The identified
Industrial, Commercial, and Mixed-Use parcels were sorted by their classification of vacant, partially
vacant/infill, and redevelopable per the Metro dataset. From this filtering, Mackenzie prepared tables
showing the employment area by jurisdiction (acres) and parcel size distribution.

Non-Metro Jurisdictions

For incorporated jurisdictions outside of the Metro UGB, this analysis used BLI data provided by each City
from the respective EOA reports. These jurisdictions are Canby (2023), Estacada (2019), Molalla (2025),
and Sandy (2024). The datasets provided by each City were developed when the City completed its
Economic Opportunity Analysis. As such, these datasets are from different years, noted parenthetically
above. The status of parcels may be outdated and not reflective of current parcel status at the time of this
report.

The most notable example of outdated data is in the City of Estacada. The BLI data for Estacada is from
2019, but the City has since updated its Comprehensive Plan Zoning Map in 2023, rezoning some Industrial
land in northern parts of the City to residential (North City Residential), and some Industrial land
throughout the City to commercial and mixed Use (Outdoor Commercial, Commercial Mixed Use, Mill
Area Mixed Use, and Highway Commercial). As a result, there is currently approximately 200 acres less
industrial land (approximately 100 acres have been rezoned to residential and 100 acres rezoned to
commercial and mixed use) than what is shown in the 2019 EOA and what is included in this report’s
analysis, due to this rezoning.

Additionally, the methodologies for each BLI are slightly different. Each city has its own definitions for the
classifications of status: vacant, partially vacant, and redevelopable. For example, Estacada defines
“vacant” as land with less than $10,000 in improvements or no functional improvements, whereas Canby
defines vacant as lands with no structures or with improvement value less than $5,000 and the
improvement value is 5% or less than the land value, and the Canby EOA also explains they made some



                                                                                                            1
determinations based on aerial imagery. Sandy and Molalla have their own unique definitions too. These
differing definitions are further described in Table 1, below.

Furthermore, the BLI methodology for Molalla and Sandy did not include “Redevelopable” as a separate
status classification, whereas Canby and Estacada do include redevelopable. The non-Metro jurisdictions
also did not include mixed-use as a separate employment zone. See each jurisdiction’s EOA for further
details on their BLI methodology.

After data was obtained from each jurisdiction via Clackamas County staff, the GIS data was filtered to
identify parcels designated Industrial and Commercial per their Comprehensive Plan Designation. Next,
each data set was filtered by status, retaining parcels identified as vacant, partially vacant, and
redevelopable. From this filtering, Mackenzie prepared tables summarizing the employment area
(unconstrained acres) by jurisdiction, status, zone, and parcel size distribution.

Site Aggregation

As part of this analysis, Mackenzie was asked to identify parcels that may be suitable for aggregation to
create a larger development site. In the event parcels identified as Vacant, Partially Vacant/Infill, and
Redevelopable had a common property line extending at least 100', these parcels were categorized as a
site. In some cases, this would lead to two (2) parcels becoming a site, and in other situations, up to 22
parcels becoming a site. Parcel aggregation did not take into consideration ownership, access, status
classification, or infrastructure. This parcel aggregation process also treated the filtered employment-
zoned parcels as one, meaning some sites could be composed of parcels within different zones –
Industrial, Commercial, and/or Mixed-Use – and different status – vacant, partially vacant/infill, and/or
redevelopable.

 Public hearings on
potential data center
    moratorium
     Wednesday, Oct. 21, 6 p.m.
     Thursday, Oct. 22, 10 a.m.
Overview
• ORS 197.520 allows local governments to adopt moratoria on certain
  land uses.
   • Requires a public hearing.
      • We are holding two public hearings.
   • Requires 45 days’ advance notice to DLCD.
      • Notice was provided on August 13, 2026.
   • Requires findings.
      • Proposed findings are included in the packet.
• Initial moratorium may not exceed 120 days.
   • May be extended for six months.
Proposed Resolution
• Would prohibit the development of new or the expansion of existing
  data centers as primary uses in unincorporated areas for 120 days.
• Defines “data center” as a facility for the storage, management,
  processing, and/or transmission of digital data.
   • Includes facilities used for cloud computing services, artificial intelligence training
     or inference services, etc.
   • Excludes telecommunications facilities.
• Defines “primary use” as a principal activity on a site.
Proposed Findings
• ORS 197.520(3): “A moratorium * * * may be justified only by a
  demonstration of compelling need. Such a demonstration * * * shall
  include * * * findings:”
   • ORS 197.520(3)(a)(A): “That application of existing development ordinances
     or regulations and other applicable law is inadequate to prevent irrevocable
     public harm from development in affected geographical areas;”
      • Noise, heat, and air impacts.
      • Water and electricity demands.
      • Employment density.
Proposed Findings
• ORS 197.520(3): “A moratorium * * * may be justified only by a
  demonstration of compelling need. Such a demonstration * * * shall
  include * * * findings:”
   • ORS 197.520(3)(a)(B): “That the moratorium is sufficiently limited to ensure
     that a needed supply of affected housing types and the supply of commercial
     and industrial facilities * * * are not unreasonably restricted * * *;”
      • Applies to only one type of industrial facility.
Proposed Findings
• ORS 197.520(3): “A moratorium * * * may be justified only by a
  demonstration of compelling need. Such a demonstration * * * shall
  include * * * findings:”
   • ORS 197.520(3)(a)(C): “Stating the reasons alternative methods of achieving
     the objectives of the moratorium are unsatisfactory;”
      • Objective is to give the County time to develop and adopt ZDO amendments.
      • Only alternative is developing and adopting ZDO amendments without moratorium.
      • Would allow data centers to develop before amendments are adopted.
Proposed Findings
• ORS 197.520(3): “A moratorium * * * may be justified only by a
  demonstration of compelling need. Such a demonstration * * * shall
  include * * * findings:”
   • ORS 197.520(3)(a)(D): “That * * * the public harm which would be caused by
     failure to impose a moratorium outweighs the adverse effects * * *, including
     shifts in demand for housing or economic development, public facilities and
     services and buildable lands, and the overall impact * * * on population
     distribution; and”
      • Unlikely to result in surge of data center development in other jurisdictions.
Proposed Findings
• ORS 197.520(3): “A moratorium * * * may be justified only by a
  demonstration of compelling need. Such a demonstration * * * shall
  include * * * findings:”
   • ORS 197.520(3)(a)(E): “That * * * sufficient resources are available to
     complete the development of needed interim or permanent changes in plans,
     regulations or procedures within the period of effectiveness of the
     moratorium.”
      • Amending the ZDO takes approximately 114 days.
      • County will need to amend its 2025-27 Long-Range Planning Work Program to
        accommodate the development and adoption of ZDO amendments during the
        moratorium period.
Proposed Findings
• ORS 197.520(3)(a) requires the foregoing findings for moratoria on
  urban and urbanizable land.
• ORS 197.520(3)(b) requires findings for moratoria on rural land.
   • The required findings for rural land are similar to the required findings for
     urban and urbanizable land.
   • The full text of each provision is set out in the packet.
Public Comment
• As of October 11, 2026, the County had received comments from nine
  individuals.
   • Four supported the proposed moratorium.
   • Two proposed ZDO amendments.
   • Three opposed data center development in general.
   • None opposed the proposed moratorium.
